Genesis 18:1–22:24. Select a Hebrew word for its morphology, lemma, root, senses and the comments anchored to it. A dotted underline marks a word a commentator quotes.

18:1

The LORD appeared to him at the terebinths of Mamre while he was sitting at the entrance of the tent in the heat of the day.

and-appeared to-him the-LORD in-terebinths-of Mamre and-he sitting at-entrance-of the-tent like-heat-of the-day

Grammar
  • The verb is wayyiqtol (the narrative sequential form). Here it is niphal: the English 'appeared' is the stem's sense 'appear, be seen'.
  • The clause 'while he was sitting' is circumstantial: the Hebrew joins a participle to the pronoun, which marks a background situation rather than a second action.
  • Construct chains: 'the entrance of the tent' and 'the heat of the day'. Both are read as single English noun phrases.
  • The etnahta on Mamre (18:1.5) divides the verse. The first part places the scene at the terebinths of Mamre; the second describes Abraham sitting at the tent in the heat.

The divine name is written YHWH in the Hebrew; the English is 'the LORD' per the decisions.

Commentary (16)
Rashinot-applicable וַיֵּרָ֤א אֵלָיו֙
Rashi: the LORD appeared to him 'to visit the sick' (לְבַקֵּר אֶת הַחוֹלֶה): it was the third day after his circumcision, and the Holy One came to ask after his welfare (Bava Metzia 86b). Rashi gives the purpose of the appearance, not a sense of the verb; the English 'appeared' stands.
Hebrew
לְבַקֵּר אֶת הַחוֹלֶה. אָמַר רַבִּי חָמָא בַּר חֲנִינָא, יוֹם שְׁלִישִׁי לְמִילָתוֹ הָיָה, וּבָא הַקָּבָּ"ה וְשָׁאַל בִּשְׁלוֹמוֹ (בבא מציעא פ"ו):
Rashifollows בְּאֵלֹנֵ֖י מַמְרֵ֑א
Rashi: Mamre is the man who gave Abraham counsel about the circumcision; therefore God revealed Himself to Abraham in Mamre's portion (Bereshit Rabba). 'The terebinths of Mamre' are the grove that belongs to Mamre, the Amorite of 14:13, and the English agrees with this.
Hebrew
הוּא שֶׁנָּתַן לוֹ עֵצָה עַל הַמִּילָה, לְפִיכָךְ נִגְלָה עָלָיו בְּחֶלְקוֹ (בראשית רבה):
Rashinot-applicable יֹשֵׁ֥ב
Rashi: the word is written ישב without a vav, so it can be read יָשַׁב 'he sat': Abraham wanted to stand, and the Holy One said to him, 'Sit, and I will stand'. This is a sign for his children that God will stand among the judges while they sit (Ps. 82:1). A homily; the English keeps the participle 'sitting'.
Hebrew
ישב כְּתִיב, בִּקֵּשׁ לַעֲמֹד, אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּבָּ"ה שֵׁב וַאֲנִי אֶעֱמֹד, וְאַתָּה סִימָן לְבָנֶיךָ שֶׁעָתִיד אֲנִי לְהִתְיַצֵּב בַּעֲדַת הַדַּיָּנִים וְהֵן יוֹשְׁבִין, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר אֱלֹהִים נִצָּב בַּעֲדַת אֵל (תהילים פ"ב) (בראשית רבה):
Rashinot-applicable פֶּֽתַח הָאֹ֖הֶל
Rashi: he sat at the entrance to watch for passers-by and bring them into his house. This gives the purpose, not the sense of the words.
Hebrew
לִרְאוֹת אִם יֵשׁ עוֹבֵר וָשָׁב וְיַכְנִיסֵם בְּבֵיתוֹ:
Rashinot-applicable כְּחֹ֥ם הַיּֽוֹם׃
Rashi: the LORD brought out the sun from its sheath so as not to trouble Abraham with guests; seeing him grieve that no guests came, He sent the angels in the form of men. A homily on the heat of the day.
Hebrew
הוֹצִיא הַקָבָּ"ה חַמָּה מִנַּרְתִּיקָהּ, שֶׁלֹּא לְהַטְרִיחוֹ בְּאוֹרְחִים, וּלְפִי שֶׁרָאָהוּ מִצְטַעֵר שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ אוֹרְחִים בָּאִים, הֵבִיא הַמַּלְאָכִים עָלָיו בִּדְמוּת אֲנָשִׁים (בבא מציעא שם):
Ibn Ezranormativefollows וַיֵּרָ֤א
Ibn Ezra: some say the Name and the three men are one and the same and cannot be divided; they forgot 'the two angels came to Sodom' (19:1). Other interpreters say the Name appeared to Abraham in prophetic vision, and afterwards he lifted his eyes and saw three angels: one to bring the news to Sarah, two to Sodom, one to destroy and one to save Lot. The English keeps 'The LORD appeared' and then 'three men'.

Ibn Ezranormativedeclines the whole verse
Ibn Ezra glosses 'and they ate' (18:8) as 'the bread was consumed', like 'which the fire consumes' (Lev. 6:3): not that the visitors ate as men eat. The comment is filed at 18:1 but bears on 18:8. The English keeps 'they ate'; see the note and the apparatus on 18:8.

Hebrew
לְשׁוֹן רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית י"ח:א') לְבַקֵּר אֶת הַחוֹלֶה. אָמַר רַבִּי חָמָא בַּר חֲנִינָא, יוֹם שְׁלִישִׁי לְמִילָתוֹ הָיָה, וּבָא הקב"ה וְשָׁאַל בּוֹ. "וַיֹּאכֵלוּ", נִרְאוּ כְּמִי שֶׁאָכְלוּ. וּבְסֵפֶר מוֹרֶה הַנְּבֻכִים (ב מב) נֶאֱמַר כִּי הַפָּרָשָׁה כְּלָל וּפְרָט, אָמַר הַכָּתוּב תְּחִלָּה כִּי נִרְאָה אֵלָיו הַשֵּׁם בְּמַרְאוֹת הַנְּבוּאָה, הַנְּבוּאָה, וְלֹא יָדַעְתִּי לָמָּה הָיָה צוֹלֵעַ עַל יְרֵכוֹ בְּהָקִיץ, וְלָמָּה אָמַר (בראשית ל"ב:ל"א) "כִּי רָאִיתִי אֱלֹהִים פָּנִים אֶל פָּנִים וַתִּנָּצֵל נַפְשִׁי", כִּי הַנְּבִיאִים לֹא מַרְאָה, וְיִשָּׁאֵר לוֹט בִּסְדוֹם. אֲבָל יַחְשֹׁב שֶׁהָיוּ הַמַּעֲשִׂים נַעֲשִׂים מֵאֲלֵיהֶם, וְהַמַּאֲמָרִים בְּכָל דָּבָר וְדָבָר מַרְאָה. וְאֵלֶּה דְּבָרִים סוֹתְרִים הַכָּתוּב, אָסוּר לְשָׁמְעָם וְאָמְרוּ (ויק"ר א יד), מָה בֵּין מֹשֶׁה לְכָל הַנְּבִיאִים, רַבָּנָן אָמְרֵי כָּל הַנְּבִיאִים רָאוּ מִתּוֹךְ אַסְפַּקְלַרְיָא שֶׁאֵינָהּ מְצֻחְצַחַת, הֲדָא הוּא דִכְתִיב (הושע יב יא) "וְאָנֹכִי חָזוֹן הִרְבֵּיתִי וּבְיַד הַנְּבִיאִים אֲדַמֶּה", וּמֹשֶׁה רָאָה מִתּוֹךְ אַסְפַּקְלַרְיָא מְצֻחְצַחַת, הֲדָא הוּא דִכְתִיב (במדבר יב ח) "וּתְמוּנַת ה' יַבִּיט", כְּמוֹ שֶׁהוּא מְפֹרָשׁ בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (שם) וּמְקוֹמוֹת אֲחֵרִים (יבמות מט), וְלֹא נָתְנוּ בְּשׁוּם מָקוֹם נְבוּאָתָם לְמַלְאָךְ. וְאַל תִּשּׁוֹמֵם בַּעֲבוּר שֶׁכָּתוּב (מלכים א יג יח) "גַּם אֲנִי נָבִיא כָּמוֹךָ וּמַלְאָךְ דִּבֶּר אֵלַי בִּדְבַר ה' לֵאמֹר", כִּי פֵּרוּשׁוֹ גַּם אֲנִי נָבִיא כָּמוֹךָ וְיוֹדֵעַ אֲנִי שֶׁהַמַּלְאָךְ שֶׁדִּבֵּר אֵלַי בִּדְבַר ה' הוּא, וְזוֹ מַדְרֵגָה מִמַּדְרֵגוֹת הַנְּבוּאָה, כַּאֲשֶׁר אָמַר אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים "כִּי כֵן צִוָּה אֹתִי בִּדְבַר ה'" (שם יג ט), וְאָמַר "כִּי דָבָר אֵלַי בִּדְבַר ה'" (שם יג יז) וּכְבָר אָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ (במד"ר כ ג) בְּעִנְיַן בִּלְעָם שֶׁאָמַר "וְעַתָּה אִם רַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ אָשׁוּבָה לִּי" (במדבר כב לד), אֲנִי לֹא הָלַכְתִּי עַד שֶׁאָמַר לִי הקב"ה "קוּם לֵךְ אִתָּם" (שם שם כ), וְאַתָּה אוֹמֵר שֶׁאֶחְזֹר, כָּךְ הוּא אֻמָּנוּתוֹ, לֹא כָּךְ אָמַר לְאַבְרָהָם לְהַקְרִיב אֶת בְּנוֹ וְאַחַר כָּךְ "וַיִּקְרָא מַלְאַךְ ה' אֶל אַבְרָהָם וַיֹּאמֶר אַל תִּשְׁלַח יָדְךָ אֶל הַנַּעַר" (בראשית כ"ב:י"ב), לָמוּד הוּא לוֹמַר דָּבָר וּמַלְאָךְ מַחְזִירוֹ וְכוּ'. הִנֵּה הַחֲכָמִים מִתְעוֹרְרִים לוֹמַר שֶׁאֵין הַנְּבוּאָה בַּדִּבּוּר הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁהִזְכִּיר בּוֹ הַשֵּׁם שָׁוָה לַדִּבּוּר הַשֵּׁנִי שֶׁאָמַר בּוֹ שֶׁהוּא עַל יְדֵי מַלְאָךְ, אֶלָּא שֶׁהוּא דֶּרֶךְ בַּנְּבִיאִים שֶׁיְּצַוֶּה בִּנְבוּאָה וִיבַטֵּל הַצַּוָּאָה בְּמַלְאָךְ, כִּי הַנָּבִיא יוֹדֵעַ כִּי דְבַר ה' הוּא. וּבִתְחִלַּת וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (א ט) אָמְרוּ, "וַיִּקְרָא אֶל מֹשֶׁה", לֹא כְּאַבְרָהָם, בְּאַבְרָהָם כָּתוּב "וַיִּקְרָא מַלְאַךְ ה' אֶל אַבְרָהָם שֵׁנִית מִן הַשָּׁמָיִם" (בראשית כ"ב:ט"ו), הַמַּלְאָךְ קוֹרֵא וְהַדִּבּוּר מְדַבֵּר, בְּרַם הָכָא אָמַר הקב"ה אֲנִי הוּא הַקּוֹרֵא וַאֲנִי הוּא הַמְדַבֵּר. כְּלוֹמַר שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה אַבְרָהָם מַשִּׂיג הַנְּבוּאָה עַד הֲכִינוֹ נַפְשׁוֹ בַּתְּחִלָּה לְהַשָּׂגַת מַלְאָךְ, וְיַעֲלֶה מִן הַמַּדְרֵגָה הַהִיא לְמַעֲלַת דִּבּוּר הַנְּבוּאָה, אֲבָל מֹשֶׁה מוּכָן לַנְּבוּאָה בְּכָל עֵת. הִנֵּה בְּכָל מָקוֹם יִתְעוֹרְרוּ הַחֲכָמִים לְהוֹדִיעֵנוּ כִּי רְאִיַּת הַמַּלְאָךְ אֵינֶנָּה נְבוּאָה, וְאֵין הָרוֹאִים מַלְאָכִים וְהַמְּדַבְּרִים עִמָּם מִכְּלַל הַנְּבִיאִים, כַּאֲשֶׁר הִזְכַּרְתִּי בְּדָנִיֵּאל, אֲבָל הִיא מַרְאָה תִּקָּרֵא "גְּלוּי עֵינַיִם", כְּמוֹ "וַיְגַל הַשֵּׁם אֶת עֵינֵי בִלְעָם וַיַּרְא אֶת מַלְאַךְ ה'" (במדבר כב לא), וְכֵן "וַיִּתְפַּלֵּל אֱלִישָׁע וַיֹּאמַר ה' פְּקַח נָא אֶת עֵינָיו וְיִרְאֶה" (מלכים ב ו יז), אֲבָל בִּמְקוֹם אֲשֶׁר יַזְכִּיר הַמַּלְאָכִים בְּשֵׁם "אֲנָשִׁים" כְּעִנְיַן הַפָּרָשָׁה הַזֹּאת וּפָרָשַׁת לוֹט, וְכֵן "וַיֵּאָבֵק אִישׁ עִמּוֹ" (בראשית ל"ב:כ"ה) וְכֵן "וַיִּמְצָאֵהוּ אִישׁ" (שם לז טו) עַל דַּעַת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ (תנחומא וישב ב), הוּא כָּבוֹד נִבְרָא בַּמַּלְאָכִים, יִקָּרֵא אֵצֶל הַיּוֹדְעִים "מַלְבּוּשׁ", יֻשַּׂג לְעֵינֵי בָּשָׂר בְּזַכֵּי הַנְּפָשׁוֹת כַּחֲסִידִים וּבְנֵי הַנְּבִיאִים, וְלֹא אוּכַל לְפָרֵשׁ. וְהַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר תִּמְצָא בּוֹ רְאִיַּת ה' וְדִבּוּר מַלְאָךְ אוֹ רְאִיַּת מַלְאָךְ וְדִבּוּר ה', כַּכָּתוּב בְּדִבְרֵי מֹשֶׁה בִּתְחִלַּת נְבוּאָתוֹ, (שמות ג ב-ד) וּבְדִבְרֵי זְכַרְיָה (ג א-ב), עוֹד אֲגַלֶּה בּוֹ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים בִּרְמִיזוֹת (עיין שמות ג ב). וְעִנְיַן "וַיֹּאכֵלוּ" אָמְרוּ חֲכָמִים (ב"ר מח יד) רִאשׁוֹן רִאשׁוֹן מִסְתַּלֵּק. וְעִנְיַן הַהִסְתַּלְּקוּת תָּבִין אוֹתוֹ מִדְּבַר מָנוֹחַ אִם תִּזְכֶּה אֵלָיו. וְהִנֵּה פֵּרוּשׁ הַפָּרָשָׁה הַזֹּאת אַחֲרֵי שֶׁאָמַר כִּי בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה נִמּוֹל אַבְרָהָם (בראשית י"ז:כ"ו), אָמַר שֶׁנִּרְאָה אֵלָיו הַשֵּׁם בִּהְיוֹתוֹ חוֹלֶה בְּמִילָתוֹ יוֹשֵׁב וּמִתְקָרֵר בְּפֶתַח אָהֳלוֹ מִפְּנֵי חֹם הַיּוֹם אֲשֶׁר יַחֲלִישֶׁנּוּ. וְהִזְכִּיר זֶה לְהוֹדִיעַ שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה מִתְכַּוֵּן לִנְבוּאָה, לֹא נוֹפֵל עַל פָּנָיו וְלֹא מִתְפַּלֵּל, וְאַף עַל פִּי כֵן בָּאָה אֵלָיו הַמַּרְאָה הַזֹּאת.
Ramban בְּאֵלֹנֵ֖י מַמְרֵ֑א
Hebrew
לְהוֹדִיעַ הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ נִמּוֹל, וְזֶה גִּלּוּי הַשְּׁכִינָה אֵלָיו לְמַעֲלָה וְכָבוֹד לוֹ, כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁבָּא בַּמִּשְׁכָּן "וַיֵּצְאוּ וַיְבָרֲכוּ אֶת הָעָם וַיֵּרָא כְבוֹד ה' אֶל כָּל הָעָם" (ויקרא ט כג), כִּי מִפְּנֵי הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם בְּמִצְוַת הַמִּשְׁכָּן זָכוּ לִרְאִיַּת הַשְּׁכִינָה. וְאֵין גִּלּוּי הַשְּׁכִינָה כָּאן וְכָאן לְצַוּוֹת לָהֶם מִצְוָה אוֹ לְדִבּוּר כְּלָל, אֶלָּא גְּמוּל הַמִּצְוָה הַנַּעֲשֵׂית כְּבָר, וּלְהוֹדִיעַ כִּי רָצָה הָאֱלֹהִים אֶת מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם, כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (תהלים יז טו) "אֲנִי בְּצֶדֶק אֶחֱזֶה פָנֶיךָ אֶשְׂבְּעָה בְהָקִיץ תְּמוּנָתֶךָ", וְכֵן בְּיַעֲקֹב אָמַר (בראשית ל"ב:ב') "וַיִּפְגְּעוּ בוֹ מַלְאֲכֵי אֱלֹהִים", וְאֵין שָׁם דִּבּוּר וְלֹא שֶׁחִדְּשׁוּ בּוֹ דָּבָר רַק שֶׁזָּכָה לִרְאִיַּת מַלְאֲכֵי עֶלְיוֹן וְיָדַע כִּי מַעֲשָׂיו רְצוּיִים. וְכֵן הָיָה לְאַבְרָהָם בִּרְאִיַּת הַשְּׁכִינָה זְכוּת וְהַבְטָחָה. וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (מכילתא שירתא ג) בְּיוֹרְדֵי הַיָּם שֶׁאָמְרוּ "זֶה אֵלִי וְאַנְוֵהוּ", רָאֲתָה שִׁפְחָה עַל הַיָּם מָה שֶׁלֹּא רָאָה יְחֶזְקֵאל הַנָּבִיא, זְכוּת לָהֶם בְּעֵת הַנֵּס הַגָּדוֹל שֶׁהֶאֱמִינוּ בַּה' וּבְמֹשֶׁה עַבְדּוֹ. וּפְעָמִים יָבֹא בִּשְׁעַת הַקֶּצֶף, "וַיֹּאמְרוּ כָּל הָעֵדָה לִרְגּוֹם אֹתָם בָּאֲבָנִים וּכְבוֹד ה' נִרְאָה בְּאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד אֶל כָּל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל" (במדבר יד י), וְיִהְיֶה זֶה לְהָגֵן עַל עֲבָדָיו הַצַּדִּיקִים וְלִכְבוֹדָם. וְאַל תָּחוּשׁ לְהֶפְסֵק הַפָּרָשָׁה, כִּי הָעִנְיָן מְחֻבָּר, וְלָכֵן אָמַר "וַיֵּרָא אֵלָיו" וְלֹא אָמַר "וַיֵּרָא ה' אֶל אַבְרָהָם", אֲבָל בַּפָּרָשָׁה רָצָה לְסַדֵּר כָּבוֹד הַנַּעֲשֶׂה לוֹ בְּעֵת שֶׁעָשָׂה הַמִּילָה, וְאָמַר כִּי נִגְלֵית עָלָיו הַשְּׁכִינָה וְשָׁלַח אֵלָיו מַלְאָכָיו לְבַשֵּׂר אֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ וְגַם לְהַצִּיל לוֹט אָחִיו בַּעֲבוּרוֹ, כִּי אַבְרָהָם נִתְבַּשֵּׂר בְּבֵן מִפִּי הַשְּׁכִינָה כְּבָר, וְשָׂרָה מִפִּי הַמַּלְאָךְ שֶׁדִּבֵּר עִם אַבְרָהָם כְּדֵי שֶׁתִּשְׁמַע שָׂרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר "וְשָׂרָה שׁוֹמַעַת", וְזוֹ כַּוָּנָתָם שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סוטה יד) לְבַקֵּר אֶת הַחוֹלֶה, שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לְדִבּוּר אֶלָּא לְכָבוֹד לוֹ, וְעוֹד אָמְרוּ (ב"ר מח ד) "מִזְבַּח אֲדָמָה תַּעֲשֶׂה לִּי" (שמות כ כד), וּמָה אִם זֶה שֶׁבָּנָה מִזְבֵּחַ לִשְׁמִי הֲרֵינִי נִגְלֶה עָלָיו וּמְבָרְכוֹ, אַבְרָהָם (משלי טז טו) "בְּאוֹר פְּנֵי מֶלֶךְ חַיִּים":

Radak: the LORD appeared where Abraham lived (14:13), after the circumcision, to make Sodom's fate known to him, since Abraham was the greatest man of his generation. He allows that the whole account to 18:33 was a prophetic vision, begun while Abraham sat at the tent door. The English reads a narrated event and records the vision reading.

Ancient Near East
  • אֵלוֹן is a large, long-lived tree, usually rendered terebinth or oak; the exact species is uncertain. Prominent trees were landmarks and places of meeting, judging and worship in Canaan, and the narrative names this camp by its trees (see also 13:18, 14:13).
  • Abraham lives as a herder in a tent. Resting in the shade at the tent entrance in the middle of the day is the ordinary habit of a household in a hot country.
  • Mamre is a place near Hebron (13:18); the same word names a man, an Amorite ally of Abraham (14:13, 24). Rashi takes the name here as that man; the English takes the place.
Apparatus
  • Ramban: the appearance is honour and reward for the circumcision (not a message). Radak: it came after the circumcision to tell Abraham of Sodom, and he allows that the whole account to 18:33 was a prophetic vision. Neither is adopted as the plain reading of the narrative; both are recorded.
  • Ibn Ezra reads the three 'men' as angels in human form (see his comment on 18:1); the Hebrew calls them אֲנָשִׁים, and the English keeps 'men'.
18:2

He lifted his eyes and saw, and look, three men were standing before him. When he saw them, he ran from the entrance of the tent to meet them, and bowed down to the ground.

and-lifted his-eyes and-saw and-look three men standing upon-him and-saw and-ran to-meet-them from-entrance-of the-tent and-bowed-down to-the-ground

Grammar
  • The verbs form a chain: he lifted, he saw, (he saw), he ran, he bowed. The second וַיַּרְא resumes the narrative, 'when he saw them', and is the turning point from sight to action.
  • הִנֵּה introduces what Abraham sees and draws the reader into his view: 'and look, three men'.
  • נִצָּבִים is a niphal participle, masculine plural, agreeing with 'men'; with עָלָיו it means standing at his side or in front of him, in attendance.
  • לִקְרָאתָם is lamed with the infinitive construct of קרא 'meet' and a 3mp suffix: 'to meet them'. וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ is the short wayyiqtol of the reflexive stem of שחה, 'bow down'; אָרְצָה carries the directional ending.

The second וַיַּרְא is read as 'again' (Radak), as 'saw that they stood there' (Ramban) or as 'understood' (Rashi). The English 'When he saw them' keeps the plain verb. The Hebrew calls them אֲנָשִׁים; Ibn Ezra takes them to be angels (see 18:1), and the English keeps 'men'.

Commentary (16)
Rashinot-applicable וְהִנֵּה֙ שְׁלֹשָׁ֣ה אֲנָשִׁ֔ים
Rashi: the three are three messengers with three tasks (one to tell Sarah, one to overturn Sodom, one to heal Abraham), since one angel does not do two missions; the text uses the plural throughout (they ate, they said). Midrash on the purpose of the visitors. Ibn Ezra gives other tasks (one to announce, one to destroy, one to save Lot). The English keeps 'three men'.

Radakfollows נִצָּבִ֖ים עָלָ֑יו
Radak: 'standing upon him' means standing near him, in attendance for his benefit or to meet his wish, as in 1 Sam. 22:7, unlike Gen. 28:13. Abraham saw them standing and not going on, as if waiting for him to call them, and ran to meet them. The English 'before him' keeps the sense of attendance.

Ancient Near East
  • The visitors are called 'men' (אֲנָשִׁים). The narrator has just said that the LORD appeared; Ibn Ezra takes the three men to be angels in human form, and 19:1 calls two of them angels. The text does not say that Abraham knew who they were.
  • To bow to the ground (hishtaḥavah) was the ordinary gesture of respect to a superior or honoured stranger across the ancient Near East. The verb is also used of worship; the context decides, and here it is the courtesy of a host.
18:3

He said, "My lord, if I have found favour in your sight, please do not pass by your servant.

and-said my-lord if now I-found favour in-your-eyes not now pass-over from-upon your-servant

Grammar
  • The condition (protasis) 'if I have found favour' leads to the request, a negative jussive: 'do not pass on'. The conditional clause often opens a polite request.
  • אִם־נָא 'if now': נָא softens the condition into a courteous request. The second נָא in אַל־נָא makes the prohibition an entreaty, rendered 'please'.
  • 'Your servant' (עַבְדֶּךָ) is the speaker's self-reference: 'I, your servant' (the pack lists this as sense 6). It is the usual courteous form before a superior.
  • מֵעַל עַבְדֶּךָ 'from upon your servant' with the verb 'pass': 'do not pass on from me'. The silluq ends the verse; the tipḥa on 'pass' sets 'do not pass' apart from 'from your servant'.

אֲדֹנָי with qamats may address God or a person. The English 'my lord' (lower case) is the reading consistent with Ibn Ezra's view that the three are angels in human form (his comment on 18:1; the pack has no comment of his on this word). Rashi's second view and Radak's second, that Abraham addresses the LORD, is recorded in the apparatus.

Commentary (7)
Rashirecords וַיֹּאמַ֑ר אֲדֹנָ֗י אִם נָ֨א
Rashi: Abraham spoke to the greatest of the three but called them all 'lords' (אֲדוֹנִים); he asked the greatest not to pass by, since if he stayed his companions would stay with him. In this reading the word is profane (Shevuot 35b). Another reading: the word is holy, and Abraham asked the Holy One to wait for him while he ran and brought in the guests; the words were said before 'he ran to meet them', though written after. Both readings are in Bereshit Rabba. The English keeps the singular address 'My lord' to the greatest of them; Rashi's plural 'lords' and his holy reading are recorded.

עִם כָּל אֶחָד יְדַבֵּר כְּדֶרֶךְ כָּל הַתּוֹרָה, "וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם אֶת (כל) חֻקֹּתַי (ועשיתם אותם) עֶרְוַת אָבִיךָ וְעֶרְוַת אִמְּךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה" (ויקרא יח ה ז), "וּבְקֻצְרְכֶם אֶת קְצִיר אַרְצְכֶם לֹא תְכַלֶּה" (שם יט ט), "וּבִקַּשְׁתֶּם מִשָּׁם אֶת ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ וּמָצָאתָ כִּי תִדְרְשֶׁנּוּ בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ וּבְכָל נַפְשֶׁךָ" (דברים ד כט), וְרֹב מִשְׁנֵה הַתּוֹרָה כֵּן, וְהֶפֶךְ מִזֶּה "רְאֵה אָנֹכִי נוֹתֵן לִפְנֵיכֶם הַיּוֹם" (שם יא כו). וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ אָמְרוּ (ב"ר מח ו), לַגָּדוֹל שֶׁבָּהֶם אָמַר. וְגַם זֶה יִתָּכֵן, שֶׁאָמַר לַגָּדוֹל אַל נָא תַּעֲבֹר, וְאַתָּה וְרֵעֶיךָ אֲשֶׁר יִשָּׁאֲרוּ עִמְּךָ תִּרְחֲצוּ רַגְלֵיכֶם. וְהַנָּכוֹן בְּעֵינַי שֶׁקָּרָא אֶת כֻּלָּם אֲדוֹנִים וּפָנָה אֶל כָּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד, לָרִאשׁוֹן אָמַר אִם נָא מָצָאתִי חֵן בְּעֵינֶיךָ אַל נָא תַעֲבֹר, וְכֵן אָמַר לַשֵּׁנִי, וְכֵן אָמַר לַשְּׁלִישִׁי, לְכָל אֶחָד בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ יִתְחַנֵּן, אִם נָא מָצָאתִי חֵן בְּעֵינֶיךָ אַל נָא תַעֲבֹר מֵעַל עַבְדֶּךָ וְיֻקַּח נָא מְעַט מַיִם וְרַחֲצוּ רַגְלֵיכֶם כֻּלְּכֶם. וְזֶה דֶּרֶךְ מוּסָר וְכָבוֹד מֵרֹב חֶפְצוֹ לְהִתְנַדֵּב עִמָּהֶם. וְהִנֵּה הִכִּיר בָּהֶם שֶׁהֵם עוֹבְרֵי דֶּרֶךְ וְאֵין חֶפְצָם לָלוּן שָׁם, וְלָכֵן לֹא בִּקֵּשׁ מֵהֶם רַק שֶׁיֻּקַּח מְעַט מַיִם לִרְחֹץ רַגְלֵיהֶם מְעַט מִפְּנֵי הַחֹם, לָתֵת מַיִם קָרִים עַל נֶפֶשׁ עֲיֵפָה, וְיִשָּׁעֲנוּ תַּחַת הָעֵץ לְרוּחַ הַיּוֹם, לֹא יָבוֹאוּ בְּאֹהֶל וּבְמִשְׁכָּן:
Radakrecords וַיֹּאמַ֑ר אֲדֹנָ֗י
Radak: the rabbis differ. Some say the word is secular and Abraham spoke to the greatest of the three angels, who rank above one another; he said אֲדֹנָי with qamats out of respect, as Gideon did to an angel (Judg. 6:15). Others say it is holy and Abraham spoke to the LORD, asking Him to wait; from this they learned that welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Presence. The English follows the first view and records the second.

Ancient Near East
  • To 'find favour in someone's eyes' is the ordinary polite formula for asking a superior's goodwill, and 'your servant' the ordinary self-designation of a speaker before a superior; neither describes Abraham's actual standing.
  • The form אֲדֹנָי with qamats is the one the tradition reads as divine; the commentators disagree whether Abraham addresses the LORD or the visitors (see the apparatus).
Apparatus
  • אֲדֹנָי with qamats: Rashi, second view (Shevuot 35b), and Radak, second view: the word is a name of God, and Abraham asked the LORD to wait while he welcomed the guests. Not adopted: the English addresses the visitors.
  • Rashi, first view and Radak: Abraham spoke to the greatest of the three. Ramban: he spoke to each of the three in turn, urging each. The singular verbs do not decide between these; the English leaves it open.
18:4

Please, let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree.

let-be-brought please little-of water and-wash your-feet and-rest-yourselves under the-tree

Grammar
  • The passive jussive 'let [water] be brought' has no stated agent. Rashi takes it that a servant brings it.
  • The imperatives (wash, rest) are in the plural; they address the three men together.
  • The etnahta on feet (18:4.6) divides the verse: the water and washing first, the resting place second.
  • The construct me'at-mayim: 'a little of water', a quantity phrase.
Commentary (8)
Rashifollows יֻקַּֽח נָ֣א
Rashi: the passive 'let be brought' means through an agent, a servant, just as the LORD paid Israel through an agent (Num. 20:11, where Moses struck the rock). The English keeps the passive, which leaves the agent unstated.
Hebrew
עַל יְדֵי שָׁלִיחַ, וְהַקָּבָּ"ה שִׁלֵּם לְבָנָיו עַל יְדֵי שָׁלִיחַ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וַיָּרֶם מֹשֶׁה אֶת יָדוֹ וַיַּךְ אֶת הַסֶּלַע (במדבר כ'):
Rashinot-applicable וְרַחֲצ֖וּ רַגְלֵיכֶ֑ם
Rashi: Abraham took them for Arabs who bow down to the dust of their feet, and so was careful not to bring idolatry into his house. Lot, who was not careful, gave lodging before washing (Gen. 19:2). A reason for the request, not a reading of the words.

, רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר עַל יְדֵי אֶחָד מִן הָעֲבָדִים, אֲבָל עַל הַפַּת אָמַר ״וְאֶקְחָה פַת לֶחֶם״ (בראשית יח:ה) – הוּא בְּעַצְמוֹ.

Ancient Near East
  • Travellers went on foot, in sandals or barefoot, over dusty tracks; the host's first courtesy was water for the feet, often through a servant (compare 19:2, 24:32, 43:24).
  • The shade of a large tree in the heat of the day is offered as a place to rest, not as lodging.
18:5

Let me fetch a morsel of bread, and sustain your hearts; afterward you may go on, since you have passed by your servant." They said, "Do so, as you have said."

and-let-me-fetch a-morsel-of bread and-sustain your-hearts after you-will-pass-on for on-this-account you-passed upon your-servant and-they-said so you-do as-you-spoke

Grammar
  • The speech has two parts: Abraham's offer (a cohortative, 'let me fetch', then an imperative, 'sustain', then a yiqtol of permission, 'you may go on') and the visitors' reply.
  • The compound כִּי־עַל־כֵּן: 'since, for this reason'. Ibn Ezra: it means 'since' (הואיל), as in 19:8. The qatal 'you have passed' is the reason clause.
  • The visitors speak as a group (plural verb, 'they said') but answer Abraham in the singular (תַּעֲשֶׂה, דִּבַּרְתָּ). The yiqtol תַּעֲשֶׂה 'you do' has the force of a polite command.
  • The etnaḥta on עַבְדְּכֶם divides the verse: the offer comes first, the reply (after the new וַיֹּאמְרוּ) second.
Commentary (14)
Rashifollows וְסַעֲד֤וּ לִבְּכֶם֙
Rashi: in the Torah, the Prophets and the Writings, bread is 'the support of the heart': 'sustain your hearts' here, 'sustain your heart with a morsel of bread' (Judg. 19:5), 'bread that sustains the heart of man' (Ps. 104:15). R. Hama: the text writes לִבְּכֶם, not לְבַבְכֶם (with two bets, the two inclinations), which shows that the evil inclination does not rule over angels. The English follows the plain sense.
Hebrew
בַּתּוֹרָה, בַנְּבִיאִים וּבַכְּתוּבִים מָצִינוּ דְּפִתָּא סַעֲדָתָא דְלִבָּא. בַּתּוֹרָה וְסַעֲדוּ לִבְּכֶם, בַּנְּבִיאִים סְעָד לִבְּךָ פַּת לֶחֶם (שופטים י"ט), בַּכְּתוּבִים וְלֶחֶם לְבַב אֱנוֹשׁ יִסְעָד (תהל' ק"ד). אָמַר רַבִּי חָמָא, לְבַבְכֶם אֵין כְּתִיב כָּאן אֶלָּא לִבְּכֶם, מַגִּיד שֶׁאֵין יֵצֶר הָרַע שׁוֹלֵט בַּמַּלְאָכִים (בראשית רבה):
Rashifollows אַחַ֣ר תַּעֲבֹ֔רוּ
Rashi: 'afterward you may go on' means afterwards you may go on your way. The English follows this.
Hebrew
אַחַר כֵּן תֵּלְכוּ:
Rashifollows כִּֽי עַל כֵּ֥ן עֲבַרְתֶּ֖ם
Rashi: 'I ask this of you, since you have passed by me to honour me.' The English 'since you have passed by your servant' follows the reason clause.

Ancient Near East
  • 'A morsel of bread' is courteous understatement: the meal that follows (18:6–8) is lavish. The Hebrew idiom for refreshing oneself with food is 'sustain the heart'; in Hebrew thought the heart (לֵב) is the seat of mind, will and appetite as well as feeling.
18:6

Abraham hurried to the tent, to Sarah, and said, "Hurry! Three seahs of fine flour: knead it and make cakes."

Grammar
  • The imperatives מַהֲרִי, לוּשִׁי and עֲשִׂי are feminine singular, addressed to Sarah.
  • The numeral 'three' (שְׁלֹשׁ) is feminine to agree with the feminine noun סְאָה (plural סְאִים).
  • קֶמַח סֹלֶת: the two nouns stand together, 'meal, fine flour'; 'to the tent' ends in the directional הָ- (הָאֹהֱלָה), and the preposition אֶל introduces Sarah.

Ancient Near East
  • A seah is a dry measure, a third of an ephah. Its modern value is uncertain; estimates run from about seven to more than ten litres. Three seahs is a very large quantity for three guests; the commentators explain it as lavish hospitality or as food for the household.
  • סֹלֶת is fine wheat flour, a luxury; עֻגוֹת are round flat loaves baked quickly on hot stones or in embers (compare 1 Kgs 19:6). Kneading and baking were the work of the women of the household.
18:7

Abraham ran to the herd and took a young bull, tender and good, and gave it to the young servant, and hurried to prepare it.

and-to the-herd ran Abraham and-took son-of herd tender and-good and-gave to the-lad and-hurried to-prepare it

Grammar
  • The sentence begins with the fronted prepositional phrase 'to the herd'; the verb ran (qatal) follows, then a chain of wayyiqtols.
  • Ben bakar is a construct: 'son of the herd', the idiom for a young bull. The adjectives tender and good are masculine singular, agreeing with it.
  • The infinitive construct with the object marker (la-'asot oto) gives 'to prepare it'.
  • The accents: the tipha on 'hurried' (18:7.13) marks the last clause; the silluq comes at the end of the verse.

Rashi's midrash is that there were three bulls, so that the three guests could be fed three tongues in mustard (Bava Metzia 87a). The Hebrew is singular (בֶּן־בָּקָר), and Radak reads a single small male, so the English keeps 'a young bull' and the reading is recorded in the commentary. The subject of וַיְמַהֵר is not marked: Radak takes it as Abraham's zeal; the servant is also possible.

וּלְוַת תּוֹרֵי רְהַט אַבְרָהָם וּדְבַר בַּר תּוֹרֵי רַכִּיךְ וְטַב וִיהַב לְעוּלֵמָא וְאוֹחִי לְמֶעְבַּד יָתֵיהּ:
Ancient Near East
  • Meat was a rare luxury for a household of herders, who lived mostly on milk, curds and bread; slaughtering a choice young animal for a guest marks great honour (compare 1 Sam. 28:24).
  • Abraham's household includes many servants (14:14, 17:23), one of whom prepares the animal.
18:8

He took curds and milk and the young bull which he had prepared, and set them before them, and he stood by them under the tree, and they ate.

and-took curds and-milk and-son-of the-herd which he-made and-set before-them and-he standing upon-them under the-tree and-they-ate

Grammar
  • The chain of wayyiqtols (he took, he set, they ate) carries the meal forward; 'and he stood' is a circumstantial clause in the middle (a waw, the pronoun and a participle).
  • The relative clause 'which he had prepared' (אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה) is a qatal that precedes the setting-out; Radak adds 'through the servant'.
  • The Hebrew names no bread; Radak supposes bread was served first, as 18:6 implies, and the verse lists only the further dishes. Rashi has a midrash (Sarah's niddah) for the omission. The English names no bread.
  • The etnaḥta on לִפְנֵיהֶם divides the verse: the serving comes first, the standing and the eating second.

Ibn Ezra (comment on 18:8, filed at 18:1): וַיֹּאכֵלוּ means 'the bread was consumed', as in 'which the fire consumes' (Lev. 6:3), that is, he does not take it that the visitors ate as men do. The English keeps 'they ate': the narrative sets the food before them and Lot's visitors also 'eat' (19:3), and the reading of Ibn Ezra rests on a view of what angels are, not on the Hebrew grammar of the verse (the subject is plural and active). The reading is recorded in the apparatus and the commentary. Rashi's 'appeared to eat' is also recorded.

Commentary (13)
Rashinot-applicable וַיִּקַּ֨ח חֶמְאָ֜ה
Rashi: no bread is mentioned because Sarah's period began that day, which made the dough unclean (Bava Metzia 86b). A midrash on the omission. Radak holds that bread was certainly served first (18:6) and the verse lists only the further dishes. The English names no bread because the Hebrew names none.

Ancient Near East
  • חֶמְאָה is a milk product; the exact food is uncertain (curds, soured or clotted milk, or butter). Cow's milk and meat are served together: the later rabbinic separation of milk and meat is not in this narrative and is not read into it.
  • A host who stands by his guests while they eat attends on them; it shows deference, not distance.
Apparatus
  • Ibn Ezra: ויאכלו = 'the bread was consumed' (compare Lev. 6:3), not that the visitors ate. Not adopted; the active plural verb is read as the plain sense (question for the editor, since Ibn Ezra is normative).
  • Rashi (Bava Metzia 87a): they appeared to eat. Ramban cites the rabbis (Genesis Rabbah): each visitor in turn departed as the meal went on. Radak: the whole scene is a prophetic vision.
18:9

They said to him, "Where is Sarah your wife?" He said, "Look, in the tent."

and-they-said to-him where Sarah your-wife and-he-said look in-the-tent

Grammar
  • The two wayyiqtol verbs (וַיֹּאמְרוּ, וַיֹּאמֶר) carry the narrative sequence: first the visitors speak, then the one addressed answers.
  • The question has no verb: אַיֵּה שָׂרָה אִשְׁתֶּךָ is 'where Sarah your wife', and the English supplies 'is'.
  • The etnaḥta on אִשְׁתֶּךָ closes the question; the silluq on בָאֹהֶל closes the verse.
  • The letters א, י and ו of אֵלָיו carry dots above them (puncta extraordinaria). Rashi and Radak, after Bereshit Rabbah, read the dotted letters as אַיּוֹ, 'where is he?': the visitors asked Sarah about Abraham too. The English reads the word as written, 'to him'.

The answer 'in the tent' is taken as the modest place of a woman who stays inside (Rashi). The English states the place only.

Commentary (7)
Rashinot-applicable וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ אֵׄלָ֔יׄוׄ
Rashi: the letters אי"ו of אֵלָיו are dotted. R. Shimon ben Elazar: where the undotted letters outnumber the dotted, one expounds the writing; where the dotted outnumber the undotted, one expounds the dots, and here they spell אַיּוֹ 'where is he?': they asked Sarah too where Abraham was. Hence a guest asks the man about the wife and the wife about the man. Bava Metzia: the angels knew where Sarah was, but asked to make known that she was modest and so endear her to her husband; R. Yose bar Ḥanina: to send her the cup of blessing. A midrash on the dots; the English reads 'to him' as written.

Apparatus
  • Puncta extraordinaria over the letters א, י, ו of אֵלָיו (WLC note 4). Rashi and Radak, citing R. Shimon ben Elazar (Bereshit Rabbah 48), read the dotted letters as אַיּוֹ, 'where is he?'.
18:10

He said, "I will surely return to you at this time next year, with Sarah alive, and Sarah your wife will have a son." And Sarah was listening at the entrance of the tent, and he was behind it.

and-he-said return I-will-return to-you as-the-time living and-look son to-Sarah your-wife and-Sarah listening opening-of the-tent and-he behind-it

Grammar
  • The infinitive absolute שׁוֹב before the yiqtol אָשׁוּב is the emphatic form: 'I will surely return'.
  • כָּעֵת חַיָּה is an adverbial phrase: כְּ with the article, 'at the time', and the feminine adjective חַיָּה, 'living'. Ibn Ezra: this time next year, with Sarah alive; Radak: Sarah giving birth; Onkelos: 'when you are alive'.
  • וְהִנֵּה־בֵן לְשָׂרָה is verbless: 'and look, a son to Sarah'; the English supplies 'will have'.
  • The etnaḥta on אִשְׁתֶּךָ divides the verse: the promise, then the scene at the tent. Both clauses after it are circumstantial, a subject before a participle (וְשָׂרָה שֹׁמַעַת) and a pronoun before a preposition (וְהוּא אַחֲרָיו).

Ibn Ezra reads כָּעֵת חַיָּה as 'at this time next year, with Sarah alive' (like כֹּה לֶחָי, 1 Sam 25:6); the English follows him and supplies 'next year' and Sarah's name from the feminine adjective. Rashi's second reading and Onkelos ('when you are alive') and Radak (Sarah giving birth) are in the commentary and the notes. In the last clause the English follows Ibn Ezra: 'he' is the visitor who speaks and 'it' the tent; Rashi and Radak read 'the entrance was behind him'.

Commentary (17)
Rashifollows שׁ֣וֹב אָשׁ֤וּב
Rashi: the angel does not promise his own return; he speaks on the errand of the Place (בִּשְׁלִיחוּתוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם), as in 16:10 where the angel says 'I will multiply', so the words are God's. The English keeps the first person of the speech.

Rashi: הַפֶּתַח הָיָה אַחַר הַמַּלְאָךְ, the entrance was behind the angel; so Radak and Sforno. The English follows Ibn Ezra, 'he was behind it', and records this.
Hebrew
הַפֶּתַח הָיָה אַחַר הַמַּלְאָךְ:

Ibn Ezra: 'at this time in the next year' (כעת הזאת בשנה האחרת), and חַיָּה is Sarah, alive (ושרה חיה), like the greeting כֹּה לֶחָי, 'so to the living' (1 Sam 25:6). The English follows: 'at this time next year, with Sarah alive'.

Ibn Ezra: 'he' is the angel who was speaking with Abraham; he was behind the tent, and Abraham, sitting at the entrance of the tent, did not see Sarah. Others say the entrance of Sarah's tent was behind Abraham's tent (וי"א פתח האהל שלה היה אחרי אהל אברהם). The English follows his first reading, 'he was behind it'.

הַ

Hebrew
הָיָה אַחֲרֵי הַמַּלְאָךְ הַמְדַבֵּר, לְפִיכָךְ לֹא דִּבֵּר עִמָּהּ לְנוֹכַח כְּמוֹ שֶׁעָשָׂה אֱלִישָׁע.
Ancient Near East
  • Genesis pictures Abraham as a herdsman living in tents (12:8, 13:3, 18:1). Elsewhere in Genesis wives have tents of their own (24:67, 31:33), which is the picture behind the reading, given by Ibn Ezra, that Sarah's tent stood behind Abraham's.
18:11

Now Abraham and Sarah were old, advanced in days; Sarah had ceased to have the way of women.

and-Abraham and-Sarah old coming in-days; ceased to-be for-Sarah way as-women

Grammar
  • חָדַל לִהְיוֹת is 'ceased to be': a qatal of cessation with an infinitive construct; its subject is אֹרַח. Rashi glosses it as 'ceased from her'.
  • בָּאִים בַּיָּמִים is the idiom for old age: 'coming into days', the participle of בּוֹא with ב.
  • אֹרַח כַּנָּשִׁים is a noun phrase with כ of comparison: 'a way like women's'. The silluq on כַּנָּשִׁים closes the verse.
  • The etnaḥta on בַּיָּמִים divides the verse: the age of the couple, then the cessation in Sarah.

The English 'the way of women' is the Hebrew's own euphemism. Rashi names it as the custom of the menstrual course; the English does not name it.

Targum Onkelos the whole verse
Hebrew
וְאַבְרָהָם וְשָׂרָה סִיבוּ עַלּוּ בְּיוֹמִין פְּסַק מִלְּמֶהֱוֵי לְשָׂרָה אוֹרַח כִּנְשַׁיָּא:
18:12

Sarah laughed to herself, saying, "After I am worn out, shall I have delight, when my lord is old?"

and-she-laughed Sarah within-her-inward-part saying after my-being-worn-out she-was to-me delight and-my-lord old

Grammar
  • The verse has no interrogative particle; the question is Ibn Ezra's reading of Sarah's words: 'how shall the delight of youth be renewed for me?'.
  • The verb הָיְתָה is a qatal used for the future (Ibn Ezra: כמו תהיה לי); the English 'shall I have' gives that sense.
  • The verse turns on two clauses: 'after I am worn out' (the infinitive of בלה with the suffix) and 'my lord is old' (a qatal of זקן, with the subject אֲדֹנִי).
  • The wayyiqtol וַתִּצְחַק and the infinitive לֵאמֹר introduce the speech; after בְּקִרְבָּהּ it is said within herself, not aloud.

עֶדְנָה is 'delight' (Ibn Ezra, and the lexicon). Rashi reads softness of flesh, and a second reading 'the time of the menstrual course'; both are recorded in the commentary.

Commentary (12)
Rashirecords בְּקִרְבָּ֣הּ

Ancient Near East
  • Sarah calls her husband אֲדֹנִי, 'my lord', the respectful term of a woman for the man of her household (compare Judg 19:26–27); Hebrew also calls a husband בַּעַל, 'master'.
18:13

The LORD said to Abraham, "Why is it that Sarah laughed, saying, 'Is it even true that I shall bear a child, now that I have grown old?'

and-said the-LORD to Abraham why this laughed Sarah saying is-it-even truly I-shall-bear and-I have-grown-old

Grammar
  • The LORD speaks in the wayyiqtol of the narrative, and the speech is direct: the double quotes are the LORD's words, and Sarah's words are inside them in single quotes.
  • לָמָּה זֶּה: the enclitic זֶה after the interrogative sharpens the question, 'why is it that'. The verb is a qatal (צָחֲקָה), the past reported to Abraham.
  • הַאַף אֻמְנָם: the interrogative הַ, אַף 'even', and אֻמְנָם 'truly', before the yiqtol אֵלֵד: 'is it even true that I shall bear?'.
  • The closing clause is a qatal, 1st person singular, וַאֲנִי זָקַנְתִּי, where Sarah had said 'and my lord is old' (18:12).

The LORD's words say 'I have grown old' where Sarah had thought 'after I am worn out ... and my lord is old' (18:12). Ibn Ezra: 'I have grown old' renders her 'after I am worn out', and the words are true. Rashi and Ramban add that 'my lord is old' was left out for the sake of peace. The English keeps the words as written.

Commentary (9)
Rashifollows הַאַ֥ף אֻמְנָ֛ם
Rashi: הַאַף אֻמְנָם is הֲגַם אֱמֶת אֵלֵד, 'shall I truly, in truth, bear?'. The English reads 'Shall I truly bear a child'.

Rashifollows וַאֲנִ֥י זָקַֽנְתִּי׃
Rashi: Scripture changed Sarah's 'and my lord is old' to 'and I am old' for the sake of peace (מִפְּנֵי הַשָּׁלוֹם). The English keeps 'I am old'.

שִׁנָּה הַכָּתוּב מִפְּנֵי הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהֲרֵי הִיא אָמְרָה וַאדֹנִי זָקֵן:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows וַאֲנִ֥י זָקַֽנְתִּי׃

The word ומ"ם is the opening of the comment filed as ibn-ezra:18:13:3: 'and the mem [of אֻמְנָם] is added, as the mem of שִׁלְשֹׁם'. The anchoring split one sentence; its sense is given there.

ומ"ם
Ibn Ezranormativefollows אֻמְנָ֛ם
Ibn Ezra: the mem of אֻמְנָם is added, as in שִׁלְשֹׁם (31:5). He then reports other commentators: the three men were prophets; to the objection that a prophet does not come to a prophet, they answer that the men came to Sarah (hence 'where is Sarah your wife'), and two went on to Sodom; on that reading 'they ate' is literal and אֲדֹנַי in 18:3 means 'my masters'. He gives further views on the order of the chapter and says no scribal correction is needed; his own view, he says, is hinted at in the portion of Shemot. The English 'truly' follows his first words.

(בראשית יח ג) שדבר בתחלה עם הגדול שבהם ואחר כן עם כולם ומצאנו שנקרא הנביא מלאך "בחגי", וי"א כי אברהם בקש רשות מהשכינה, וי"א שהוא מוקדם ומאוחר, וכן הוא וישא, וכבר נשא עיניו ועשה כך וכך, ואח"כ נראה אליו השם ואמר המכסה אני מאברהם גם זעקת סדום ואלו ההולכים הגיעו אל סדום, ואברהם עודנו עומד לפני ד', ועל כל פנים "וד' אמר" (בראשית יח יז) עם אברהם ידבר או עם המלאכים שיאמרו לו, רק "ויאמר ד' זעקת סדום" (בראשית יח כ) עם אברהם דבר ואברהם נגש ואמר "האף תספה" (בראשית יח כג) ונכנס פסוק "ויפנו משם האנשים" (בראשית יח כב) להודיע כי בעת שבאו אל סדום, אז אמר השם לאברהם זעקת סדום וכן "אמור לנער ויעבור לפנינו ויעבור ואתה עמוד כיום" (ש"א ט כט) ואין לנו צורך לתיקון סופרים, והעד שאמר באחרונה "אל המקום אשר עמד שם את פני ד'" (בראשית יט כז), והנכון בעיני תמצאנו רמוז בפרשת ואלה שמות:

Apparatus
  • Sarah's words 'and my lord is old' (18:12) and the LORD's 'and I have grown old' (18:13) differ; the English follows the words of each speaker, and the commentators' accounts are in the commentary.
  • The ibn-ezra:18:13:2 entry (ומ"ם) is the first word of the comment on אֻמְנָם filed as ibn-ezra:18:13:3; the anchoring has split one sentence in two.
18:14

Is anything hidden from the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you, at this time next year, with Sarah alive, and Sarah will have a son."

is-it-hidden from-the-LORD anything to-the-appointed-time I-will-return to-you as-the-time living and-to-Sarah son

Grammar
  • הֲיִפָּלֵא is a question with the interrogative ה and a nifal yiqtol: 'is anything hidden from the LORD?'.
  • לַמּוֹעֵד, 'at the appointed time', is a noun with ל and the article: the time set in 17:21. כָּעֵת חַיָּה repeats the words of 18:10.
  • וּלְשָׂרָה בֵן is verbless: 'and to Sarah a son'; the English supplies 'will have'.
  • The etnaḥta on דָּבָר divides the verse: the question, then the promise repeated.

Rashi and Ibn Ezra take הֲיִפָּלֵא as 'hidden' (היתכסי, היעלם), and the English follows them. The lexicon's Niph senses ('beyond one's power, difficult') are the other reading; Radak takes it so, and it is recorded.

Commentary (7)
Rashifollows הֲיִפָּלֵ֥א
Rashi: הֲיִפָּלֵא is הֲיִתְכַּסִּי, 'is it concealed?' (as its Targum). Is any wondrous, separated or hidden thing hidden from me in doing my will? The English reads 'hidden from the LORD'.
Hebrew
כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ הֲיִתְכַּסִּי? וְכִי שׁוּם דָּבָר מֻפְלָא וּמֻפְרָד וּמְכֻסֶּה מִמֶּנִּי מִלַּעֲשׂוֹת כִּרְצוֹנִי:
Rashifollows לַמּוֹעֵ֞ד
Rashi: לַמּוֹעֵד is that appointed time that was set for you yesterday, at this time next year. The English gives 'at the appointed time' and 'at this time next year'.

Ibn Ezra: הֲיִפָּלֵא means היעלם, is hidden. Others say it means 'not a wonder for God', but then the mem would not be attached to the Name; he rejects that. The English follows 'hidden'.

Radakrecords הֲיִפָּלֵ֥א
Radak (not normative): things that seem strange to people are hidden from them, but nothing is hard for the LORD (לֹא יִפָּלֵא מִמֶּנּוּ דָּבָר). The English does not adopt this reading; it is recorded here.

  • 18:14.2 vowels: WLC reads מֵיְהוָה; the base text reads מֵיְהֹוָה. The English is the same.

18:15

Sarah denied, saying, "I did not laugh," for she was afraid. He said, "No, but you did laugh."

and-she-denied saying not I-laughed for she-was-afraid and-he-said no but you-laughed

Grammar
  • The first כִּי gives the reason for the denial ('for she was afraid'); the second corrects it ('no, but you did laugh'), as Rashi reads the two.
  • The wayyiqtol וַתְּכַחֵשׁ is piel, the denial; the two qatal forms (צָחַקְתִּי, יָרֵאָה) are the past of the speech.
  • The etnaḥta on יָרֵאָה closes the clause of the reason, and the silluq on צָחָקְתְּ closes the verse on the correction.
  • The English 'did laugh' supplies the auxiliary for the second person feminine qatal.

Sarah's denial is a lie told out of fear (Radak); the LORD answers that she laughed. The English keeps both quotations in direct speech.

Commentary (8)
Rashifollows כִּ֣י יָרֵ֑אָה כִּ֥י צָחָֽקְתְּ׃
Rashi: the first כִּי means 'for' (הָרִאשׁוֹן ... דְּהָא), giving the reason for the denial: she was afraid. The second means 'but' (אֶלָּא): 'No, but you did laugh'. The English follows both.
Hebrew
הָרִאשׁוֹן מְשַׁמֵּשׁ לְשׁוֹן דְּהָא, שֶׁנּוֹתֵן טַעַם לַדָּבָר וַתְּכַחֵשׁ שָׂרָה – לְפִי שֶׁיָּרְאָה; וְהַשֵּׁנִי מְשַׁמֵּשׁ בִּלְשׁוֹן אֶלָּא, וַיֹּאמֶר לֹא כִדְבָרֵךְ הוּא אֶלָּא צָחַקְתְּ, שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ כִּי מְשַׁמֵּשׁ בְּאַרְבַּע לְשׁוֹנוֹת, אִי, דִּלְמָא, אֶלָּא, דְּהָא:
Ramban וַתְּכַחֵ֨שׁ שָׂרָ֧ה לֵאמֹ֛ר
Hebrew
אֲנִי תָּמֵהַּ בַּנְּבִיאָה הַצַּדֶּקֶת, אֵיךְ תְּכַחֵשׁ בַּאֲשֶׁר אָמַר הַשֵּׁם לַנָּבִיא, וְגַם לָמָּה לֹא הֶאֱמִינָה לְדִבְרֵי מַלְאֲכֵי אֱלֹהִים. וְהַנִּרְאֶה בְּעֵינַי כִּי הַמַּלְאָכִים הָאֵלֶּה הַנִּרְאִים כַּאֲנָשִׁים בָּאוּ אֶל אַבְרָהָם, וְהוּא בְּחָכְמָתוֹ הִכִּיר בָּהֶם, וּבִשֵּׂר אוֹתוֹ "שׁוֹב אָשׁוּב אֵלֶיךָ וּלְשָׂרָה בֵן", וְשָׂרָה שׁוֹמַעַת וְלֹא יָדְעָה כִּי מַלְאֲכֵי עֶלְיוֹן הֵם, כָּעִנְיָן בְּאֵשֶׁת מָנוֹחַ (שופטים יג ו), וְאוּלַי לֹא רָאֲתָה אוֹתָם כְּלָל. וַתִּצְחַק בְּקִרְבָּהּ , לְלַעַג, כְּמוֹ "יוֹשֵׁב בַּשָּׁמַיִם יִשְׂחָק ה' יִלְעַג לָמוֹ" (תהלים ב ד), כִּי הַשְּׂחוֹק לְשִׂמְחָה הוּא בַּפֶּה, "אָז יִמָּלֵא שְׂחוֹק פִּינוּ" (שם קכו ב), אֲבָל הַשְּׂחֹק בַּלֵּב לֹא יֵאָמֵר בַּשִּׂמְחָה. והקב"ה הֶאֱשִׁים אוֹתָהּ לְאַבְרָהָם, לָמָּה הָיָה הַדָּבָר נִמְנָע בְּעֵינֶיהָ, וְרָאוּי לָהּ שֶׁתַּאֲמִין אוֹ שֶׁתֹּאמַר "אָמֵן כֵּן יַעֲשֶׂה ה'". וְהִנֵּה אַבְרָהָם אָמַר אֵלֶיהָ, לָמָּה צָחַקְתְּ, הֲיִפָּלֵא מֵה' דָּבָר, וְלֹא פֵּרֵשׁ אֵלֶיהָ כִּי הַשֵּׁם גִּלָּה אֵלָיו סוֹדָהּ, וְהִיא מִפְּנֵי יִרְאָתוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם תְּכַחֵשׁ, כִּי חָשְׁבָה שֶׁאַבְרָהָם בְּהַכָּרַת פָּנֶיהָ יֹאמַר כֵּן, אוֹ מִפְּנֵי שֶׁשָּׁתְקָה וְלֹא נָתְנָה שֶׁבַח וְהוֹדָאָה בַּדָּבָר וְלֹא שָׂמְחָה. וְהוּא אָמַר "לֹא כִּי צָחָקְתְּ", אָז הֵבִינָה כִּי בִּנְבוּאָה נֶאֱמַר לוֹ כֵּן, וְשָׁתְקָה וְלֹא עָנְתָה אוֹתוֹ דָּבָר. וְרָאוּי שֶׁנֹּאמַר עוֹד כִּי אַבְרָהָם לֹא גִּלָּה לָהּ הַנֶּאֱמָר לוֹ מִתְּחִלָּה (בראשית י"ז:י"ט) "אֲבָל שָׂרָה אִשְׁתְּךָ יֹלֶדֶת לְךָ בֵּן", אוּלַי הִמְתִּין עַד שְׁלֹחַ הַשֵּׁם אֵלֶיהָ הַבְּשׂוֹרָה בְּיוֹם מָחָר, כִּי יָדַע "כִּי לֹא יַעֲשֶׂה ה' אֱלֹהִים דָּבָר כִּי אִם גָּלָה סוֹדוֹ אֶל עֲבָדָיו הַנְּבִיאִים" (עמוס ג ז), אוֹ מֵרֹב זְרִיזוּתוֹ בַּמִּצְוֹת הָיָה טָרוּד בְּמִילָתוֹ וּמִילַת עַם רַב אֲשֶׁר בְּבֵיתוֹ, וְאַחַר כֵּן בְּחֻלְשָׁתוֹ יָשַׁב לוֹ פֶּתַח הָאֹהֶל, וְהַמַּלְאָכִים בָּאוּ טֶרֶם שֶׁהִגִּיד לָהּ דָּבָר:

18:16

The men rose from there and looked down toward Sodom, and Abraham was going with them to escort them.

and-they-rose from-there the-men and-they-looked-down over face-of Sodom and-Abraham walking with-them to-escort-them

Grammar
  • Two wayyiqtol verbs (וַיָּקֻמוּ, וַיַּשְׁקִפוּ) carry the narrative; the subject הָאֲנָשִׁים stands after the first verb and its adverb.
  • וַיַּשְׁקִפוּ is the hiphil of שׁקף, 'look down' from a height; with עַל־פְּנֵי, 'over the face of', it is the view down over Sodom.
  • וְאַבְרָהָם הֹלֵךְ: subject before participle, a circumstantial clause, 'while Abraham was going with them'. The infinitive לְשַׁלְּחָם gives the purpose.
  • The piel of שׁלח, 'send off', is here seeing guests on their way (Rashi and Radak: לְלַוּוֹתָם).

Rashi reads the verb of looking down as a look for evil; the English keeps the neutral 'looked down' and records this. Rashi reads לְשַׁלְּחָם as escort, as one who supposes they are guests.

Commentary (10)
Rashirecords וַיַּשְׁקִ֖פוּ
Rashi: every הַשְׁקָפָה in Scripture is for harm, except 'look down from your holy dwelling' (Deut 26:15), for great is the power of gifts to the poor, which turns the attribute of anger into mercy. The English keeps the neutral 'looked down'.
Hebrew

Rashi: לְשַׁלְּחָם means לְלַוּוֹתָם, to escort them, as one who supposes they are guests (כַּסָּבוּר אוֹרְחִים הֵם). The English reads 'to escort them'.

הוּא הָיָה מִתְעַסֵּק בְּמִצְוַת גְּמִילוּת חֲסָדִים לְלַוּוֹת אֶת הָאוֹרְחִים, וַה' אָמַר שֶׁיְּגַלֶּה לוֹ
Ancient Near East
  • Genesis places Sodom in the plain of the Jordan near the Dead Sea (13:10–12, 14:3). Its site is disputed, at the south end of the sea or north of it in the Jordan plain, and has not been identified with certainty. From the hill country near Hebron the land falls steeply east to that basin, the picture of 'looked down' here and in 19:28.
18:17

The LORD said, "Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do,

and-the-LORD said: question-covering I from-Abraham what I doing?

Grammar
  • וַיהוָה אָמָר: a vav, then the subject, then a qatal (pausal אָמָר). Because the subject stands before the verb, this is not the plain wayyiqtol of narrative: it is a clause that pauses the story ('now the LORD had said'), or reports a thought (Ramban). The Hebrew gives no addressee.
  • הַמְכַסֶּה: a piel participle with the interrogative ה, 'am I hiding?'; Rashi reads the ה as a question of astonishment (בִּתְמִיהָ), 'can I hide?'.
  • אֲשֶׁר אֲנִי עֹשֶׂה is a relative clause with an active participle, which can mean an act in progress or one about to happen; the object is not stated (Rashi supplies 'in Sodom').
  • The tipḥa on וַיהוָה and the etnaḥta on אָמָר set off the introduction; the mahpakh on הַמְכַסֶּה begins the question, and the silluq closes the verse at עֹשֶׂה.

The English keeps the question form. Rashi supplies 'in Sodom' as the object of 'what I am doing'; the English does not add it, and the commentary records it. The quotation is not closed here: the speech runs to the end of 18:19.

Rashifollows הַֽמְכַסֶּ֤ה אֲנִי֙
Rashi: the הֲ of הַמְכַסֶּה marks astonishment (בִּתְמִיהָ), so God asks in wonder whether he can hide the matter from Abraham. The English keeps the question.

בִּתְמִיהָ:
Rashirecords אֲשֶׁ֖ר אֲנִ֥י עֹשֶֽׂה׃

It is not fitting for God to do this without Abraham's knowledge: God gave him this land, and these five cities are his (he cites Gen. 10:19, the border of the Canaanite 'toward Sodom and Gomorrah'); God called him Abraham, father of a multitude of nations, so will he destroy the sons and not tell the father, who loves him? The English 'what I am about to do' does not name Sodom; the supplied object is recorded here.

Apparatus
  • Addressee of the saying: Ramban takes it to be the host of heaven or the messengers, or an inner thought ('every saying with the heart is a thought'); Radak takes it as the God who appeared to Abraham telling him of Sodom in the same vision. The Hebrew names no one.
18:18

seeing that Abraham shall surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed through him?

and-Abraham surely-become shall-become to-a-nation great and-mighty and-shall-be-blessed through-him all nations-of the-earth

Grammar
  • הָיוֹ יִהְיֶה: the infinitive absolute before the yiqtol of the same verb intensifies it: 'surely shall become'.
  • לְגוֹי גָּדוֹל וְעָצוּם: the predicate after הָיָה is marked by the lamed, and the two adjectives are joined by the vav.
  • וְנִבְרְכוּ בוֹ: the weqatal of the nifal continues the yiqtol of 18:18.3; its subject is 'all the nations', and the verb is passive in Ibn Ezra's reading.
  • The zaqef qaton on the first word and the tipḥa on גָּדוֹל divide the clause; the silluq closes the verse at הָאָרֶץ.

Rashi's midrash is that the name is repeated for a blessing (זֵכֶר צַדִּיק לִבְרָכָה); the plain sense is that God would not hide from one dear to him. The English gives the plain sense. The verse continues the quoted speech begun in 18:17.

Commentary (7)

Hebrew
וּבִהְיוֹתוֹ לְנֵס עַמִּים רַבִּים תִּהְיֶה תּוֹכַחְתּוֹ רַבַּת הַתּוֹעֶלֶת.
18:19

For I have known him, so that he may charge his sons and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD by doing righteousness and justice, in order that the LORD may bring upon Abraham what he spoke concerning him."

for I-have-known-him, in-order-that he-will-charge [object-marker] his-sons and-[object-marker] his-household after-him, and-they-keep the-way-of the-LORD to-do righteousness and-justice, in-order-that the-LORD bring upon-Abraham [object-marker] that he-spoke concerning-him

Grammar
  • כִּי יְדַעְתִּיו: qatal, first person singular, with the suffix 'him'; the clause gives the reason why God will not hide the matter. יָדַע with a person as object is 'know a person' (acquaintance, regard, choice).
  • לְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר יְצַוֶּה: לְמַעַן is a preposition of purpose; with אֲשֶׁר it opens a purpose clause and the yiqtol is 'may charge'. The same word opens the second purpose clause (לְמַעַן הָבִיא).
  • וְשָׁמְרוּ: the weqatal continues the yiqtol of יְצַוֶּה, so the sons and the household are to keep the way of the LORD; לַעֲשׂוֹת states how: by doing righteousness and justice.
  • הָבִיא is a hifil infinitive construct with לְמַעַן: 'in order that the LORD may bring'.
  • The revia on יְדַעְתִּיו closes the first clause; the zaqef on אַחֲרָיו and the etnaḥta on וּמִשְׁפָּט mark the later divisions; the silluq closes the verse at עָלָיו.

Rashi glosses לְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר as 'because' and יְצַוֶּה as a present; but the word is a preposition of purpose and the English reads it so, as Ramban does. The English keeps 'known' for יְדַעְתִּיו, which is Ramban's own choice (knowledge as God's regard for the righteous); Rashi's 'affection' and Ramban's 'I raised him up' are recorded in the commentary. The quotation of the LORD's speech closes here.

Commentary (14)
Rashifollows כִּ֣י יְדַעְתִּ֗יו
Rashi: ידעתיו is a word of affection (לְשׁוֹן חִבָּה), like מוֹדָע לְאִישָׁהּ (Ruth 2); the root sense of all such words is knowledge, since one who loves draws near and knows the beloved. The English keeps 'known'.
Hebrew
לְשׁוֹן חִבָּה, כְּמוֹ מוֹדָע לְאִישָׁהּ (רות ב'), הֲלֹא בֹעַז מֹדַעְתָּנוּ (שם ג'), וָאֵדָעֲךָ בְּשֵׁם (שמות ל"ג). וְאָמְנָם עִקַּר לְשׁוֹן כֻּלָּם אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא לְשׁוֹן יְדִיעָה, שֶׁהַמְחַבֵּב אֶת הָאָדָם מְקָרְבוֹ אֶצְלוֹ וְיוֹדְעוֹ וּמַכִּירוֹ, וְלָמָּה יְדַעְתִּיו?
Rashideclines לְמַ֩עַן֩ אֲשֶׁ֨ר יְצַוֶּ֜ה
Rashi: לְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר יְצַוֶּה means 'because he commands his sons concerning me to keep my ways'. He adds that if one explains it like the Targum ('I know that he will command ...'), לְמַעַן would not fit the wording. The English declines 'because': it reads לְמַעַן as 'so that', a purpose.
Hebrew
לְפִי שֶׁהוּא מְצַוֶּה אֶת בָּנָיו עָלַי לִשְׁמֹר דְּרָכַי. וְאִם תְּפָרְשֵׁהוּ כְתַרְגּוּמוֹ, יוֹדֵעַ אֲנִי בוֹ שֶׁיְּצַוֶּה אֶת בָּנָיו וְגוֹ', אֵין לְמַעַן נוֹפֵל עַל הַלָּשׁוֹן:
Rashirecords יְצַוֶּ֜ה
Rashi: יְצַוֶּה is present tense (לְשׁוֹן הוֹוֶה), like 'so Job did' (Job 1:5). The English takes it as the subjunctive of the purpose clause, 'may charge'; his present is recorded here.
Hebrew
לְשׁוֹן הוֹוֶה, כְמוֹ כָּכָה יַעֲשֶׂה אִיּוֹב (איוב א'):
Rashifollows לְמַ֗עַן הָבִ֤יא
Rashi: this is how Abraham commands his sons, 'keep the way of the LORD', in order that the LORD may bring upon Abraham what he spoke. He notes that the verse says 'upon Abraham' and not 'upon the house of Abraham', and draws the homily that whoever leaves a righteous son is as if he had not died. The English reads the second לְמַעַן as purpose; the homily is not the plain sense.
Hebrew
כָּךְ הוּא מְצַוֶּה לְבָנָיו, שִׁמְרוּ דֶּרֶך ה' כְּדֵי שֶׁיָּבִיא ה' עַל אַבְרָהָם וְגוֹ'; עַל בֵּית אַבְרָהָם לֹא נֶאֱמַר אֶלָּא עַל אַבְרָהָם, לָמַדְנוּ, כָּל הַמַּעֲמִיד בֵּן צַדִּיק כְּאִלוּ אֵינוֹ מֵת:
Rambanfollows כִּ֣י יְדַעְתִּ֗יו לְמַ֩עַן֩ אֲשֶׁ֨ר יְצַוֶּ֜ה
Ramban: he first repeats Rashi (ידעתיו as a word of affection, like 'known to her husband') and adds that if it is explained 'I know that he will command', לְמַעַן does not fit. Another possibility: 'I raised him up so that he would command his sons' (compare Exod. 33:12). He holds that the right sense is knowledge itself: God's knowledge is his providence, which watches the righteous in particular. The English keeps 'known' and reads לְמַעַן as purpose; the 'raised him up' reading is recorded here.
Hebrew
לְשׁוֹן רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית י"ח:י"ט), "אֲרִי יְדַעְתִּנֵּיהּ" כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ, לְשׁוֹן חִבָּה, כְּמוֹ "מוֹדָע לְאִישָׁהּ" (רות ב א), "וָאֵדָעֲךָ" (שמות לג יז). אָמְנָם עִקַּר כֻּלָּם לְשׁוֹן יְדִיעָה, שֶׁהַמְחַבֵּב אֶת הָאָדָם וּמְקָרְבוֹ אֶצְלוֹ יוֹדְעוֹ וּמַכִּירוֹ. וְאִם תְּפָרְשֵׁהוּ יוֹדֵעַ אֲנִי בּוֹ שֶׁיְּצַוֶּה אֶת בָּנָיו, אֵין "לְמַעַן" נוֹפֵל עַל הַלָּשׁוֹן. וְיִתָּכֵן שֶׁיִּהְיֶה "יְדַעְתִּיו", גִּדַּלְתִּיו וְרוֹמַמְתִּיו בַּעֲבוּר אֲשֶׁר יְצַוֶּה אֶת בָּנָיו אַחֲרָיו לַעֲשׂוֹת אֶת הַיָּשָׁר לְפָנַי, וּלְכָךְ אֲשִׂימֶנּוּ לְגוֹי גָּדוֹל וְעָצוּם שֶׁיַּעַבְדוּנִי, וְכָמוֹהוּ "יְדַעְתִּיךָ בְשֵׁם" (שמות לג יב), "מָה אָדָם וַתֵּדָעֵהוּ" (תהלים קמד ג). אוֹ יֹאמַר יְדַעְתִּיו שֶׁיְּצַוֶּה, וְכֵן "לְמַעַן יָנוּחַ שׁוֹרְךָ וַחֲמֹרֶךָ" (שמות כג יב), שֶׁיָּנוּחַ. וְהַנָּכוֹן בְּעֵינַי שֶׁהִיא יְדִיעָה בּוֹ מַמָּשׁ, יִרְמֹז כִּי יְדִיעַת הַשֵּׁם שֶׁהִיא הַשְׁגָּחָתוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַשָּׁפָל הִיא לִשְׁמֹר הַכְּלָלִים, וְגַם בְּנֵי הָאָדָם מֻנָּחִים בּוֹ לַמִּקְרִים עַד בֹּא עֵת פְּקֻדָּתָם, אֲבָל בַּחֲסִידָיו יָשׂוּם אֵלָיו לִבּוֹ לָדַעַת אוֹתוֹ בִּפְרָט, לִהְיוֹת שְׁמִירָתוֹ דְּבֵקָה בּוֹ תָּמִיד, לֹא תִּפָּרֵד הַיְּדִיעָה וְהַזְּכִירָה מִמֶּנּוּ כְּלָל, כְּטַעַם "לֹא יִגְרַע מִצַּדִּיק עֵינָיו" (איוב לו ז). וּבָאוּ מִזֶּה פְּסוּקִים רַבִּים, כְּדִכְתִיב (תהלים לג יח) "הִנֵּה עֵין ה' אֶל יְרֵאָיו" וְזוּלַת זֶה:

Ancient Near East
  • The verb 'know' with a person as object can be covenant language: in the treaties of the ancient Near East a great king 'knows' a vassal when he recognizes him as his own partner. Many scholars read 'I have known him' in that sense, 'I have chosen him', and compare Amos 3:2. The medieval commentators differ: Rashi, affection; Ramban, God's attentive regard (and, as a second possibility, 'raised him up').
18:20

The LORD said to Abraham, "The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has grown great, and their sin is very heavy.

and-said the-LORD outcry-of Sodom and-Gomorrah that-has-grown-great and-their-sin that is-heavy very

Grammar
  • וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה: the wayyiqtol introduces the speech, and the Hebrew does not name the one addressed.
  • זַעֲקַת סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה is a construct chain; the outcry is the subject of the first clause.
  • כִּי רָבָּה: a qatal, third feminine singular, agreeing with זַעֲקָה; the accent above the resh is Rashi's evidence for 'has grown'.
  • וְחַטָּאתָם כִּי כָבְדָה מְאֹד: a second clause with the same כִּי, so the two clauses stand side by side; the adverb מְאֹד intensifies the qatal.

Rashi has the speech addressed to Abraham, and the English says so; Ramban says all the commentators read it that way. The English keeps 'outcry' for זַעֲקַת, which covers both Ibn Ezra's readings; the note records them. The lexicon entry for רבב given in the pack is an adjective; see the note on 18:20.7.

Commentary (14)
Rashifollows וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהֹוָ֔ה
Rashi: 'to Abraham', who had done as God said (not to hide the matter from him). Ramban reports that all the commentators take the speech to Abraham. The English adds 'to Abraham'.
Hebrew
אֶל אַבְרָהָם שֶׁעָשָׂה כַּאֲשֶׁר אָמַר, שֶׁלֹּא יְכַסֶּה מִמֶּנּוּ:
Rashifollows כִּי רָ֑בָּה
Rashi: every רַבָּה in Scripture has its accent below the bet, because it translates 'great'; this one has it above the resh, because it translates גָּדְלָה, 'has grown'. The English 'has grown great' follows him.
Hebrew
כָּל רַבָּה שֶׁבַּמִּקְרָא הַטַּעַם לְמַטָּה בַּבֵּי"ת, לְפִי שֶׁהֵן מְתֻרְגָּמִין גְּדוֹלָה, אוֹ גְּדֵלָה וְהוֹלֶכֶת, אֲבָל זֶה טַעֲמוֹ לְמַעְלָה בָּרֵי"ש, לְפִי שֶׁמְּתֻרְגָּם גָדְלָה כְּבָר כְּמוֹ שֶׁפֵּרַשְׁתִּי וַיְהִי הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ בָּאָה, הִנֵּה שָׁבָה יְבִמְתֵּךְ:
Ibn Ezranormativerecords זַעֲקַ֛ת סְדֹ֥ם
Ibn Ezra: the outcry is either words spoken against God, or the outcry of violence (זעקת החמס). The English keeps 'outcry', and the note records both readings.

Ramban וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהֹוָ֔ה זַעֲקַ֛ת סְדֹ֥ם וַעֲמֹרָ֖ה

לְשׁוֹן רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית י"ח:כ'), וַיֹּאמֶר ה' אֶל אַבְרָהָם שֶׁעָשָׂה כַּאֲשֶׁר אָמַר, שֶׁלֹּא יְכַסֶּה מִמֶּנּוּ. וְאָמַר רַבִּי אַבְרָהָם (אבן עזרא על בראשית י"ח:י') כִּי נִכְנַס פָּסוּק "וַיִּפְנוּ מִשָּׁם הָאֲנָשִׁים" בֵּנְתַיִם, לְהוֹדִיעַ כִּי בְּעֵת שֶׁבָּאוּ לִסְדוֹם אָז אָמַר הַשֵּׁם לְאַבְרָהָם "זַעֲקַת סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה כִּי רָבָּה". וְכֵן דַּעַת כָּל הַמְּפָרְשִׁים כִּי עִם אַבְרָהָם יְדַבֵּר, וּלְפִי זֶה הַנָּכוֹן בַּפָּסוּק "וַיִּפְנוּ מִשָּׁם הָאֲנָשִׁים" לוֹמַר כִּי כַּאֲשֶׁר אָמַר הַשֵּׁם לְאַבְרָהָם בִּנְסֹעַ הָאֲנָשִׁים מִמֶּנּוּ "זַעֲקַת סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה כִּי רָבָּה", עָמַד אַבְרָהָם בִּתְפִלָּה וּתְחִנָּה לְפָנָיו לִמְחֹל לָהֶם וְלָתֵת לוֹ רְשׁוּת לְדַבֵּר, וְהֶאֱרִיךְ בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ עַד שֶׁבָּאוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים סְדֹמָה, וְאָז נִגַּשׁ אַבְרָהָם וְאָמַר, "הַאַף תִּסְפֶּה". אוֹ יִהְיֶה פֵּרוּשׁוֹ שֶׁשָּׁב לְבָאֵר "עוֹדֶנּוּ עֹמֵד לִפְנֵי ה'", כִּי נִגַּשׁ אַבְרָהָם וְאָמַר "הַאַף תִּסְפֶּה". וְהִנֵּה הֶאֱרִיךְ בִּתְחִנָּה לְפָנָיו בְּכָל פַּעַם לֵאמֹר "אַל יִחַר אַף ה'", וְהָיָה עוֹד מְכַוֵּן דַּעְתּוֹ בְּכָל פַּעַם לִנְבוּאָה עַד שֶׁשָּׁמַע תְּשׁוּבָה לִדְבָרָיו מִפִּיו שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, וְהֶאֱרִיכוּ כָּל הַיּוֹם בָּזֶה, וַיֵּלֶךְ ה' בָּעֶרֶב כַּאֲשֶׁר כִּלָּה לְדַבֵּר אֶל אַבְרָהָם, וּבָאוּ שְׁנֵי הַמַּלְאָכִים סְדֹמָה:

Ancient Near East
  • Sodom and Gomorrah are named in the text among the cities of the plain: Gen. 13:12 has Lot settle among them, and Gen. 14:2 names five kings and their cities, Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Bela (that is Zoar). The text does not say how many people lived in them.
  • זְעָקָה is the cry of someone who has been wronged and appeals for redress (compare Gen. 4:10 and Exod. 22:22). In the text's picture of the world such a cry goes up to the deity as judge, who then hears the case.
18:21

Let me go down now and see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to me; and if not, I will find out."

I-will-go-down please and-I-will-see whether-according-to-its-outcry the-coming to-me they-have-done completion, and-if not I-will-know

Grammar
  • אֵרְדָה־נָּא וְאֶרְאֶה: two cohortatives, first person singular, 'let me go down' and 'let me see'; נָא softens them.
  • הַכְּצַעֲקָתָהּ: the interrogative ה, 'whether', with כְּ 'according to' and the noun 'outcry' with the feminine suffix ('its outcry', the outcry of the city; Rashi 'of the city'). הַבָּאָה: the article before the qatal makes a relative clause, 'that has come to me'.
  • עָשׂוּ כָּלָה: a qatal, third common plural, with כָּלָה. Rashi, Radak and the first view that Ibn Ezra reports take כָּלָה as the consequence ('they will be made an end of'); the pesiq between the words points that way. Ibn Ezra's own view, and Sforno's, take it as 'altogether, all of them'.
  • וְאִם־לֹא אֵדָעָה: the other half of the alternative, 'and if not, I will know'; the sense is 'see and discern' (Qal 1.c).

The English reads one question: God goes down to see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry, and if not, to find out. This is Ibn Ezra's own reading ('I will see whether they all did like this evil'); the apodosis reading ('then I will make an end', Rashi, Radak, and the view he reports first) is recorded. The vowel variant at 18:21.1 does not change the reading.

Commentary (16)
Rashirecords אֵֽרְדָה נָּ֣א
Rashi gives two readings of 'I will go down and see': first a homily (the LORD's descent teaches judges to decide capital cases only on evidence); second, 'I will go down to the end of their deeds'. The English keeps 'go down and see'; the second reading is recorded here.
Hebrew
לִמֵּד לַדַּיָּנִים שֶׁלֹא יִפְסְקוּ דִינֵי נְפָשׁוֹת אֶלָּא בִרְאִיָּה, הַכֹּל כְּמוֹ שֶׁפֵּרַשְׁתִּי בְפָרָשַׁת הַפַּלָּגָה. דָּבָר אַחֵר, אֵרְדָה נָא לְסוֹף מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם:
Rashirecords הַכְּצַעֲקָתָ֛הּ
Rashi: הַכְּצַעֲקָתָהּ means 'of the city' (שֶׁל מְדִינָה), the outcry of the city. The English 'the outcry' does not name the city; Rashi's reading is recorded here.
Hebrew
שֶׁל מְדִינָה:
Rashirecords הַבָּ֥אָה אֵלַ֖י עָשׂ֣וּ
Rashi: if they stand in their rebellion, 'I am making an end of them' (כָּלָה אֲנִי עוֹשֶׂה בָהֶם); if they do not, 'I will know what to do' to punish them with afflictions and not destroy them (compare Exod. 33:5). A pesiq separates עָשׂוּ from כָּלָה. The English does not supply a consequence: it takes כָּלָה as 'altogether', as Ibn Ezra does, and Rashi's reading is recorded here.

Ibn Ezra reports a view ('some say') on הכצעקתה: 'if so, they did, I will make an end of them' (אם כן עשו אעשה בהם כלה), taking כלה as the consequence. His own view is in the next comment ('I will see whether they all did'); the English follows that, not this reading.

Apparatus
  • 18:21.1 vowels: WLC reads אֵֽרֲדָה; the base text reads אֵֽרְדָה. The verb is the same; only the vowels differ.
  • 18:21.7–8 עָשׂוּ ׀ כָּלָה: a pesiq stands between the two words. Rashi, Radak and the first view in Ibn Ezra read 'if they have done according to the outcry, I will make an end (of them)'; Ibn Ezra's own view and Sforno read כָּלָה as 'altogether, all of them'.
  • אֵֽרְדָה — WLC reads אֵֽרֲדָה (vowels)
18:22

The men turned from there and went to Sodom, but Abraham still stood before the LORD.

and-turned from-there the-men and-went Sodom-to and-Abraham still standing before the-LORD

Grammar
  • וַיִּפְנוּ and וַיֵּלְכוּ are wayyiqtol forms narrating the departure of the men.
  • עוֹדֶנּוּ עֹמֵד: the participle with עוֹד gives a continuing state: 'still standing'.
  • וְאַבְרָהָם opens a clause of contrast with the wayyiqtol chain before it.
  • The mahpakh on וַיִּפְנוּ and the merkha on לִפְנֵי divide the verse; the silluq closes it at יְהֹוָה.

Rashi reads the clause as a scribal correction (תִּקּוּן סוֹפְרִים): he holds that God came to Abraham and that the original text read that the LORD still stood over Abraham. The English translates the Hebrew as pointed, since the unit is translated from the witness, and records Rashi's view in the commentary.

Ancient Near East
  • To 'stand before' a king or a god is the idiom for serving or petitioning him in his presence (compare Deut. 10:8; 1 Kgs 10:8). The tradition that the wording is a scribal correction (תִּקּוּן סוֹפְרִים) is rabbinic; the text as pointed has Abraham standing before the LORD.
18:23

Abraham drew near and said, "Will you indeed sweep away a righteous person along with a wicked one?

and-drew-near Abraham and-said: will-also sweep-away you a-righteous with a-wicked?

Grammar
  • וַיִּגַּשׁ אַבְרָהָם וַיֹּאמַר: two wayyiqtol verbs; the approach comes first, and the speech follows it.
  • הַאַף: the interrogative ה (pointed with pataḥ before the guttural alef; the article would take qamets) and the adverb אַף, 'also, even': 'will you also ...?'. The Targum and Radak read אַף as 'anger'.
  • תִּסְפֶּה: the yiqtol is second person singular, Abraham speaking to God; the verb is transitive (Ibn Ezra) with an object left unsaid.
  • צַדִּיק עִם־רָשָׁע: two singular adjectives without the article, 'a righteous person with a wicked one'; the question is whether one sentence may fall on both.

Rashi's own gloss of הַאַף is הֲגַם, 'even, also'; the Targum's 'in anger' is the reading he introduces for Onkelos. The English follows the data (אַף 'also') and keeps the anger reading in the apparatus. Ibn Ezra takes the verb as transitive, 'consume'. The quotation runs on into 18:24.

Commentary (9)
Rashirecords וַיִּגַּ֥שׁ אַבְרָהָ֖ם
Rashi: the verb וַיִּגַּשׁ is used for approach to battle, to appease, and to pray; Abraham drew near for harsh words, for appeasement and for prayer. The English keeps 'drew near' and does not name one purpose.

Rashifollows הַאַ֣ף תִּסְפֶּ֔ה

Ancient Near East
  • צַדִּיק and רָשָׁע are also court words: the צַדִּיק is the one declared in the right and the רָשָׁע the one declared in the wrong (compare Deut. 25:1). Abraham's question is whether a judge may pass one sentence on both.
Apparatus
  • 18:23.4 הַאַף: Onkelos (בִּרְגַז) and Radak take אַף as 'anger', 'will you in anger sweep away?'; Rashi's own gloss is הֲגַם, 'even, also'.
18:24

Perhaps there are fifty righteous within the city. Will you indeed sweep away, and not spare Sodom for the sake of the fifty righteous who are within it?

perhaps there-are fifty righteous within the-city; will-also you-sweep-away and-not you-will-bear the-place for-the-sake-of fifty the-righteous who within-her

Grammar
  • אוּלַי introduces a tentative question: 'perhaps there are fifty'.
  • יֵשׁ חֲמִשִּׁים צַדִּיקִם בְּתוֹךְ הָעִיר: an existential clause with יֵשׁ; the city is where the righteous would be found.
  • הַאַף תִּסְפֶּה וְלֹא־תִשָּׂא: a second question, with the same verb as 18:23 and the negative on the verb of sparing.
  • לְמַעַן חֲמִשִּׁים הַצַּדִּיקִם אֲשֶׁר בְּקִרְבָּהּ: a purpose phrase; the relative clause 'who are within it' refers back to the righteous.

Abraham's argument opens here and the quotation continues into 18:25, so the English has no closing quotation mark. Rashi's count is ten for each of the five cities; the English keeps the Hebrew's singular 'the city'. The English names Sodom as Ibn Ezra does, and 'spare' follows his 'forgive'.

Commentary (8)
Rashirecords אוּלַ֥י יֵ֛שׁ חֲמִשִּׁ֥ים צַדִּיקִ֖ם
Rashi: the fifty righteous are ten for each of the five cities, since there are five places; he also asks why the righteous are destroyed if they cannot save the wicked. The English keeps 'within the city' and records Rashi's distribution.

צַדִּיקִם בְּתוֹךְ הָעִיר שֶׁיִּשָּׂא לַמָּקוֹם וְלֹא יַשְׁחִיתֶנּוּ מִכֹּל וָכֹל, כִּי בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל לֹא הָיָה אֶלָּא נֹחַ בְּכָל הַדּוֹר הַהוּא שֶׁהָיָה צַדִּיק, לְפִיכָךְ נִשְׁחַת כָּל הָאָרֶץ וְהוּא נִצַּל, אֲבָל אִם יֵשׁ חֲמִשִּׁים צַדִּיקִים בְּתוֹךְ הָעִיר שֶׁיִּשָּׂא לַמָּקוֹם וְיִכְלוּ הָרְשָׁעִים וְהַיִּשּׁוּב יִתְקַיֵּם בְּאוֹתָם הַצַּדִּיקִים אַחַר כְּלוֹת הָרְשָׁעִים. וּמַה שֶּׁאָמַר ״וָאֲבַקֵּשׁ מֵהֶם אִישׁ גֹּדֵר גָּדֵר וְעֹמֵד בַּפֶּרֶץ לְפָנַי בְּעַד הָאָרֶץ לְבִלְתִּי שַׁחֲתָהּ״ (יחזקאל כב:ל), אוֹתָהּ הַשְׁחָתָה אֵינָהּ הַשְׁחָתָה גְּמוּרָה לַעֲשׂוֹתָהּ כָּלָה, אֶלָּא לְהַשְׁחִית יוֹשְׁבֶיהָ מִמֶּנָּה וְהַיִּשּׁוּב יִשָּׁאֵר, וְעַד שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אוֹתוֹ הָאִישׁ צַדִּיק גָּמוּר כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר ״גֹּדֵר גָּדֵר וְעֹמֵד בַּפֶּרֶץ״ (שם), שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בּוֹ כֹּחַ לְהַצִּיל עַל הָאֲחֵרִים מֵרֹב צִדְקָתוֹ וּמַחֲזִירָם לְמוּטָב כַּאֲשֶׁר יוּכַל, וּבִלְבַד שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה הֶחָמָס גּוֹבֵר בְּאוֹתוֹ הַמָּקוֹם, כִּי עִם רֹב הֶחָמָס לֹא יַעֲמֹד הַיִּשּׁוּב. אֲבָל אִם שְׁאָר עֲוֹנוֹת גּוֹבְרִים, אֵינוֹ דִּין הָאֵל לְהַשְׁחִית הַמָּקוֹם, אֶלָּא לִשְׁפֹּט הָרְשָׁעִים בַּחֶרֶב וּבָרָעָב אוֹ לְהַגְלוֹתָם מִן הָאָרֶץ, וּבָזֶה יִלְקוּ מְעַט הַצַּדִּיקִים בִּכְלַל רֹב הָרְשָׁעִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר ״וְהִכְרַתִּי מִמְּךָ צַדִּיק וְרָשָׁע״ (יחזקאל כא:ח), וְאוֹמֵר ״כִּי עַד צֶדֶק יָשׁוּב מִשְׁפָּט״ (תהלים צד:טו), וְאוֹמֵר ״נָתְנוּ אֶת נִבְלַת עֲבָדֶיךָ וְגוֹ׳״ (תהלים עט:ב). וּמַה שֶׁאָמַר ״וּבַקְּשׁוּ בִרְחוֹבוֹתֶיהָ אִישׁ אִם יֵשׁ מְבַקֵּשׁ אֱמוּנָה וְאֶסְלַח לָהּ״ (ירמיה ה:א), הָיוּ בָהֶם צַדִּיקִים בְּעַצְמָם, אֲבָל לְהָשִׁיב אֲחֵרִים מֵעָוֹן וְשֶׁיֵּלְכוּ בַּחוּצוֹת וּבָרְחוֹבוֹת לְהָשִׁיבָם מֵעָוֹן לֹא הָיוּ בָהֶם, כִּי הָיוּ יְרֵאִים לְנַפְשׁוֹתָם פֶּן יֵהָרְגוּ, וְלֹא הָיוּ מוֹסְרִים נַפְשָׁם כְּדֵי לְהָשִׁיב הַפּוֹשְׁעִים. אִם כֵּן אֵין כֹּחַ בְּצִדְקָתָם לִסְלֹחַ לָעִיר בַּעֲבוּרָם, אֶלָּא מֵהֶם יֵלְכוּ עִם הָרְשָׁעִים וּמֵהֶם יִנָּצְלוּ לְעַצְמָם, הַכֹּל לְפִי צִדְקָתָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר ״וְהָיוּ שְׁלֹשֶׁת הָאֲנָשִׁים הָאֵלֶּה בְּתוֹכָם נֹחַ דָּנִיֵּאל וְאִיּוֹב״ (יחזקאל יד:יד), ״הֵמָּה בְצִדְקָתָם יְנַצְּלוּ נַפְשָׁם״, וְאוֹמֵר ״וְאִם בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת יַצִּילוּ״ (יחזקאל יד:טז).

18:25

Far be it from you to do such a thing, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous and the wicked would be alike. Far be it from you! Will not the Judge of all the earth do justice?"

far-be-it to-you from-doing like-the-thing the-this to-kill righteous with wicked and-would-be like-the-righteous like-the-wicked far-be-it to-you will-the-judge-of all the-earth not do justice

Grammar
  • The two infinitive constructs, מֵעֲשֹׂת and לְהָמִית, depend on חָלִילָה לְךָ: 'far be it from you to do ... to kill'. Each carries its own preposition (מ, ל).
  • וְהָיָה (18:25.10) is a weqatal after the infinitives and states the result. The paired comparison כַצַּדִּיק כָּרָשָׁע, 'like the righteous, like the wicked', means 'the one like the other' (Ibn Ezra, Radak; compare כָמוֹךָ כְּפַרְעֹה, 44:18).
  • The question הֲשֹׁפֵט כָּל־הָאָרֶץ (18:25.15) takes the interrogative he. The English puts 'Will not' at the front to make the question clear.
  • The etnaḥta on כָּרָשָׁע (18:25.12) divides the verse: the first part names the act Abraham calls unthinkable, the second appeals to God's justice. The silluq on מִשְׁפָּט closes it.
  • לָּךְ (18:25.14) is the pausal form of לְךָ.

Both occurrences of חָלִילָה are rendered 'Far be it'. The second opens the appeal, and the English keeps it as a separate sentence.

Commentary (13)
Rashifollows חָלִ֨לָה לְּךָ֜
Rashi glosses חָלִילָה לְךָ as חֻלִּין הוּא לְךָ, 'it is profane (not holy) for you'. He adds that people would say God's craft is to sweep away all, righteous and wicked alike, as in the flood and the dispersal. The English adopts the sense 'far be it'; the charge itself is not in the English.
Hebrew
חֻלִּין הוּא לְךָ, יֹאמְרוּ כָךְ הוּא אֻמָּנוּתוֹ, שׁוֹטֵף הַכֹּל, צֵדִּיקִים וּרְשָׁעִים, כָּךְ עָשִׂיתָ לְדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל וּלְדוֹר הַפַּלָּגָה:
Rashifollows כַּדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֗ה
Rashi: כַּדָּבָר הַזֶּה means 'not this, and not anything like it' (לֹא הוּא וְלֹא כַּיּוֹצֵא בוֹ). The English 'such a thing' follows this.
Hebrew
לֹא הוּא וְלֹא כַּיּוֹצֵא בוֹ:
Rashirecords חָלִ֣לָה לָּ֔ךְ
Rashi refers the second חָלִילָה לָּךְ to the world to come (לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא). The English does not adopt this temporal reference; it is recorded here.
Hebrew
לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא:
Rashifollows הֲשֹׁפֵט֙ כׇּל הָאָ֔רֶץ
Rashi: the he of הֲשֹׁפֵט takes a hataf patah and gives the clause an interrogative tone: 'וְכִי מִי שֶׁהוּא שׁוֹפֵט לֹא יַעֲשֶׂה מִשְׁפַּט אֱמֶת', is it possible that a judge would not do true justice? The English is a question.
Hebrew
נָקוּד בַּחֲטַף פַּתָּח ה"א שֶׁל הֲשׁוֹפֵט, לְשׁוֹן תְּמִיהָ, וְכִי מִי שֶׁהוּא שׁוֹפֵט לֹא יַעֲשֶׂה מִשְׁפַּט אֱמֶת:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows חָלִ֨לָה
Ibn Ezra: חָלִלָה is 'a thing that cannot be' (דָּבָר שֶׁלֹּא יִתָּכֵן); some say the word has the sense of חָלוּל, 'hollow, with nothing in it'. The English 'far be it' carries the impossibility.
Hebrew
דבר שלא יתכן וי"א שהמלה כטעם חלול שאין בו כלום:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows וְהָיָ֥ה כַצַּדִּ֖יק כָּרָשָׁ֑ע
Ibn Ezra: when two כ's are joined it is a short way of speaking: 'the righteous would be like the wicked, and the wicked like the righteous', as in 'you are like Pharaoh' (44:18), 'as my people, so your people' (1 Kgs 22:4), 'darkness and light are alike' (Ps 139:12). He ends: how could the judge of all the earth not do justice? Radak reads the same. The English 'the righteous and the wicked would be alike' follows.

Ancient Near East
  • 'Judge of all the earth' gives the LORD a title that the neighbouring literatures gave to gods of justice: in Mesopotamia the sun god Shamash was invoked as judge of heaven and earth and as guardian of right, and he is shown giving the laws on the stele of Hammurabi. Abraham's appeal rests on the same idea, that the highest judge is bound to judge rightly.
Apparatus
  • The Hebrew also allows the one-way reading, 'so that the righteous would be like the wicked'; the English follows Ibn Ezra's two-way reading.
18:26

The LORD said, "If I find in Sodom fifty righteous people within the city, I will spare the whole place for their sake."

and-said the-LORD if I-find in-Sodom fifty righteous in-midst-of the-city and-I-spare to-all-of the-place for-their-sake

Grammar
  • וַיֹּאמֶר (18:26.1) is a wayyiqtol. It introduces the LORD's answer, which is this verse; Abraham speaks again in 18:27.
  • The condition is אִם with the yiqtol אֶמְצָא. The consequence is the weqatal וְנָשָׂאתִי: 'if I find ... I will spare'.
  • The etnaḥta on הָעִיר (18:26.9) divides the verse. The first part is the condition, the second the consequence.
  • נָשָׂא with לְ of the person or place is 'bear with, forgive': here 'spare'.

Ibn Ezra (18:29) rejects the reading that counts the five cities, since the text speaks of Sodom alone; the English 'the whole place' is the city, and Rashi's reading is recorded.

Grammar
  • וַיַּעַן (18:27.1) and וַיֹּאמַר (18:27.3) are two wayyiqtol forms. Together they open the speech, which runs on into 18:28.
  • הוֹאַלְתִּי is a hifil qatal 1cs of יָאַל. Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it as 'I wished', the English 'I have been willing'.
  • הִנֵּה־נָא is an interjection with an entreaty: 'look, please'. The English 'Now, please' keeps both.
  • וְאָנֹכִי עָפָר וָאֵפֶר is verbless: 'and I dust and ashes'. The ו is contrastive, and the English supplies 'am'.

Ancient Near East
  • Dust and ashes belong to the rites of mourning and self-abasement known across the ancient Near East: mourners strewed dust on their heads and sat in ashes, as El does on hearing of Baal's death in the Ugaritic Baal cycle. Abraham names himself by the stuff of those rites.
18:28

Perhaps the fifty righteous will be five short. Will you destroy the whole city for the lack of five?" He said, "I will not destroy if I find there forty-five."

perhaps will-be-lacking fifty the-righteous five will-you-destroy for-five [obj] the-whole-of the-city and-he-said not I-will-destroy if I-find there forty and-five

Grammar
  • הֲתַשְׁחִית (18:28.6) is the interrogative he with the hifil yiqtol 2ms of שָׁחַת. The question is Abraham's protest, addressed to God.
  • יַחְסְרוּן is Qal 2 'be lacking': five are missing from the fifty. The construction with אוּלַי (perhaps) expresses doubt; Abraham does not assert that five are lacking.
  • The etnaḥta on הָעִיר (18:28.10) closes Abraham's question. The reply, וַיֹּאמֶר (18:28.11), begins God's answer.
  • Abraham's speech begins in 18:27 and runs through 18:28, so the English opens the quotation in 18:27 and closes it after 'five?'.

18:29

He spoke to him again and said, "Perhaps forty will be found there." He said, "I will not do it for the sake of the forty."

and-added again to-speak to-him and-said perhaps will-be-found there forty and-said not I-will-do for-the-sake-of the-forty

Grammar
  • וַיֹּסֶף עוֹד לְדַבֵּר is a hifil wayyiqtol of יָסַף with an infinitive: 'went on to speak'. The English gives the adverb 'again'.
  • אוּלַי with the nifal yiqtol יִמָּצְאוּן is a proposal: 'perhaps forty will be found there'. The numeral אַרְבָּעִים, after the verb, is its subject.
  • The answer is לֹא with the yiqtol אֶעֱשֶׂה. The object, destruction, is not written; the English 'I will not do it' keeps the Hebrew's ellipsis.
  • The etnaḥta on אַרְבָּעִים (18:29.9) divides the verse at Abraham's proposal; the answer follows.

The English keeps 'do it' for the ellipsis. Ibn Ezra makes the object 'destruction' explicit (commentary).

Commentary (5)
Rashideclines אוּלַ֛י יִמָּצְא֥וּן שָׁ֖ם אַרְבָּעִ֑ים
Rashi: forty would save four of the cities, thirty three, twenty two, and ten one. Ibn Ezra rejects any count by the five cities, since the text speaks of Sodom alone; the English keeps the plain sense, forty righteous people in Sodom.
Hebrew
וְיִמָּלְטוּ ד' הַכְּרַכִּים וְכֵן ל' יַצִּילוּ ג' מֵהֶם אוֹ כ' יַצִּילוּ ב' מֵהֶם אוֹ י' יַצִּילוּ אֶחָד מֵהֶם:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows לֹ֣א אֶֽעֱשֶׂ֔ה בַּעֲב֖וּר הָאַרְבָּעִֽים׃
Ibn Ezra: 'I will not do' means 'I will not do destruction'. After the tenth and the ninth, Abraham did not go on joining the two lacks, but asked next for a quarter, a third and a half to be lacking (forty to thirty, twenty, ten). Some say he went no lower than ten because there would be two in each of the five cities; this is not right, since he said 'in Sodom' alone. Though the sages taught that there is no public prayer with fewer than ten, this verse too supports that tradition. The English 'I will not do it' follows.

Grammar

18:33

And the LORD went away when he had finished speaking to Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place.

and-went the-LORD as-which finished to-speak to-Abraham and-Abraham returned to-his-place

Grammar
  • The first verb is wayyiqtol (the sequential narrative form, 'and went'); the second half of the verse changes to a disjunctive clause, 'and Abraham returned', with the subject first.
  • The clause 'when he had finished speaking' is circumstantial: kaf and asher make a temporal conjunction, and the piel qatal kilah gives the completed action before the departure.
  • The etnahta on Abraham (18:33.7) divides the verse: the first part is the LORD's departure, the second Abraham's return to his place.
  • The place to which Abraham returns is not named; the commentators identify it (Ibn Ezra: Hebron). See the commentary.

The sense is Qal I.1 'go' (of persons); 'went away' adds only the departure that the context gives. The vision-reading of Radak is in the apparatus.

Rashi's midrash: when the advocate (Abraham) fell silent, the judge (the LORD) went away. The English gives the plain sense of the departure after the speech; the allegory is recorded here.
