Apparatus
  • Onkelos renders the subject as 'the Glory of the LORD' (yeqara d'Adonai); the English keeps 'the LORD', the Hebrew word.
  • Radak (not normative) reads the departure as the end of the prophetic vision: Abraham found himself back in his house where he had been sitting. Sforno: Abraham waited there until the Shekhinah withdrew. Neither is adopted.
19:1

The two angels came to Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting in the gate of Sodom. When Lot saw them, he rose to meet them and bowed down, nose to the ground.

and-came two the-angels to-Sodom in-the-evening and-Lot sitting in-gate-of Sodom and-saw Lot and-rose to-meet-them and-bowed-down nostrils to-the-ground

Grammar
  • The chain of wayyiqtols (came, saw, rose, bowed down) gives the narrative sequence: the arrival, the sighting, the rising and the bowing.
  • The dual shenei (two) with the definite noun 'the angels' is a construct phrase: 'two of the angels' is read as 'the two angels'.
  • yoshev (19:1.7) is a participle: the English 'was sitting' gives the state that Lot is in when the angels arrive.
  • The dual apayim (19:1.15), 'nostrils', is the adverbial accusative of the bowing: 'bowed down, nostrils to the ground'; the hitpael of shaḥah means 'prostrate oneself'.

The English 'he rose to meet them' keeps the subject Lot; the verb 'rose' with the lamed infinitive is a sequence of two actions.

Commentary (13)
Rashinot-applicable שְׁנֵ֨י
Rashi (after the Talmud and Bereshit Rabbah): of the three visitors of 18:2, one went to destroy Sodom, one to save Lot (the same who had come to heal Abraham), and the third, who came to tell Sarah, left once his task was done. A midrash on the errands; the English 'two' is the text's own number.

The English 'angels' is the plain word; Rashi's reasons for the change of term are recorded.

Ancient Near East
  • The city gate was the public space of an ancient town: a roofed or chambered passage where people met, did business and sat in judgment. A man sitting in the gate is a townsman in the public place.
  • Bowing to the ground was the formal greeting to a superior or an honoured guest; it expresses courtesy and respect and is not an act of worship.
Apparatus
  • Targum Onkelos renders the bowing as 'on his face (al apohi) on the ground'; Ibn Ezra takes the dual as the nostrils, and the English follows him. 'Face' (BDB 2) is the other sense.
19:2

And he said, "Here now, my lords, turn aside, please, to your servant's house and spend the night, and wash your feet; then you can rise early and go on your way." But they said, "No, but we will spend the night in the square."

and-said Here now my-lords turn-aside please to house-of your-servant and-spend-the-night and-wash your-feet and-rise-early and-go to-your-way and-said no for in-the-square we-spend-the-night

Grammar
  • The imperatives suru, vilinu and verahatsu (plural) address the men; the vav links the imperatives in a request.
  • Hinneh na is an exclamation with the particle na: 'here now'. The second na (19:2.6) is an exhortation, 'please'.
  • The qatal forms vehishkamtem and vahalakhtem (19:2.13-14) continue the imperatives: 'then you can rise early and go on your way'.
  • lo ... ki (19:2.17-18) is 'No, but': ki is adversative here, as Rashi reads it.

The imperative 'spend the night' (lun) and the yiqtol 'we will spend the night' (19:2.20) use the same verb: the men refuse Lot's offer of a night in his house.

Ancient Near East
  • Washing the feet of a guest was an ordinary act of hospitality in a land of dusty roads and open sandals (see 18:4).
  • A traveller who reached a town at nightfall without a host could spend the night in the open square inside the town; a parallel scene is Judges 19:15-21. Taking a stranger into one's house put him under the host's protection.
Apparatus
  • WLC note v on 19:2.14 (vahalakhtem): one or more vowels in the Leningrad codex are read differently from BHS. The pointing in the pack is followed.
19:3

But he urged them strongly, and they turned aside to him and came into his house. He made a feast for them and baked unleavened bread, and they ate.

and-urged in-them greatly and-turned-aside to-him and-came to-house-of-him and-made for-them feast and-unleavened-cakes baked and-ate

Grammar
  • The wayyiqtols (urged, turned aside, came, made, ate) carry the narrative. The vav of 'urged' is adversative: the men had refused, and Lot presses them.
  • The adverb me'od (19:3.3) intensifies the verb: 'greatly'. The preposition beth on the 3mp suffix gives the object of the urging.
  • The meal is named by two nouns, mishteh and matsot, and one verb, afah: the Hebrew names the feast before the baking. The English reverses the order.

The verb 'turned aside' (vayyasuru) is the same as 19:2.5 'turn aside'. The men who refused the road now turn to Lot's house.

Commentary (8)
Rashirecords וַיָּסֻ֣רוּ אֵלָ֔יו
Rashi: 'they turned aside to him' means they bent the road toward his house (as in his comment at 19:2, that Lot bent the road so as not to be seen). The English 'turned aside to him' is the plain departure from the road; Rashi's crooked-road sense is recorded.

עִקְּמוּ אֶת הַדֶּרֶךְ לְצַד בֵּיתוֹ:

Rashi: the unleavened bread shows that it was Passover. The English keeps 'unleavened bread' and does not name the feast; the Passover reading is recorded here.

פֶּסַח הָיָה:

Ancient Near East
  • Unleavened bread is flat bread baked at once, without waiting for the dough to rise; it was what a host could prepare in a short time for guests who arrived late (see 18:6 for the same hurry). The text does not tie it to a festival; Rashi reads it as Passover.
Apparatus
  • Targum Onkelos (19:3) renders the urging as 'and he pressed them'; the English keeps 'urged' with the adverb 'strongly'.
19:4

Before they lay down, the men of the city, the men of Sodom, surrounded the house, from boys to old men, all the people, from the far edge of the city.

before they-lay-down the-men-of the-city the-men-of Sodom surrounded upon the-house from-youth and-to old all the-people from-end

Grammar
  • Teram with the yiqtol (before they lay down) is a temporal clause. The English uses the past, since the narrative is past.
  • The phrase 'the men of the city, the men of Sodom' is an apposition: the men of the city are the men of Sodom, the wicked.
  • nasabu is nifal (Niph) qatal, 'they surrounded'. The stem gives a middle sense, 'close round the house'.

The verse is a single long sentence: the time clause, the subject and the verb, then the range of ages and the closing phrase.

19:5

And they called to Lot and said to him, "Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, that we may lie with them."

and-called to Lot and-said to-him where the-men who-came to-you the-night bring-them-out to-us and-that-we-know them

Grammar
  • The imperative hotsi (19:5.12) carries the 3mp suffix 'them'; the English gives 'bring them out to us'.
  • The cohortative venedaah (19:5.14) is 'let us know' with the vav of purpose: 'that we may know'. Ibn Ezra calls the verb a euphemism for lying (כנוי לשכיבה); BDB Qal 3, 'know a person'. The English 'lie with' keeps the euphemism.
  • The construction qara' el (19:5.1) means 'call to'. The homograph qara' 'meet' is not used here.

The speech is direct: the men speak to Lot and the English puts it in double quotes. 'Know' is the verb of 19:5.14; the English is the commentators' reading of it.

מְאֹד", שֶׁהָיוּ מַכְעִיסִים וּמוֹרְדִים בְּשַׁלְוָתָם וּבְעִנּוּי הָאֶבְיוֹנִים, וְהוּא שֶׁאָמַר (יחזקאל טז נ) "וַתִּגְבְּהֶינָה וַתַּעֲשֶׂינָה תוֹעֵבָה לְפָנָי וָאָסִיר אֶתְהֶן כַּאֲשֶׁר רָאִיתִי". וְעַל דַּעַת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ (עיין סנהדרין קט) הָיוּ בָּהֶם כָּל מִדּוֹת רָעוֹת, אֲבָל נִגְמַר דִּינָם עַל אוֹתוֹ הֶעָוֹן, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁלֹּא הֶחֱזִיקוּ יַד עָנִי וְאֶבְיוֹן, כִּי הָיוּ תְּדִירִים בְּאוֹתוֹ עָוֹן יוֹתֵר מִכֻּלָּם. וְגַם כִּי כָל הָעַמִּים עוֹשִׂים צְדָקוֹת עִם רֵעֵיהֶם וְעִם עֲנִיֵּיהֶם, לֹא הָיָה בְּכָל הַגּוֹיִם כִּסְדוֹם לְאַכְזָרִיּוּת. וְדַע כִּי מִשְׁפַּט סְדוֹם הָיָה לְמַעֲלַת אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, כִּי הִיא מִכְּלַל נַחֲלַת ה' וְאֵינָהּ סוֹבֶלֶת אַנְשֵׁי תּוֹעֵבוֹת, וְכַאֲשֶׁר תָּקִיא אֶת הַגּוֹי כֻּלּוֹ מִפְּנֵי תּוֹעֲבוֹתָם הִקְדִּימָה וְקָאֲתָה אֶת הָעָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהָיוּ רָעִים מִכֻּלָּם לַשָּׁמַיִם וְלַבְּרִיּוֹת, וְשָׁמְמוּ עֲלֵיהֶם הַשָּׁמַיִם וְהָאָרֶץ וְהֻשְׁחֲתָה הָאָרֶץ בְּלֹא רְפוּאָה לְעוֹלָם, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁבַּעֲבוּר טוֹבָה נִתְגָּאוּ. וְרָאָה הקב"ה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לְאוֹת לִבְנֵי מֶרִי, לְיִשְׂרָאֵל הָעֲתִידִים לְיָרְשָׁהּ, כַּאֲשֶׁר הִתְרָה בָּהֶן "גָּפְרִית וָמֶלַח שְׂרֵפָה כָל אַרְצָהּ כְּמַהְפֵּכַת סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה אַדְמָה וּצְבוֹיִם אֲשֶׁר הָפַךְ ה' בְּאַפּוֹ וּבַחֲמָתוֹ" (דברים כט כב), כִּי יֵשׁ בָּאֻמּוֹת רָעִים וְחַטָּאִים מְאֹד וְלֹא עָשָׂה בָּהֶם כָּכָה, אֲבָל לְמַעֲלַת הָאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת הָיָה הַכֹּל, כִּי שָׁם הֵיכַל ה'. וְעוֹד אֲנִי עָתִיד לְבָאֵר זֶה בְּסֵדֶר אַחֲרֵי מוֹת (ויקרא יח כד), אִם יְחַיֵּנִי הַמֵּמִית וְהַמְּחַיֶּה:
Radakrecords וְנֵדְעָ֖ה אֹתָֽם׃
Radak (not normative): 'who are they, and how did they not fear to come to our city, being strangers?' - that is, they said it to kill them, as ונדעה in the concubine at Gibeah (Judg. 19:22), where the man says 'they meant to kill me' (Judg. 20:5). Some explain it as lying with a male. The English takes Rashi's and Ibn Ezra's sexual sense; Radak's 'kill' is recorded.
Hebrew
מִי הֵם וְאֵיךְ לֹא יָרְאוּ לָבוֹא לְעִירֵנוּ אֲנָשִׁים זְכָרִים, רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר שֶׁאָמְרוּ לְהָרְגָם כְּמוֹ ״וְנֵדְעָה״ דְּפִלֶגֶשׁ בְּגִבְעָה (שופטים יט:כב) וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר הָאִישׁ בְּסַפְּרוֹ הַמַּעֲשֶׂה, ״אוֹתִי דִּמּוּ לְהָרֹג״ (שופטים כ:ה). וְיֵשׁ מְפָרְשִׁים יְדִיעַת מִשְׁכַּב זָכוּר.
Targum Onkelos the whole verse
Hebrew
וּקְרוֹ לְלוֹט וַאֲמָרוּ לֵיהּ אָן גֻּבְרַיָּא דִּי אֲתוֹ לְוָתָךְ לֵילְיָא אַפֵּקִנּוּן לְוָתָנָא וְנִדַּע יָתְהוֹן:
Ancient Near East
  • The demand is for sexual abuse of strangers, which breaks the duty of hospitality; Judges 19:22-25 tells a parallel scene. The verb 'know' with a person as object is the usual Hebrew euphemism for sexual relations, but some commentators (Radak) read it here as 'to question' or 'to do them harm'.
Apparatus
  • Ramban (not normative) says the men's aim was to put an end to the traffic of strangers, as in Sanhedrin 109: they feared that the land's goodness would draw many to it, and they despised charity (Ezek. 16:49). The English follows Ibn Ezra's euphemism for lying.
19:6

Lot went out to them, to the doorway, and shut the door behind him.

and-went-out to-them Lot to-the-doorway and-the-door shut behind-him

Grammar
  • The wayyiqtol 'went out' is followed by the qatal 'shut' in a second clause: the narrative continues with the act of closing.
  • The directional he on petah (19:6.4) gives the place towards which Lot goes: the doorway.
  • The preposition achar with the 3ms suffix gives 'behind him'.

The subject of the shutting is Lot in the English; Radak allows the man inside to have shut it.

Commentary (3)
Ibn Ezranormativefollows הַפֶּ֑תְחָה
Ibn Ezra glosses הַפֶּתְחָה as אל הפתח, 'to the opening', the final he being directional; he adds that the tav of דלת is the sign of the feminine and that the noun is 'found lacking'. A grammatical note; the English 'to the doorway' is the sense he gives.
Hebrew
אל הפתח תי"ו דלת סימן נקבה ונמצא חסר:
Radakrecords סָגַ֥ר אַחֲרָֽיו׃
Radak (not normative): 'shut' may mean that the man inside shut the door, or that Lot shut it from outside. The English gives Lot's act; Radak's alternative is recorded.
Hebrew
סָגַר הַסּוֹגֵר שֶׁהָיָה בִּפְנִים, אוֹ לוֹט סָגַר מִבַּחוּץ.
Targum Onkelos the whole verse
Hebrew
וּנְפַק לְוָתְהוֹן לוֹט לְתַרְעָא וְדָשָׁא אֲחַד בַּתְרוֹהִי:
19:7

And he said, "Please, my brothers, do not act wickedly.

and-said do-not please my-brothers act-wickedly

Grammar
  • al with the yiqtol (19:7.2 and 19:7.5) is a prohibition: 'do not act wickedly'.
  • The particle na (19:7.3) softens the prohibition to a request: 'please'.
  • The hifil of ra'a (19:7.5) carries the sense 'do evil': the English 'act wickedly' takes the second sense listed.

Lot's speech is a plea, not a command: the English 'please' keeps the particle na.

Commentary (3)
Radakfollows אַל נָ֥א
Radak (not normative): 'please' is a request that the men do not harm these people. The English 'please' and the prohibition follow his reading.
Hebrew
בְּבַקָּשָׁה מִכֶּם אַל תָּרֵעוּ לָאֵלֶּה הָאֲנָשִׁים, כִּי
Radakrecords אַחַ֖י
Radak: 'my brothers' means 'my neighbours', and the request is that they leave these men for the sake of his honour. The English keeps 'my brothers', the Hebrew word; the neighbour reading is recorded here.
Hebrew
וּשְׁכֵנַי אַתֶּם וְלִכְבוֹדִי הַנִּיחוּ אוֹתָם.
Targum Onkelosfollows the whole verse
Targum Onkelos renders 'do not act wickedly' as la tav'ishun, 'do not do evil, do not harm'. This is the same sense as the English; it does not mean 'shame'.
Hebrew
וַאֲמַר בְּבָעוּ כְעַן אַחַי לָא תַבְאִישׁוּן:
19:8

Look, please, I have two daughters who have never known a man. Let me bring them out to you now, and do to them as you see fit. Only, to these men do not do anything, since they have come under the shelter of my roof."

look-please to-me two-of daughters who not knew man let-me-bring-out now them to-you and-do to-them as-the-good in-eyes-of-you only to-the-men these not do a-thing for-on-account-of-this came in-shadow-of roof-of-me

Grammar
  • הִנֵּה and נָא open Lot's speech to the men of Sodom: an interjection and an entreaty, 'look' and 'please'. The whole verse is direct speech, so it is set in double quotation marks.
  • יָדְעוּ is a qatal, 3rd plural, with the daughters as subject, and the negative לֹא belongs to it. The verb has the lexicon sense 'know a person', the biblical euphemism for sexual relations. Ibn Ezra notes that the one form serves masculine and feminine plural.
  • אוֹצִיאָה is a cohortative (hifil, 1st singular, 'let me bring out'); the particle נָא comes after it, so the offer is softened by the cohortative and again by נָא. The imperative וַעֲשׂוּ then gives the crowd leave to act.
  • הָאֵל is a short form of הָאֵלֶּה, 'these', and follows its noun: 'the men these' (Ibn Ezra, Rashi).
  • כִּי עַל כֵּן (the lexicon: 'forasmuch as') gives the ground of Lot's plea: the men have come under his roof, so they are not to be harmed. Rashi and Radak read it 'because they came'.
  • The pashta on יָדְעוּ is a minor pause; the zaqef qaton on אִישׁ closes the relative clause, the etnaḥta on בְּעֵינֵיכֶם divides the offer from the protection of the guests, and the silluq on קֹרָתִי ends the verse.

Lot's offer to the crowd is the plain sense of the verse: his daughters in place of his guests. The English keeps the offer as Lot makes it and does not comment on it; the commentators (Ramban, Sforno) discuss his motive.

Commentary (11)
Rashifollows הָאֵל֙
Rashi, like Ibn Ezra, reads הָאֵל as כְּמוֹ הָאֵלֶּה, 'these'.
Hebrew
כְּמוֹ הָאֵלֶּה:
Rashirecords כִּֽי עַל כֵּ֥ן בָּ֖אוּ
Rashi paraphrases the clause as 'you will do this good for my honour, because they came under the shelter of my roof'. The English keeps the causal link and does not add the honour.
Hebrew
כִּי הַטּוֹבָה הַזֹּאת תַּעֲשׂוּ לִכְבוֹדִי עַל אֲשֶׁר בָּאוּ בְּצֵל קֹרָתִי; תַּרְגּוּם בִּטְלַל שָׁרוּתֵי, תַּרְגּוּם שֶׁל קוֹרָה – שָׁרוּתָא:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows יָדְעוּ֙ אִ֔ישׁ
Ibn Ezra says יָדְעוּ is the plural of the past tense used of masculine and feminine alike, with no added vav and the same vowel in both. The English takes the verb with the two daughters as its subject.
Hebrew
לשון רבים ורבות בפעל שעבר בלא תוספות וי"ו פתוח שוה:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows הָאֵל֙
Ibn Ezra: הָאֵל is the same as הָאֵלֶּה, 'these'. The Gaon said it was written so because of the third man who had not come; Ibn Ezra calls that reason remote, since both forms, the short and the long, are found in Aramaic. The English 'these' follows him.
Hebrew
. כמו האלה ויאמר הגאון, כי בעבור השלישי שלא בא אמר כן וזה הטעם רחוק, כי גם שתי הלשונות תמצאם בלשון ארמית:
Ramban אוֹצִֽיאָה נָּ֤א אֶתְהֶן֙ אֲלֵיכֶ֔ם
Hebrew
מִתּוֹךְ שִׁבְחוֹ שֶׁל הָאִישׁ הַזֶּה בָּאנוּ לִידֵי גְּנוּתוֹ, שֶׁהָיָה טוֹרֵחַ מְאֹד עַל אַכְסַנְיָא שֶׁלּוֹ לְהַצִּיל אוֹתָם מִפְּנֵי שֶׁבָּאוּ בְּצֵל קוֹרָתוֹ, אֲבָל שֶׁיְּפַיֵּס אַנְשֵׁי הָעִיר בְּהֶפְקֵר בְּנוֹתָיו – אֵין זֶה כִּי אִם רֹעַ לֵב, שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה עִנְיַן הַזִּמָּה בַּנָּשִׁים מְרֻחָק בְּעֵינָיו, וְלֹא הָיָה עוֹשֶׂה לִבְנוֹתָיו חָמָס גָּדוֹל כְּפִי דַּעְתּוֹ. לְכָךְ אָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ (תנחומא וירא יב), בְּנֹהַג שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם אָדָם מוֹסֵר עַצְמוֹ עַל בְּנוֹתָיו וְעַל אִשְׁתּוֹ, וְהוֹרֵג אוֹ נֶהֱרָג, וְזֶה מוֹסֵר בְּנוֹתָיו לְהִתְעוֹלֵל בָּהֶן. אָמַר לוֹ הקב"ה, לְעַצְמְךָ אַתָּה מְשַׁמְּרָן. וְהִנֵּה לוֹט הָיָה מִתְיָרֵא עֲלֵיהֶם כִּי הָיָה חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁהֵם אֲנָשִׁים, אֲבָל כַּאֲשֶׁר הִכּוּ בַּסַּנְוֵרִים אֶת אַנְשֵׁי הָעִיר וְאָמְרוּ לוֹ "כִּי מַשְׁחִתִים אֲנַחְנוּ אֶת הַמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה וַיְשַׁלְּחֵנוּ ה' לְשַׁחֲתָהּ", אָז הִכִּיר בָּהֶם וְהֶאֱמִין לַעֲשׂוֹת כָּל אֲשֶׁר צִוּוּ. וְדַע וְהָבֵן כִּי עִנְיַן פִּילֶגֶשׁ בַּגִּבְעָה (שופטים יט) אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא נִדְמֶה לָעִנְיָן הַזֶּה אֵינֶנּוּ כָּמוֹהוּ לָרֹעַ, כִּי הָרְשָׁעִים הָהֵם לֹא הָיָה דַּעְתָּם לְכַלּוֹת הָרֶגֶל מִמְּקוֹמָם, אֲבָל הָיוּ שְׁטוּפֵי זִמָּה וְרָצוּ גַּם בְּמִשְׁכַּב הָאִישׁ הָאוֹרֵחַ, וְכַאֲשֶׁר הוֹצִיאוּ אֲלֵיהֶם פִּילַגְשׁוֹ נִתְפַּיְּסוּ בָּהּ. וְהָאִישׁ הַזָּקֵן שֶׁאָמַר לָהֶם "הִנֵּה בִתִּי הַבְּתוּלָה וּפִילַגְשֵׁהוּ אוֹצִיאָה נָּא אוֹתָם וַעֲשׂוּ לָהֶם הַטּוֹב בְּעֵינֵיכֶם" (שם יט כד), יוֹדֵעַ הָיָה שֶׁלֹּא יַחְפְּצוּ בְּבִתּוֹ וְלֹא יַעֲשׂוּ עִמָּהּ רָעָה, וְעַל כֵּן לֹא אָבוּ לִשְׁמֹעַ לוֹ, וְכַאֲשֶׁר הוֹצִיא אֶת פִּילַגְשׁוֹ לְבַדָּהּ שָׁתְקוּ מִמֶּנּוּ. וְהָאִישׁ בַּעַל הַבַּיִת גַּם הָאוֹרֵחַ כֻּלָּם הָיוּ חֲפֵצִים לְהַצִּיל אֶת הָאִישׁ בְּפִילַגְשׁוֹ, כִּי פִּילֶגֶשׁ הָיְתָה לֹא אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ, וּכְבָר זָנְתָה עָלָיו. וּבַפֶּרֶץ הַהוּא עוֹד לֹא הָיוּ בּוֹ כָּל אַנְשֵׁי הָעִיר כַּאֲשֶׁר בִּסְדוֹם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בּוֹ "מִנַּעַר וְעַד זָקֵן כָּל הָעָם מִקָּצֶה", אֲבָל בַּגִּבְעָה נֶאֱמַר וְהִנֵּה "אַנְשֵׁי הָעִיר אַנְשֵׁי בְנֵי בְלִיַּעַל" (שם יט כב) מִקְצָתָם שֶׁהָיוּ שָׂרִים וְתַקִּיפִים בָּעִיר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר הָאִישׁ (שם כ ה) "וַיָּקֻמוּ עָלַי בַּעֲלֵי הַגִּבְעָה", וְעַל כֵּן לֹא מִחוּ הָאֲחֵרִים בְּיָדָם. וְהִנֵּה פִּנּוֹת כָּל הָעָם מִכָּל שִׁבְטֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל רָצוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת גָּדֵר גָּדוֹל בַּדָּבָר לְהָמִית אוֹתָם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (שם כ יג) "וְעַתָּה תְּנוּ אֶת הָאֲנָשִׁים בְּנֵי בְלִיַּעַל אֲשֶׁר בַּגִּבְעָה וּנְמִיתֵם". וְדָבָר בָּרוּר הוּא שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ חַיָּבִין מִיתָה בְּדִין תּוֹרָה, שֶׁלֹּא עָשׂוּ מַעֲשֶׂה זוּלָתִי עִנּוּי הַפִּילֶגֶשׁ הַזּוֹנָה, וְלֹא נִתְכַּוְּנוּ לַמִּיתָה שֶׁלָּהּ, וְגַם לֹא מֵתָה בְּיָדָם, וַיְשַׁלְּחוּהָ מֵאִתָּם כַּעֲלוֹת הַשַּׁחַר, וְהָלְכָה מֵאִתָּם לְבֵית אֲדוֹנֶיהָ וְאַחַר כָּךְ מֵתָה, אוּלַי נֶחְלְשָׁה מֵרֹב הַבִּיאוֹת וְנִתְקָרְרָה בַּפֶּתַח עַד הָאוֹר וּמֵתָה שָׁם. אֲבָל מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהָיוּ חֲפֵצִים וְאוֹמְרִים לַעֲשׂוֹת נְבָלָה כְּאַנְשֵׁי סְדוֹם, רָאוּ הַשְּׁבָטִים לַעֲשׂוֹת סְיָג לַתּוֹרָה, שֶׁלֹּא יֵעָשֶׂה וְלֹא יֵאָמֵר כֵּן בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ "וּנְבַעֲרָה רָעָה מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל" (שם). וְזֶה הַדִּין הוּא מִמָּה שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ (סנהדרין מו), בֵּית דִּין מַכִּין וְעוֹנְשִׁין שֶׁלֹּא מִן הַתּוֹרָה, וְלֹא לַעֲבֹר עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֶלָּא לַעֲשׂוֹת סְיָג לַתּוֹרָה. וְשֵׁבֶט בִּנְיָמִין לֹא הִסְכִּימוּ בְּדָבָר זֶה, שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בָּהֶם חִיּוּב מִיתָה בְּעִנּוּי הַפִּלֶגֶשׁ. וְאוּלַי הִקְפִּידוּ עוֹד בְּנֵי בִּנְיָמִין עַל אֲשֶׁר לֹא שָׁלְחוּ לָהֶם מִתְּחִלָּה, וְעָשׂוּ הַהַסְכָּמָה שֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתָּם. וּלְפִי דַּעְתִּי שֶׁזֶּה עָנְשָׁם שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל לְהִנָּגֵף בַּתְּחִלָּה, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁלֹּא הָיְתָה הַמִּלְחָמָה נַעֲשֵׂית מִן הַדִּין, וְהַגָּדֵר עַצְמוֹ – עַל שֵׁבֶט בִּנְיָמִין הָיָה מוּטָל לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ וְלֹא עֲלֵיהֶם, שֶׁמִּצְוָה עַל הַשֵּׁבֶט לָדוּן אֶת שִׁבְטוֹ (ספרי קמד). וְהִנֵּה שְׁתֵּי הַכִּתּוֹת רְאוּיוֹת לְהֵעָנֵשׁ, כִּי בִּנְיָמִין מַרְשִׁיעַ, שֶׁאֵינוֹ חוֹשֵׁשׁ לְיַסֵּר הָרָעִים וְלֹא לִגְעֹר בָּהֶם כְּלָל, וְיִשְׂרָאֵל עוֹשִׂין מִלְחָמָה שֶׁלֹּא מִן הַדִּין, וְגַם אֶת פִּי ה' לֹא שָׁאֲלוּ בָּזֶה, אֲבָל אָמְרוּ "מִי יַעֲלֶה לָּנוּ בַתְּחִלָּה לַמִּלְחָמָה עַל בְּנֵי בִנְיָמִין" (שופטים כ יח), כִּי מֵעַצְמָם הִסְכִּימוּ לַמִּלְחָמָה עַל כָּל פָּנִים. וְכֵן לֹא שָׁאֲלוּ בְּעִנְיַן הַנִּצּוּחַ "אִם תִּתְּנֵם בְּיָדִי" כִּי בָּטְחוּ בִּזְרוֹעַ בָּשָׂר, שֶׁהָיוּ רַבִּים מְאֹד, כִּי עַתָּה כְּמוֹהֶם עֲשָׂרָה פְּעָמִים וְיוֹתֵר, וְלֹא שָׁאֲלוּ אֶלָּא "מִי יַעֲלֶה לָּנוּ בַתְּחִלָּה", וְהוּא כְּמוֹ גּוֹרָל בֵּינֵיהֶם, אוּלַי הָיָה כָּל שֵׁבֶט אוֹמֵר "לֹא אֶעֱלֶה אֲנִי תְּחִלָּה", אוֹ אוֹמֵר "אֲנִי רִאשׁוֹן", וְהקב"ה הֵשִׁיב כְּפִי שְׁאֵלָתָם "יְהוּדָה בַּתְּחִלָּה", לֵאמֹר כִּי יְהוּדָה הוּא בָּרֹאשׁ לְעוֹלָם, "כִּי בִיהוּדָה בָּחַר ה' לְנָגִיד" (דהי"א כח ד), וּלְכָךְ לֹא אָמַר "יְהוּדָה יַעֲלֶה" כִּשְׁאָר הַמְּקוֹמוֹת (עיין שופטים א ב), כִּי לֹא הִרְשָׁה אוֹתָם, אֲבָל לֹא מְנָעָם וְלֹא אָמַר לָהֶם "לֹא תַעֲלוּ וְלֹא תִלָּחֲמוּ" מִפְּנֵי עָנְשׁוֹ שֶׁל בִּנְיָמִין. וְהִנֵּה הָלַךְ הַשֵּׁם עִם שְׁנֵיהֶם בְּקֶרִי וְהִנִּיחָם לַמִּקְרִים, וּבְנֵי בִּנְיָמִין הָיוּ גִּבּוֹרִים וְעָרֵיהֶם בְּצוּרוֹת, וְהִשְׁחִיתוּ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל הַבּוֹטְחִים בִּזְרוֹעַ בָּשָׂר, וְהוֹסִיפוּ עֹנֶשׁ עַל עָנְשָׁם, כִּי דַּי הָיָה לָהֶם לְהַבְרִיחַ יִשְׂרָאֵל מִן הַגִּבְעָה, וְהֵם הִכּוּ בָּהֶם לְמַשְׁחִית אֵיבַת עוֹלָם וְהִפִּילוּ מֵהֶם עַם רַב וְעָצוּם כ"ב אֲלָפִים. וְהִנֵּה יִשְׂרָאֵל כַּאֲשֶׁר הֻכּוּ מַכָּה רַבָּה נוֹדְעָה לָהֶם שִׁגְגָתָם כִּי עָשׂוּ מִלְחָמָה עִם אֲחֵיהֶם שֶׁלֹּא בִּרְשׁוּת גָּבוֹהַּ וְשֶׁלֹּא כְּדִין תּוֹרָה, וְעַל כֵּן שָׁאֲלוּ בַּיּוֹם הַשֵּׁנִי "הַאוֹסִיף לָגֶשֶׁת לַמִּלְחָמָה עִם בְּנֵי בִנְיָמִן אָחִי" (שם כ כג), וְהִזְכִּירוּ עַתָּה הָאַחְוָה, לִשְׁאֹל אִם הוּא אוֹסֵר עֲלֵיהֶם הַמִּלְחָמָה. וְהַשֵּׁם הִרְשָׁה אוֹתָם עַתָּה בַּיּוֹם הַשֵּׁנִי, וְאָמַר "עֲלוּ אֵלָיו", כִּי עַתָּה מֻתָּר לָהֶם לִדְרֹשׁ דַּם אֲחֵיהֶם הַשָּׁפוּךְ. וְהֵם לֹא שָׁאֲלוּ הַנִּצּוּחַ, כִּי עֲדַיִן הָיוּ בּוֹטְחִים בְּרֻבָּם לְנַצֵּחַ עַל כָּל פָּנִים, וְהַשֵּׁם לֹא בֵּאֵר לָהֶם רַק כִּי הַמִּלְחָמָה מֻתֶּרֶת לָהֶם, וּמִפְּנֵי שֶׁעֲדַיִן לֹא נִתְכַּפֵּר עָנְשָׁם הָרִאשׁוֹן נָפְלוּ מֵהֶם גַּם בַּיּוֹם הַשֵּׁנִי י"ח אֲלָפִים. וּבַיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי גָּזְרוּ תַּעֲנִית וַיָּצוּמוּ וַיִּבְכּוּ לִפְנֵי ה', וְהִקְרִיבוּ עוֹלוֹת לְכַפֵּר עַל הִרְהוּרֵי הַלֵּב אֲשֶׁר בָּטְחוּ בִּזְרֹעָם, וְהִקְרִיבוּ שְׁלָמִים וְהֵם שַׁלְמֵי תּוֹדָה, כִּי רָאוּ עַצְמָם כְּאִלּוּ כֻּלָּם פְּלֵטִים מֵחֶרֶב בִּנְיָמִין, וְזֶה מִשְׁפַּט כָּל הַנִּמְלָטִים לְהַקְרִיב תּוֹדָה, כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (תהלים קז כב) "וְיִזְבְּחוּ זִבְחֵי תוֹדָה וִיסַפְּרוּ מַעֲשָׂיו בְּרִנָּה", וְכָתוּב (שם כז ו) "וְעַתָּה יָרוּם רֹאשִׁי עַל אֹיְבַי סְבִיבוֹתַי וְאֶזְבְּחָה בְאָהֳלוֹ זִבְחֵי תְרוּעָה אָשִׁירָה וַאֲזַמְּרָה לַה'". וְהִנֵּה הָיוּ בִּשְׁנֵי הַיָּמִים הַמֵּתִים מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל אַרְבָּעִים אֶלֶף, וּמִבִּנְיָמִן נָפְלוּ בַּסּוֹף כ"ה אֲלָפִים אַנְשֵׁי חַיִל (שופטים כ לה), וּמֵעִיר מְתֹם עַד כָּל הַנִּמְצָא (שם כ מח) רַבִּים, וְיִתָּכֵן שֶׁיִּהְיוּ ט"ו אֲלָפִים בֵּין אֲנָשִׁים וְנָשִׁים וְהַטַּף, וְהָיָה עֹנֶשׁ שְׁתֵּי הַכִּתּוֹת בְּשָׁוֶה. וּמַה נִּכְבְּדוּ דִּבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ (סנהדרין קג) שֶׁהָיָה הַקֶּצֶף בְּפִסְלוֹ שֶׁל מִיכָה, אָמַר הקב"ה בִּכְבוֹדִי לֹא מְחִיתֶם בִּכְבוֹד בָּשָׂר וָדָם מְחִיתֶם, לוֹמַר בִּכְבוֹדִי לֹא מְחִיתֶם, בִּמְחֻיְּבֵי מִיתָה וּפוֹשְׁטִים יְדֵיהֶם בָּעִקָּר, בִּכְבוֹד בָּשָׂר וָדָם מְחִיתֶם יוֹתֵר מִשּׁוּרַת הַדִּין. וְעַל כֵּן סִכֵּל עֲצַת שְׁתֵּי הַכִּתּוֹת וְאִמֵּץ אֶת לְבָבָם, וְלֹא זָכְרוּ בְּרִית אַחִים. וְאַחַר הַמַּעֲשֶׂה נִתְחָרְטוּ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (שופטים כא ב) "וַיָּבֹא הָעָם בֵּית אֵל וַיֵּשְׁבוּ שָׁם עַד הָעֶרֶב לִפְנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים וַיִּבְכּוּ בְּכִי גָּדוֹל וַיֹּאמְרוּ לָמָה ה' אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הָיְתָה זֹאת בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל לְהִפָּקֵד הַיּוֹם מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל שֵׁבֶט אֶחָד", כִּי הִכִּירוּ טָעוּתָם וְעָנְשָׁם. וְהִנֵּה בְּדֶרֶךְ גְּרָרָא פֵּרַשְׁנוּ עִנְיַן מַהוּתָם, וְאֵינוֹ מְבֹאָר, וְהִזְכַּרְנוּ סִבּוֹתָיו:
Radak הִנֵּה נָ֨א
Hebrew
פֵּרַשׁ: עַתָּה, כְּלוֹמַר הִנֵּה עַתָּה לְהַעֲבִיר יִצְרֵיכֶם שֶׁהוּא לְהָמִית הָאֲנָשִׁים, הִנֵּה אֶמְסֹר לָכֶם שְׁתֵּי בְנוֹתַי וְהַעֲבִירוּ יִצְרֵיכֶם בָּהֶן וְתַעֲנּוּ אוֹתָן כִּי עֲדַיִן
Radak לֹֽא יָדְעוּ֙ אִ֔ישׁ

, אוֹ תַּהַרְגוּן, זֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר
Radak כַּטּ֖וֹב בְּעֵינֵיכֶ֑ם אַל תַּעֲשׂ֣וּ דָבָ֔ר

אַל תַּעֲשׂוּ דָּבָר רָע.
Radak כִּֽי עַל כֵּ֥ן בָּ֖אוּ

כִּי עַל כֵּן שֶׁבָּאוּ לָלוּן בְּצֵל קֹרָתִי, תָּחוּסוּ לִכְבוֹדִי כִּי טוֹב לִי שֶׁתַּעֲנּוּ אֶת בְּנוֹתַי אוֹ תַּהַרְגֵן אִם תִּרְצוּ מִשֶּׁתַּעֲשׂוּ דָּבָר רָע לָאֵלֶּה הָאֲנָשִׁים.

Sforno אוֹצִֽיאָה נָּ֤א אֶתְהֶן֙ אֲלֵיכֶ֔ם
Hebrew
חָשַׁב שֶׁיָּקוּמוּ לוֹקְחֵי בְנוֹתָיו, וְקָאם שָׁאוֹן בֵּינֵיהֶם (הושע י:יד).
Ancient Near East
  • The shelter of the roof-beam (קֹרָה) names the host's protection of a guest who has come under his roof; Lot's plea rests on that duty.
  • Offering one's daughters to a crowd in place of guests recurs in Judges 19:24, where a host makes the same offer; Ramban compares the two cases.
Apparatus
  • הָאֵל (19:8.20) is read as 'these' (הָאֵלֶּה) by Ibn Ezra and Rashi. Ibn Ezra reports the Gaon's reason for the short form, 'because of the third (man) who did not come', and rejects it as remote, since both forms occur in Aramaic.
19:9

And they said, "Get out of the way!" And they said, "This one came to sojourn, and he has set himself up as a judge. Now we will treat you worse than them." And they pressed upon the man, upon Lot, very hard; and they drew near to break the door.

and-said they draw-near further-on and-said they the-one came to-sojourn and-judged judging now we-do-harm to-you more-than-them and-pressed they on-the-man on-Lot exceedingly and-drew-near they to-break the-door

Grammar
  • The two וַיֹּאמְרוּ (wayyiqtol, 3rd plural) open two separate speeches of the crowd. The wayyiqtols וַיִּפְצְרוּ and וַיִּגְּשׁוּ then carry the narrative; וַיִּשְׁפֹּט is inside the speech, 'and he has acted as judge'.
  • The first speech is one command: גֶּשׁ is the imperative of נָגַשׁ, 'draw near', with הָלְאָה, 'further on'. The two together mean 'move on, stand back' (Rashi: draw aside and keep away; Radak: go to another place). Ramban finds the clue in the verb that follows.
  • הָאֶחָד has the article: 'the one', 'this one fellow', said with contempt. The word order puts him first and the verbs follow.
  • The infinitive absolute שָׁפוֹט beside the wayyiqtol וַיִּשְׁפֹּט stresses the verb: 'and he would play the judge'.
  • נָרַע is a hifil imperfect, 1st plural, 'we will do harm'; לְךָ is the one harmed and מֵהֶם is the comparative 'than (to) them'.

The Hebrew says only 'the man' and 'Lot'; the English keeps the name and the phrase 'upon the man, upon Lot' as the repetition of the preposition has it.

Ancient Near East
  • גּוּר, 'sojourn', is the status of a resident alien: a man who settles outside his own kin among strangers, under the protection of the local people but without a native's standing. The crowd's charge is that such a newcomer presumes to judge them; Lot is said to have settled in Sodom in 13:12.
19:10

And the men stretched out their hands, and brought Lot to them, into the house, and shut the door.

and-stretched-out the-men (object) their-hand and-brought-in (object) Lot to-them housewards and-(object) the-door shut

Grammar
  • The two wayyiqtols וַיִּשְׁלְחוּ and וַיָּבִיאוּ carry the narrative; the third verb, סָגָרוּ, is a qatal with its object set first: 'and the door they shut', a closing act that goes with the bringing in.
  • הַבָּיְתָה is the directional form of בַּיִת; the ending marks motion, 'into the house'.
  • The etnaḥta on הַבָּיְתָה divides the verse; the tipḥa on אֲלֵיהֶם only separates the words within the second clause.
  • The verse ends with the silluq on סָגָרוּ.

The men who took Lot in are the two visitors of verse 1; the text calls them 'men' here and does not name them.

Targum Onkelosfollows the whole verse

19:11

And the men who were at the entrance of the house they struck with blindness, from the least to the greatest; and they wore themselves out searching for the entrance.

and-the-men who at-entrance-of the-house they-struck with-blindness from-small to-great and-they-wore-out to-find the-entrance

Grammar
  • The subject of הִכּוּ is the two visitors; the men struck are the men of Sodom 'at the entrance of the house'. The object is set first, with the particle אֶת, before the verb.
  • The pair מִקָּטֹן וְעַד־גָּדוֹל, 'from small to great', is a fixed phrase for all of the people, of every age and rank.
  • The wayyiqtol וַיִּלְאוּ continues the sequence, and its infinitive לִמְצֹא states what they wearied themselves over: they could not find the entrance.
  • The verse ends with the silluq on הַפָּתַח; the entrance is named twice, first as a place and then as the thing sought.

סַנְוֵרִים is rare; the English 'blindness' follows the lexicon and Rashi. Ibn Ezra's 'darkening of the eye and of the heart' is recorded in the commentary.

Apparatus

19:12

And the men said to Lot, "If you have anyone else here, a son-in-law, your sons, your daughters, and all that you have in the city, bring them out of this place.

and-said the-men to-Lot still who to-you here a-son-in-law and-your-sons and-your-daughters and-all which to-you in-the-city bring-out from the-place

Grammar
  • עוֹד מִי לְךָ פֹּה is an idiom: literally 'still who to you here', 'who else do you have here'. Rashi (his plain sense) and Radak take it as a question; Ibn Ezra paraphrases it as a condition, 'if you have a son-in-law', and the English follows him.
  • The list runs חָתָן (singular), בָּנֶיךָ, בְּנֹתֶיךָ (plural), then כֹּל אֲשֶׁר־לְךָ בָּעִיר, 'all that is yours in the city'. It stands before the verb as one long object, and הוֹצֵא then governs the whole list.
  • הוֹצֵא is a hifil imperative, 2nd masculine singular, addressed to Lot; the object is the list before it.
  • The etnaḥta on בָּעִיר divides the list from the command; the silluq on הַמָּקוֹם ends the verse.

The English reads the condition (Ibn Ezra) and keeps 'your sons' as the Hebrew has it. Ibn Ezra's 'sons-in-law who are as sons' and the reading of Rashi and Radak, 'the sons of your married daughters' (Lot has no sons), are recorded in the apparatus and the commentary.

Apparatus
  • ובניך (19:12.10) is 'your sons'. Ibn Ezra reads 'sons-in-law who are as your sons and daughters'; Rashi and Radak, 'the sons of your married daughters', since Lot had no sons (Radak). The English keeps 'your sons', the plain word.
19:13

For we are about to destroy this place, because their outcry has grown great before the LORD, and the LORD sent us to destroy it."

for destroying we the-place this for has-grown-great their-outcry before the-presence-of the-LORD and-sent-us the-LORD to-destroy-it

Grammar
  • כִּי opens two causal clauses: 'for we are about to destroy' and 'for their outcry has grown great'.
  • The participle מַשְׁחִתִים is a hifil, with the speakers as subject; the participle with the pronoun states an action under way or about to begin.
  • גָּדְלָה is a qatal with the feminine subject צַעֲקָתָם, and the verb agrees with its subject.
  • The verse ends with the silluq on לְשַׁחֲתָהּ; the feminine suffix refers to the city (עִיר, v. 12), not to the masculine מָקוֹם; Radak says the city is included in 'the place'.

The English keeps 'their outcry' as the Hebrew has it; Radak's reading (the cry of the oppressed against them) fits the same words and is recorded.

Commentary (4)
Radakrecords כִּֽי גָדְלָ֤ה צַעֲקָתָם֙
Radak says 'their outcry' is the cry of the oppressed who call out against those people, the suffix being the object of the cry. The English keeps the literal words, which cover this reading.

Ancient Near East
  • צְעָקָה, 'outcry', is the cry of the wronged appealing for redress; in 18:20–21 the same kind of outcry from Sodom and Gomorrah is what brings the LORD to look into the cities.
19:14

And Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, who had married his daughters, and said, "Get up, get out of this place, for the LORD is destroying the city." But to his sons-in-law he seemed like a man joking.

and-went-out Lot and-spoke to-sons-in-law-of-him takers-of daughters-of-him and-said get-up go-out from-the-place this for destroying the-LORD the-city and-was as-one-joking in-eyes-of sons-in-law-of-him

Grammar
  • וַיֵּצֵא, וַיְדַבֵּר, and וַיֹּאמֶר are wayyiqtols: Lot goes out, speaks, and says; וַיְהִי then carries the narrator's comment.
  • לֹקְחֵי בְנֹתָיו is a participle in the construct plural, 'takers of his daughters'. A participle has no tense of its own: 'who had married' follows Ibn Ezra and Radak (already taken); Rashi's betrothal reading would be 'who were to take'.
  • קוּמוּ and צְּאוּ are two plural imperatives addressed to the sons-in-law; the reason follows in a clause with the participle מַשְׁחִית.
  • וַיְהִי כִמְצַחֵק: 'he was like one jesting' (piel participle of צָחַק, BDB 'jest'), 'in the eyes of' his sons-in-law, that is, in their view.
  • The etnaḥta on הָעִיר ends Lot's words and the narrator's line follows; the silluq on חֲתָנָיו closes the verse.

The English says only 'his daughters' and does not say which daughters; Ibn Ezra holds that Lot had two other daughters, who died in Sodom, besides the two of verse 15; Rashi adds a betrothal reading for the two at home. The English follows Ibn Ezra and Radak that the men had already married.

Ancient Near East
  • A betrothed woman was treated in law as already married (Deuteronomy 22:23-24). The 'takers' of this verse may be men with a betrothal, so the status of the daughters is a question for the commentators.
Apparatus
  • לֹקְחֵי בְנֹתָיו (19:14.6–7): Ibn Ezra and Radak take the men as already married to daughters of Lot; Ibn Ezra adds that these were two daughters other than the two found at home (v. 15). Rashi also has the two at home betrothed to them. The English 'had married' follows the first.
19:15

As the dawn rose, the angels urged Lot, saying, "Get up, take your wife and your two daughters who are here, lest you be swept away in the guilt of the city."

and-as the-dawn rose and-urged the-angels in-Lot saying rise take (object) your-wife and-(object) two-of your-daughters the-ones-found lest be-swept-away in-iniquity-of the-city

Grammar
  • וּכְמוֹ הַשַּׁחַר עָלָה is a clause of time: 'and as the dawn rose'. Ibn Ezra defends the construction against R. Jonah's objection.
  • The wayyiqtol וַיָּאִיצוּ, with the subject the angels, introduces the speech with the infinitive לֵאמֹר, 'saying'.
  • קוּם and קַח are two imperatives; the two objects, 'your wife' and 'your two daughters', are the people to be taken out.
  • The participle הַנִּמְצָאֹת is nifal, feminine plural, agreeing with 'your daughters': 'who are found, who are here'. Ibn Ezra's reading of the previous verse takes it to imply other daughters who were not there.
  • The verse ends with the silluq on הָעִיר; the lest-clause (פֶּן with the imperfect) gives the danger.

The angels are called 'the men' in verses 10-12 and 'the angels' here; the verse marks the change. The English follows the Hebrew noun and keeps 'urged' for the verb.

כְּדֵי שֶׁתְּהֵא פּוּרְעָנוּתָם בִּזְרִיחַת הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ אֱלֹהֵיהֶם הַגָּדוֹל, כְּאָמְרָם זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (ברכות ז.) בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁהַחַמָּה זוֹרַחַת וְכָל מַלְכֵי מִזְרָח וּמַעֲרָב מַנִּיחִין כִּתְרֵיהֶן עַל רָאשֵׁיהֶם וּמִשְׁתַּחֲוִים לַחַמָּה, מִיָּד כּוֹעֵס.
19:16

He lingered; then the men took hold of his hand, his wife's hand and the hands of his two daughters, in the LORD's compassion for him; they brought him out and set him down outside the city.

and-lingered and-took-hold the-men in-hand-of-him and-in-hand-of-his-wife and-in-hand-of two-of-his-daughters in-compassion-of the-LORD upon-him and-brought-him-out and-set-him-down from-outside to-the-city

Grammar
  • The verbs are wayyiqtols, a chain of sequential past actions: he lingered (hitpalpel), they took hold (hifil), they brought him out (hifil), they set him down (hifil). The first has no stated subject (Lot is understood); the later ones are the men (3mp).
  • The Hebrew has the singular yad each time: 'in the hand of him', 'in the hand of his wife', 'in the hand of his two daughters'. Bet after the hifil of חָזַק means 'take hold of', so the men took hold of three hands.
  • The shalshelet on וַיִּתְמַהְמָהּ (19:16.1) is a rare accent, traditionally taken to mark hesitation, which suits the lingering. The etnaḥta on עָלָיו (19:16.12) divides the verse between the holding and the leading out.
  • 'In the compassion of the LORD upon him' is a bet phrase; bet can mean 'by' or 'while'. Ramban gives both readings, and the English 'in' keeps both open.
  • The suffixes of וַיֹּצִאֻהוּ and וַיַּנִּחֻהוּ are the object 'him'; Radak takes the singular to cover Lot, his wife and his daughters (compare the plural 'them' at 19:17).

The English says only that the men took hold of the hands and led the family out. Ibn Ezra's reason for the grip (Lot was afraid and without strength to flee), Ramban's (the men pulled him by force to hurry him) and the motive for the delay (Rashi and Radak: Lot was loath to leave his property; Sforno: sloth and an alarmed spirit) are commentary and are kept out of the English line. 'In the LORD's compassion' keeps the Hebrew bet, which Ramban reads either as 'by' (not by his merit) or as 'while' the compassion was still on him.

Commentary (12)
Rashirecords וַֽיִּתְמַהְמָ֓הּ
Rashi gives the purpose of the delay as saving his property (kedei lehatsil et mamono). The English does not state a motive; Rashi's reason is recorded.
Hebrew
כְּדֵי לְהַצִּיל אֶת מָמוֹנוֹ:
Rashirecords וַיַּחֲזִ֨יקוּ
Rashi (Bereshit Rabbah): one of the two was sent to save Lot and the other to overturn Sodom; therefore the text says 'and he said' (singular, 19:17) and not 'and they said'. A midrash on the singular verb of 19:17; the English 'he said' keeps the Hebrew number.
Hebrew

Ibn Ezra rejects the commentary of Ben Ephraim, who derived וַיִּתְמַהְמָהּ from מָה ('what'): he forgot that both heh's are sounded (mappiq). It is a word of delay (עִכּוּב); its root is triliteral and the first radical is doubled. The English 'lingered' follows him.

מהפירוש שחבר בן אפרים שאמר כי ויתמהמה מגזרת מה, והנה שכח כי שני הההי"ן מפיקין, רק הוא לשון עכוב ושרשו משולש והפ"א כפול:

19:17

As they brought them outside, he said, "Escape for your life; do not look back, and do not stop anywhere in the plain. Escape to the mountain, lest you be swept away."

and-it-came-about as-their-bringing-out them to-the-outside and-said he: escape for-your-life not look after-you and-not stand in-all the-plain to-the-mountain escape lest you-be-swept-away

Grammar
  • The clause 'as they brought them outside' is a temporal clause: wayehi with the ke-infinitive. The main verb is the next wayyiqtol, vayyomer, 'said'.
  • The speech has four commands: two imperatives (himmalet, both nifal) and two prohibitions (al with the jussives tabbit and ta'amod). Each is followed by its reason or its object.
  • Address is singular throughout: 'escape for your life', 'do not look back', 'your' (2ms). Ibn Ezra explains that the singular covers Lot with all that is his (commentary).
  • The etnahta on hakikkar (19:17.15) divides the speech: the prohibitions in the plain come before it, the command to the mountain after it.
Commentary (16)
Rashirecords הִמָּלֵ֣ט עַל נַפְשֶׁ֔ךָ
Rashi: 'it is enough for you to save lives (נְפָשׁוֹת); do not take pity on the property.' A paraphrase of 'for your life' that adds a warning against property; the English 'for your life' keeps the plain words.
Hebrew

Rashinot-applicable אַל תַּבִּ֣יט אַחֲרֶ֔יךָ
Rashi: Lot was condemned along with the others and saved for Abraham's merit, and he is not fit to look at their punishment. A homily on the prohibition; not the plain sense.
Hebrew

Rashifollows בְּכׇל הַכִּכָּ֑ר
Rashi identifies the kikkar as the plain of the Jordan (kikkar ha-Yarden). The English keeps 'the plain' and the context note records the place.

Rashi: 'the mountain' is where Abraham was; Lot flees to Abraham, who had dwelt on the mountain and whose tents reached to Hebron. The English keeps the general sense of the hills; Rashi's identification is recorded.

Ancient Near East
  • The kikkar is the plain of the Jordan, where the cities stood; the text calls them 'the cities of the kikkar' (Genesis 13:10–12).
  • The Hebrew word kikkar means 'round': it is also a round loaf and a round weight of metal (a talent); as a place it is a round district. Where the cities of the plain lay is disputed: proposals put them south of the Dead Sea or at its northern end.
19:18

Then Lot said to them, "No, please, my lords.

and-said Lot to-them: no please my-lords

Grammar
  • The etnahta on the word 'to them' (19:18.3) divides the verse: Lot's speech follows it.
  • The reply begins with al, the negation, and na, the entreaty: 'no, please'. It answers the command of 19:17 to flee; the content is understood from there.
  • The final adonai has the qamats of a pausal form, which is why its reading is disputed: profane 'my lords' for the men (Ibn Ezra, Radak), or the sacred name (Rashi, commentary).
Commentary (9)
Rashirecords אַל נָ֖א אֲדֹנָֽי׃
Rashi, following the Talmud (Shevuot 35), takes adonai here as the sacred name, the one with power to kill and to give life, and renders its Targum as 'please, Lord'. The English 'my lords' follows Ibn Ezra; Rashi's sacred reading is recorded.

Rashi: 'al na means 'do not say to me to flee to the mountain'. He reads the al as a refusal, as Ibn Ezra does.

Rashi: na is a word of request. The English 'please' follows.

לְשׁוֹן בַּקָּשָׁה:

Samuel the Nagid derived אַל נָא from הוֹאֵל ('be willing'); in Ibn Ezra's opinion it is like לֹא: when they said 'escape to the mountain', Lot answered 'not so, my masters' (לא כן רבותי). The English 'No, please, my lords' follows him.

חול ונקמץ בעבור שהוא סוף פסוק ויאמר ר' שמואל הספרדי הנגיד ז"ל כי אל נא מגזרת הואל ועל דעתי שהוא כמו לא כי כשאמרו לו ההרה המלט השיב לא כן רבותי:

The English 'my lords' follows Radak.

וַאֲמַר לוֹט לְהוֹן בְּבָעוּ כְעַן רִבּוֹנָי (נ"י יְיָ):
Apparatus
  • אֲדֹנָי with qamats (19:18.6): the Sages (Shevuot) and Rashi take it as the sacred name, 'my Lord', addressed to God; Ibn Ezra and Radak take it as profane, a pausal form of אֲדֹנַי 'my lords', addressed to the two men. The Targum is cited on both sides: Rashi reads it as 'please, O LORD', Radak as 'my master' (ribboni); some witnesses of Onkelos read the divine name. The English follows Ibn Ezra.
19:19

Look, please, your servant has found favour in your eyes, and you have shown great kindness to me by saving my life. But I cannot escape to the mountain, lest the disaster overtake me and I die.

look-please has-found your-servant favour in-your-eyes and-you-made-great your-kindness which you-did with-me to-keep-alive my-life and-I not I-am-able to-escape to-the-mountain lest it-cling-to-me the-evil and-I-die

Grammar
  • The speech moves from entreaty (hinneh na, 'look, please') to a qatal, 'has found', and then to a wayyiqtol, 'and you made great', which continues the same past.
  • The address is singular throughout: 'your servant', 'your eyes', 'you did', 'you made great'. Lot speaks to one of the two angels, the greater (Ibn Ezra, Radak; commentary).
  • The etnaḥta on נַפְשִׁי (19:19.14) divides the speech: the thanks come before it, the plea after it. The vav with the pronoun in 'but I' marks the turn.
  • After pen the imperfect תִּדְבָּקַנִי (with pataḥ under the qof, where Radak notes that tsere would be expected) gives the feared event, and the weqatal וָמַתִּי continues it as its result: 'lest ... and I die'.
Commentary (5)
Rashinot-applicable פֶּן תִּדְבָּקַ֥נִי הָרָעָ֖ה
Rashi: 'lest disaster overtake me': when I was among the men of Sodom the Holy One saw my deeds and theirs and I seemed righteous and worthy to be saved; but when I come near a righteous man I am like a wicked man, as the woman of Zarephath said to Elijah, 'you came to me to bring my iniquity to remembrance' (1 Kings 17:18). A midrash on why Lot fears; not the plain sense.
Hebrew
כְּשֶׁהָיִיתִי אֵצֶל אַנְשֵׁי סְדוֹם הָיָה הַקָּבָּ"ה רוֹאֶה מַעֲשַׂי וּמַעֲשֵׂה בְנֵי הָעִיר, וְהָיִיתִי נִרְאֶה צַדִּיק וּכְדַאי לְהִנָּצֵל, וּכְשֶׁאָבֹא אֵצֶל צַדִּיק אֲנִי כְרָשָׁע, וְכֵן אָמְרָה הַצָּרְפִית לְאֵלִיָּהוּ בָּאתָ אֵלַי לְהַזְכִּיר אֶת עֲוֹנִי (מלכים א י"ז), עַד שֶׁלֹא בָאתָ אֶצְלִי הָיָה הַקָּבָּ"ה רוֹאֶה מַעֲשַׂי וּמַעֲשֵׂה עַמִּי, וַאֲנִי צַדֶּקֶת בֵּינֵיהֶם, וּמִשֶּׁבָּאתָ אֶצְלִי, לְפִי מַעֲשֶׂיךָ אֲנִי רְשָׁעָה:
Rambanrecords וְאָנֹכִ֗י לֹ֤א אוּכַל֙ לְהִמָּלֵ֣ט הָהָ֔רָה פֶּן תִּדְבָּקַ֥נִי הָרָעָ֖ה
Ramban on Lot's words: 'lest the disaster overtake me while I am in the plain, for you will give me only a little time, as you said "hurry, escape"'. He then turns to the ban on looking back (19:17): Ibn Ezra took it as said to Lot and all that is his; Ramban holds that the angel warned them from his knowledge that harm would come from the sight, and warned Lot for his merit; Rashi's reason (Lot is not fit to see their punishment); and a further reason, that seeing a plague or contagion harms and clings, as the sight of water harms one bitten by a mad dog (Yoma); hence Lot's wife became a pillar of salt. He suggests that the destroying angel was seen in a flame between earth and heaven, as David saw one (1 Chronicles 21:16), and cites Pirkei deRabbi Eliezer: Lot's wife looked back for her married daughters and saw the back of the Shekhinah. The English states none of these causes.

19:20

Look, please, this city is near enough to flee there, and it is small. Let me escape there, please. Is it not small? And I will live."

look-please the-city this near to-flee thither and-it small let-me-escape please thither is-not small it and-may-live my-life

Grammar
  • The speech has two na's: hinneh na ('look, please') opens the plea, and na after the cohortative אִמָּלְטָה is the request ('let me escape, please'). Radak notes that אִמָּלְטָה is accented on the last syllable (milra), unlike 1 Samuel 20:29, where the accent is on the first.
  • The question 'is it not small?' (ha-lo, with מִצְעָר at 19:20.14) expects the answer yes. The repeated מִצְעָר is the argument: a small city should be spared.
  • The etnaḥta on מִצְעָר (19:20.9) divides the speech: the city's nearness and smallness come first, the request after.
  • The closing וּתְחִי נַפְשִׁי is a yiqtol 3fs of the qal of חָיָה, agreeing with the feminine נֶפֶשׁ; after the cohortative it gives the result of the request, 'that I may live'. Rashi adds 'in it' and Radak 'with them'; the English adds neither.
Commentary (11)
Rashirecords הָעִ֨יר הַזֹּ֧את קְרֹבָ֛ה
Rashi (after Shabbat): קְרוֹבָה is 'its settlement is recent' (קְרוֹבָה יְשִׁיבָתָהּ): the city was settled lately, so its measure of sin was not yet full. By his count there were fifty-two years from the Dispersion to the overturning, and Zoar was settled a year after Sodom and its neighbours, which he finds in נָא (numerical value fifty-one). A midrashic chronology; the English takes קָרֹב of distance, as Radak does.

Ancient Near East
  • Genesis 14:2 names the cities of the plain as Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Bela, and says that Bela is Zoar. Radak notes the earlier name.
Apparatus
  • 19:20.8: the WLC reads vehi (וְהִ֣יא); the base text has vehu (וְהִ֣וא). No difference of sense.

19:21

He said to him, "See, I have granted your request in this matter too, so as not to overturn the city you have spoken of.

and-said to-him see I-have-lifted-up your-face also to-the-matter this so-that-not my-overturning the-city which you-spoke

Grammar
  • The idiom nasa' panim, 'lift up the face', is the Hebrew for granting a request; the English 'granted your request' renders it, and the literal line keeps the face.
  • The purpose clause lebiltî hafkhi (with the infinitive) states what the grant serves: the city is not overturned.
  • The infinitive hafkhi carries the 1cs suffix: the speaker's own overturning. Rashi reads it as 'I overturn' (commentary).
  • The relative clause asher dibbarta returns to the city Lot named in 19:20; the English adds 'of' for the English link.
Commentary (4)
Rashirecords גַּ֖ם לַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֑ה
Rashi reads 'also in this matter' as 'not only will you be saved, but I will spare the whole city for your sake'. The English keeps 'in this matter too', the word gam with its object; Rashi's reading is recorded.

לֹא דַּיְּךָ שֶׁאַתָּה נִצָּל, אֶלָּא אַף כָּל הָעִיר אַצִּיל בִּגְלָלְךָ:
Rashifollows הׇפְכִּ֥י
Rashi: הָפְכִּי is 'hofekh ani', 'I overturn' (my overturning), like 'עַד בֹּאִי', 'אַחֲרֵי רֹאִי' and 'מִדֵּי דַבְּרִי בּוֹ': an infinitive with the first-person suffix as subject. The English 'so as not to overturn' takes the speaker as the agent.
Hebrew
הוֹפֵךְ אֲנִי, כְּמוֹ עַד בֹּאִי (בראשית מ"ח), אַחֲרֵי רֹאִי (בראשית ט״ז:י״ג), מִדֵּי דַבְּרִי בּוֹ (ירמיהו ל"א):
Radaknot-applicable וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֔יו הִנֵּה֙ נָשָׂ֣אתִי פָנֶ֔יךָ
Radak: God allows the angels to add to or subtract a little from their commission, as they judge. A remark on the angels' discretion; not the plain sense of the words.
Hebrew
נִרְאֶה מִזֶּה כִּי כְּשֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שׁוֹלֵחַ מַלְאָךְ, נוֹתֵן לָהֶם רְשׁוּת לְהוֹסִיף אוֹ לִגְרֹעַ מְעַט מִשְּׁלִיחוּתָם, כְּפִי אֲשֶׁר יִרְאוּ וְיָבִינוּ, כִּי בַּעֲלֵי שֵׂכֶל הֵם.
Targum Onkelosfollows the whole verse
Targum Onkelos renders the idiom as 'I have received (נְסֵיבִית) your face' and 'the city which you spoke' as 'the city of which you asked (דִּבְעֵיתָא עֲלַהּ)'. The English follows the idiom in sense.
Hebrew
וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ הָא נְסֵיבִית אַפָּךְ אַף לְפִתְגָּמָא הָדֵין בְּדִיל דְּלָא לְמֵהְפַּךְ יָת קַרְתָּא דִּבְעֵיתָא עֲלַהּ:
19:22

Hurry, escape there, for I cannot do anything until you arrive there." Therefore he called the name of the city Zoar.

hurry escape thither for not I-am-able to-do thing until your-coming thither upon-so he-called name-of the-city Zoar

Grammar
  • Two imperatives, piel maher and nifal malat, come first; the reason follows with ki and a negated yiqtol.
  • The speaker says 'I cannot' in the singular. Rashi takes this as the one angel who overturns, while the other saves: two angels are not sent on one matter (commentary).
  • The name tso'ar is a play on mitz'ar, 'small' (19:20). The Hebrew makes the link; the English gives the name and the note states the link.
  • The verse ends with a merkha on qara' (19:22.14) and a silluq on Zoar; the naming sentence is the closing clause of the segment.

The Hebrew verb is active, 'he called'; no subject is named. The English keeps the active voice and leaves the subject open. The name Zoar (צוֹעַר) is tied to מִצְעָר 'small' of 19:20 (Rashi); its earlier name was Bela (14:2, Radak).

Commentary (6)
Rashinot-applicable כִּ֣י לֹ֤א אוּכַל֙ לַעֲשׂ֣וֹת
Rashi: this is the punishment of the angels, who said 'we are destroyers' and attributed the matter to themselves, so they did not move until they had to say that the matter was not in their power. A homily; not the plain sense.
Hebrew

לְשׁוֹן יָחִיד; מִכָּאן אַתָּה לָמֵד שֶׁהָאֶחָד הוֹפֵךְ וְהָאֶחָד מַצִּיל, שֶׁאֵין ב' מַלְאָכִים נִשְׁלָחִים לְדָבָר א':

Radak: 'for I cannot' means 'for I was commanded not to overturn until you are saved'. The English 'until you arrive there' follows him.

כִּי כֵן צֻוֵּיתִי שֶׁלֹּא לַהֲפֹךְ עַד שֶׁתִּנָּצֵל.
Radakrecords קָרָ֥א

הַקּוֹרֵא שֵׁם הָעִיר צוֹעַר, כִּי בֶּלַע הָיָה שְׁמָהּ מִתְּחִלָּה.

Targum Onkelos: 'I cannot do the matter until you come there'. The English follows the sense.

אוֹחִי לְאִשְׁתֵּזֵב תַּמָּן אֲרֵי לָא אִכּוּל לְמֶעְבַּד פִּתְגָּמָא עַד מֵיתָךְ לְתַמָּן עַל כֵּן קְרָא שְׁמָא דְקַרְתָּא צוֹעַר:
19:23

The sun rose over the earth as Lot came to Zoar.

the-sun went-out upon the-earth and-Lot came Zoar-ward

Grammar
  • Two clauses, each with a qatal: the sun rose; Lot came. The second is a circumstantial clause, vav with a noun subject, so the English uses 'as'.
  • The etnahta on ha-arets (19:23.4) divides the verse: the sunrise first, then Lot's arrival.
Commentary (2)
Radakrecords הַשֶּׁ֖מֶשׁ וְל֖וֹט בָּ֥א צֹֽעֲרָה׃
Radak: when Lot came to Zoar, the angel sent the rain by God's command. He reads the arrival as the point at which the destruction begins. The English keeps the two clauses simultaneous; Radak's sequence is recorded.
Hebrew
וְכֵיוָן שֶׁבָּא לְצֹעַר הִמְטִיר הַמַּלְאָךְ בִּשְׁלִיחוּת הָאֵל.
Targum Onkelosfollows the whole verse
Targum Onkelos: 'the sun went out upon the earth, and Lot came to Zoar'. The English follows the sense.
Hebrew
שִׁמְשָׁא נְפַק עַל אַרְעָא וְלוֹט עַל לְצוֹעַר:
19:24

The LORD rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah brimstone and fire, from the LORD, from the heavens.

and-the-LORD rained on Sodom and-on Gomorrah brimstone and-fire from-with the-LORD from the-heavens

Grammar
  • The clause opens with the subject, and the qatal הִמְטִיר follows it. The qatal states the act as complete, and the narrative past is 'rained'.
  • The verb is hifil of מָטַר, a denominative of 'rain'. The hifil means to cause rain to fall, and עַל names the places on which it fell.
  • The etnaḥta on וָאֵשׁ marks the main division of the verse. The second half, מֵאֵת יְהוָה מִן הַשָּׁמָיִם, gives the origin twice, first with the idiom מֵאֵת and then with מִן.
  • The two origin phrases are parallel: מֵאֵת יְהוָה and מִן הַשָּׁמָיִם. The English keeps both, so the reader sees the same double statement.

The English repeats 'the LORD' for מֵאֵת יְהוָה, as the Hebrew does. Ibn Ezra takes the repetition as elegant style (לשון צחות) for 'from him'; the English keeps the name so that the repetition he describes is visible. The decisions do not themselves require the name to be kept.

Rashi ties the time of the rain to the rising of dawn and gives a midrash on sun and moon. The English does not adopt it, and it does not bear on the plain sense.

Rashirecords the whole verse
Rashi: at first it was rain (בַּתְּחִלָּה מָטָר), and it became brimstone and fire. The English keeps the plain verb 'rained' and records his change of substance.
Hebrew
בַּתְּחִלָּה מָטָר, וְנַעֲשָׂה גָּפְרִית וָאֵשׁ:
Rashifollows מֵאֵ֥ת יְהֹוָ֖ה
Rashi: it is the way of Scripture to speak so: 'wives of Lamech' and not 'my wives'; David says 'take with you the servants of your lord' and not 'my servants'; Ahasuerus has it written 'in the name of the king' and not 'in my name'. So here 'from the LORD' and not 'from me': God speaks of himself by name. The English keeps the third person.
Hebrew

Rashi cites Job 36 and the manna of Exodus 16 on the way God sends punishment and gifts from heaven. This is a homily on God's ways and does not bear on the words.
Hebrew
הוּא שֶׁאָמַר הַכָּתוּב כִּי בָם יָדִין עַמִּים וְגוֹ' (איוב ל"ו), כְּשֶׁבָּא לְיַסֵּר הֵבְּרִיוֹת מֵבִיא עֲלֵיהֶם אֵשׁ מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁעָשָׂה לִסְדוֹם, וּכְשֶׁבָּא לְהוֹרִיד הַמָּן מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם הִנְנִי מַמְטִיר לָכֶם לֶחֶם מִן הַשָּׁמָיִם (שמות ט"ז):
Ibn Ezranormativefollows מֵאֵ֥ת
Ibn Ezra: מֵאֵת ה' is an elegant turn of speech (לשון צחות); the sense is מֵאִתּוֹ, 'from him'. He adds that one finds 'the children of Israel' several times in a single verse. The English repeats 'the LORD', as the Hebrew does, and so follows him: it is the LORD who rains, and the repeated name is style, not a second person.

"מֵאֵת ה'" וְלֹא כָּתַב מֵאִתּוֹ, דֶּרֶךְ מִקְרָאוֹת לְדַבֵּר כֵּן, "נְשֵׁי לֶמֶךְ" (בראשית ד':כ"ג) וְלֹא אָמַר נָשַׁי, וְדָוִד אָמַר "קְחוּ עִמָּכֶם מֵעַבְדֵי אֲדֹנֵיכֶם" (מלכים א א לג) וְלֹא אָמַר מֵעֲבָדַי, וַאֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ "כִּתְבוּ בְּשֵׁם הַמֶּלֶךְ" (אסתר ח ח) וְלֹא אָמַר בִּשְׁמִי. וַאֲנִי תָּמֵהַּ עַל הָרַב זַ"ל שֶׁכָּתַב מִן הַהַגָּדוֹת דֵּעוֹת חֲלוּקוֹת וּמַשְׁוֶה אוֹתָם, שֶׁזֶּה מַחְלֹקֶת הוּא בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (בראשית רבה נ"א:ב'), וְשָׁם עוֹד דַּעַת שְׁלִישִׁית: אַבָּא חִלְפֵי בְּרַבִּי סֻמָּקֵי בְּשֵׁם רַבִּי יְהוּדָה ב"ר סִימוֹן, "וַה' הִמְטִיר עַל סְדֹם" זֶה גַּבְרִיאֵל, "מֵאֵת ה' מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם" זֶה הקב"ה. אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר, כָּל מָקוֹם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "וַה'" הוּא וּבֵית דִּינוֹ. אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק, בַּתּוֹרָה בַּנְּבִיאִים וּבַכְּתוּבִים מָצִינוּ שֶׁהַהֶדְיוֹט מַזְכִּיר שְׁמוֹ שְׁנֵי פְּעָמִים, בַּתּוֹרָה "וַיֹּאמֶר לֶמֶךְ לְנָשָׁיו" וְגוֹ'. הִנֵּה אֵלּוּ שָׁלֹשׁ מַחְלוֹקוֹת בַּדָּבָר, שֶׁרַבִּי יְהוּדָה ב"ר סִימוֹן יִחֵס הַשֵּׁם הָרִאשׁוֹן לְגַבְרִיאֵל, שֶׁהוּא הַשָּׁלִיחַ לְשַׁחֵת, וְנִקְרָא הַשָּׁלִיחַ בְּשֵׁם הַשּׁוֹלֵחַ; וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אָמַר כִּי הוּא וּבֵית דִּינוֹ הִסְכִּימוּ בַּמִּשְׁפָּט, וּמֵאִתּוֹ בָּא; וְרַבִּי יִצְחָק אָמַר שֶׁהוּא דֶּרֶךְ הַלָּשׁוֹן. וְאִם הֲבִינוֹתָ מָה שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְמַעְלָה תֵּדַע כַּוָּנָתָם בְּ"הוּא וּבֵית דִּינוֹ", וְיִהְיֶה פְּשׁוּטוֹ שֶׁל מִקְרָא בָּרוּר לְפָנֶיךָ. וְכֵן "וַה' אָמַר" (בראשית י"ח:י"ז) "וְשָׁמְרוּ דֶּרֶךְ ה' לְמַעַן הָבִיא ה'", שֶׁלֹּא אָמַר שִׁמְרוּ דַּרְכִּי לְמַעַן אָבִיא, וְכֵן אָמַר "כִּי גָדְלָה צַעֲקָתָם אֶת פְּנֵי ה' וַיְשַׁלְּחֵנוּ ה'" וְכֵן "וַיְהִי בְּשַׁחֵת אֱלֹהִים" וְגוֹ' (בראשית י"ט:כ"ט):

Ancient Near East
  • The plain (הַכִּכָּר) is the district around the lower Jordan where the text places Sodom and Gomorrah (13:10–12). Chapter 14 names five cities of the plain, one of them Bela, which is Zoar (14:2, 8).
  • Brimstone (גָּפְרִית) is sulphur. Some readers take the fire and sulphur to be a natural catastrophe; the text names the LORD as the one who sent it, and the English follows the text.
  • In the text's picture of the world the heavens (שָׁמַיִם) are the sky above the earth, from which rain comes, and also the place where God is. Fire, like rain, comes down from there.
Apparatus

  • וַֽיהֹוָ֗ה — WLC reads וַֽיהוָ֗ה (vowels)
19:25

He overturned these cities and all the plain and all the inhabitants of the cities and the growth of the ground.

and-he-overturned [ACC] the-cities these and-[ACC] all-of-the-plain and-[ACC] all-of dwellers-of the-cities and-growth-of the-ground

Grammar
  • The verse is a list of four objects of one verb. The first three are each marked by the object marker אֵת (the second and third joined by the vav as well); the fourth, וְצֶמַח הָאֲדָמָה, has the vav but no אֵת. The English keeps the repeated 'and all'.
  • The wayyiqtol וַיַּהֲפֹךְ continues the narrative from the qatal of v. 24 and gives the act: he overturned.
  • כׇּל־יֹשְׁבֵי הֶעָרִים is a construct chain: the participle יֹשְׁבֵי governs the noun 'the cities'. The English 'the inhabitants of the cities' keeps the chain.
  • The etnaḥta on הַכִּכָּר divides the verse. The tipḥa on צֶמַח, a construct, marks a pause before הָאֲדָמָה, and the silluq on הָאֲדָמָה ends the verse and the last object.

Rashi says the four cities sat on one rock and were overturned from top to bottom, and cites the verse of Job about the hand on the flint. This is an image, not the plain sense of the verb.

19:26

His wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.

and-she-looked wife-of-him from-behind-him and-she-became pillar-of salt

Grammar
  • The verse is two wayyiqtol clauses. The first gives the look, the second the change, and the English keeps the order.
  • The verb of the second clause is 'be' in the sense 'become', and the predicate נְצִיב מֶלַח is a noun phrase: pillar of salt.
  • The etnaḥta on מֵאַחֲרָיו divides the verse. The first half ends with the place of the look, and the second half gives the result.
  • The Hebrew says 'his wife', not Lot's wife, and the English keeps 'his wife'. The reader is told whose wife she is only by the suffix.

Ancient Near East
  • Brimstone and salt are named together in Deuteronomy 29:22 as the ruin of a land overthrown by God, so salt belongs to the picture of the destruction in the text.
  • The word נְצִיב is used elsewhere of an officer or garrison posted in a place; its root is נצב, 'stand'. Here it is a standing figure of salt. Ibn Ezra takes it as a monument (מַצֵּבָה), Radak compares a mound (תֵּל) of salt and says she became salt standing; the English has 'pillar'.
  • The shores of the Dead Sea have large deposits of salt, and many readers connect the story with such formations; the text itself does not say so.
19:27

And Abraham rose early in the morning and went to the place where he had stood before the LORD.

and-rose-early Abraham in-the-morning to the-place which he-stood there before-face-of the-LORD

Grammar
  • The verb וַיַּשְׁכֵּם is a hifil wayyiqtol. 'Rose early' is an idiom, with the time phrase 'in the morning' after it. No verb of motion follows; אֶל־הַמָּקוֹם carries it, and the English adds 'went'.
  • The relative clause אֲשֶׁר עָמַד שָׁם is a qatal with an adverb: 'where he had stood', with שָׁם repeating the place.
  • The phrase עָמַד אֶת־פְּנֵי יְהוָה, 'stood before the LORD', names the place as the one where Abraham stood in 18:22; there the wording is עֹמֵד לִפְנֵי יְהוָה, here אֶת־פְּנֵי.
  • The zaqef qaton on הַמָּקוֹם and the tipḥa on שָׁם divide the relative clause. The silluq ends the verse on the divine name.

19:28

And he looked down over the face of Sodom and Gomorrah, and over all the face of the land of the plain. And he saw, and look, the smoke of the land rose like the smoke of a furnace.

and-he-looked-down upon face-of Sodom and-Gomorrah and-upon all-face-of land-of the-plain and-he-saw and-look rose smoke-of the-land like-smoke-of the-furnace

Grammar
  • The two wayyiqtol verbs, וַיַּשְׁקֵף and וַיַּרְא, give the look and the seeing in sequence.
  • The repeated noun פְּנֵי ('face') means the surface of the ground over the cities. The English repeats 'over the face of' to keep the parallel.
  • וְהִנֵּה introduces the seen thing. Its qatal עָלָה is rendered 'rose': after הִנֵּה the qatal states what is there to be seen.
  • The etnaḥta on הַכִּכָּר ends the first half of the verse, the looking; the second half gives what he saw. The silluq closes the verse on הַכִּבְשָׁן.
Commentary (11)
Rashirecords קִיטֹ֣ר
Rashi glosses קִיטוֹר as תִּמּוּר של עָשָׁן, a column of smoke. The English says 'smoke' and does not take the column.
Hebrew
תִּמּוּר שֶׁל עָשָׁן, טורק"א בלע"ז:
Rashirecords הַכִּבְשָֽׁן׃
Rashi: הַכִּבְשָׁן is a pit in which stones are burned to make lime, and so every kiln in the Torah. The English takes 'furnace' on Ibn Ezra's reading, and Rashi's lime-kiln is the alternative.
Hebrew
חֲפִירָה שֶׁשּׂוֹרְפִין בָּה אֶת הָאֲבָנִים לְסִיד, וְכֵן כָּל כִּבְשָׁן שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה:

Ibn Ezra: כְּקִיטֹר means 'like smoke', of the same root as incense (קְטֹרֶת). The English keeps 'smoke'.

Ancient Near East
  • A kiln (כִּבְשָׁן) was used to burn stone to lime or to fire clay. Exodus 19:18 uses the same word for the smoke of Sinai, so the simile is a sight the first readers knew.
  • The word translated 'furnace' in the English is the word for a kiln. Its use for a fire kept burning, as Ibn Ezra takes it, is a reading, not a fact of the text.
19:29

When God destroyed the cities of the plain, God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow, when he overturned the cities in which Lot had lived.

and-it-came-to-pass in-destroying God [ACC] cities-of the-plain and-he-remembered God [ACC] Abraham and-sent [ACC] Lot out-of-midst-of the-overthrow in-overturning [ACC] the-cities which dwelt in-them Lot

Grammar
  • The sentence has two temporal clauses, both built with בְּ and an infinitive construct: 'when God destroyed' and 'when he overturned'. The English makes both 'when' clauses.
  • The main clause has two verbs, וַיִּזְכֹּר and וַיְשַׁלַּח: God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out. The cause and the result are joined by the vav.
  • The noun הֲפֵכָה and the infinitive בַּהֲפֹךְ share the root of the verb in v. 25, so the 'overthrow' is the same act as the overturning.
  • The etnaḥta on אַבְרָהָם divides the verse: the first half is the remembering, and the second half is the sending and the overturning.

Rashi וַיִּזְכֹּ֥ר אֱלֹהִ֖ים אֶת אַבְרָהָ֑ם

Ancient Near East
  • In this text God 'remembering' someone is God acting on a commitment to that person; it is not a recalling of something forgotten (compare Noah, 8:1).
19:30

And Lot went up from Zoar and lived in the mountain, and his two daughters with him, because he feared to live in Zoar, and he lived in the cave, he and his two daughters.

and-went-up Lot from-Zoar and-dwelt in-the-mountain and-two daughters-of-him with-him for feared to-dwell in-Zoar and-dwelt in-the-cave he and-two daughters-of-him

Grammar
  • Three wayyiqtols move the narrative: Lot went up, he dwelt in the mountain, and he dwelt in the cave.
  • The clause כִּי יָרֵא לָשֶׁבֶת gives the reason: 'for he feared to dwell'. The infinitive construct with לְ is the object of the fear.
  • The independent pronoun הוּא comes after the verb and resumes the subject, so the English 'he and his two daughters' repeats the subject.
  • The etnaḥta on בְּצוֹעַר divides the verse, and the silluq on בְנֹתָיו ends it with the daughters.
Commentary (7)
Rashirecords כִּ֥י יָרֵ֖א לָשֶׁ֣בֶת בְּצ֑וֹעַר
Rashi: Lot feared to dwell in Zoar because it was near Sodom. The English states the fear without a reason, and Ramban's different reason is recorded.
Hebrew
לְפִי שֶׁהָיְתָה קְרוֹבָה לִסְדוֹם:

Ramban rejects Rashi's reason: Zoar was among the places marked for overthrow, and it was spared only at Lot's plea. Lot feared that the delay would not last, since he had time to reach the mountain. The English does not choose between them.

Ancient Near East
  • Zoar is named in the text as a small town that Lot asked to be spared (19:20–22); the text ties its name to the word 'small' (19:20, 22). It is the Bela of 14:2, 8.
  • Caves in hill country served as shelter and dwelling places.
19:31

And the firstborn said to the younger, "Our father is old, and there is no man in the land to come to us as is the way of all the earth.

and-she-said the-firstborn to the-younger our-father old and-man there-is-not in-the-land to-come upon-us as-way-of all-the-earth

Grammar
  • The speech is the words of the elder daughter, in direct speech after the verb of saying. The English gives them in double quotation marks.
  • אָבִינוּ זָקֵן: the qatal of זָקֵן is stative, 'is old', and the subject 'our father' is first. The speech is a reason for what follows.
  • לָבוֹא עָלֵינוּ: 'come upon us' is an idiom; in this context it is a euphemism for sexual union, here with the aim of children. The English 'come to us' keeps the euphemism.
  • כְּדֶרֶךְ כׇּל־הָאָרֶץ: 'as is the way of all the earth'. The custom is taken for granted and the text does not describe it. The plan that follows is in v. 32.
Commentary (9)
Rashinot-applicable אָבִ֣ינוּ זָקֵ֑ן
Rashi glosses the daughters' reason: 'if not now, when?', lest their father die or stop begetting. This gives their motive, which the English does not state.

Ancient Near East
  • The daughters speak of 'coming in to' a woman as the normal way to marriage and children. In the text's world a family was continued through its children, and marriages were arranged by the father; the text gives their words without comment.
19:32

Come, let us make our father drink wine, and let us lie with him, and let us preserve offspring from our father."

come, let-us-make-drink (object marker) our-father wine, and-let-us-lie with-him, and-let-us-keep-alive from-our-father seed

Grammar
  • לְכָה is the one word of address in the verse. It is singular and masculine, but Radak notes that such interjections do not vary for number or gender, since they express agreement.
  • The three verbs that follow are all first common plural: נַשְׁקֶה, וְנִשְׁכְּבָה, וּנְחַיֶּה. Each one is a step in the proposal, and the English 'let us' carries them all.
  • The verb נַשְׁקֶה is a yiqtol in form, a causative (hifil) of שָׁקָה. The English 'make ... drink' keeps the causative and the object.
  • The second and third steps are joined to the first by ו (and). The English keeps 'and' only where the Hebrew has the conjunction on the verb.

Ramban the whole verse

וְטַעַם
Rambannot-applicable וּנְחַיֶּ֥ה מֵאָבִ֖ינוּ זָֽרַע׃
Ramban: perhaps they reasoned that they should do what was fitting, that God would have mercy, and that a male and a female would be born and the world would continue through them ('the world is built by kindness', Ps 89:3), since the LORD had not saved them for nothing. They were modest and did not tell their father to take them, because a descendant of Noah may marry his daughter, or because the thing was very ugly in the eyes of those generations and had never been done; and our rabbis in the aggadot condemn Lot severely. This is the motive the daughters may have had; it is not a gloss on any word, so the English gives none.

Ancient Near East
  • In the world of the text a family line continues through children, above all sons, and the name of a dead man is kept alive by his descendants. To be left without offspring was to be cut off; many stories in Genesis turn on this. The daughters give exactly this aim: to preserve offspring from their father.
19:33

And they made their father drink wine that night, and the firstborn came in and lay with her father, and he did not perceive when she lay down and when she rose.

and-they-made-drink (object marker) their-father wine in-the-night that, and-came-in the-firstborn and-lay with(אֵת) her-father, and-not he-perceived in-her-lying-down and-in-her-rising

Grammar
  • The narrative is in the wayyiqtol throughout (וַתַּשְׁקֶין, וַתָּבֹא, וַתִּשְׁכַּב): the sequence of past events.
  • The verb of perception is the qatal יָדַע, negated, and the two infinitives that follow are what he did not notice. The sentence says the father did not notice either act.
  • The verb שָׁכַב takes אֵת here and עִם in 19:35. The English uses 'lay with' for both, so the difference of preposition is kept in the literal line.
  • The infinitives בְּשִׁכְבָהּ and וּבְקוּמָהּ are a fixed pair: the first is the lying down, the second the rising, and the verse denies notice of both.

A moral reading of the wording; the English renders both acts alike.

Apparatus
  • The ו of וּבְקוּמָהּ carries a puncta extraordinaria in the Masoretic text (the WLC note in the pack). Rashi and Radak cite the midrash that the point means he knew at her rising; the English declines it.
19:34

On the next day the firstborn said to the younger, "Look, I lay with my father last night. Let us make him drink wine tonight also, and go in and lie with him, and let us preserve offspring from our father."

and-it-came-to-pass from-the-morrow and-said the-firstborn to the-younger: look, I-lay last-night with(אֵת) my-father; let-us-make-drink-him wine also the-night, and-go-in (f.) lie (f.) with-him, and-let-us-keep-alive from-our-father seed

Grammar
  • The speech changes person: the elder speaks of her completed act in the first singular (שָׁכַבְתִּי), then proposes in the first plural (נַשְׁקֶנּוּ, וּנְחַיֶּה), and gives the younger her part in the second feminine singular (וּבֹאִי, שִׁכְבִי).
  • נַשְׁקֶנּוּ is the hifil cohortative with the suffix 'him' joined by a doubled nun (an energic ending): 'let us make him drink'. The clause repeats the act of 19:33 for the next night: 'also tonight' is the English of גַּם הַלַּיְלָה.
  • The reported act of the elder is in the qatal, and she gives its time as אֶמֶשׁ, the night just past.
  • The speech ends with the same clause as the elder's proposal in 19:32 (וּנְחַיֶּה מֵאָבִינוּ זָרַע), now spoken to the younger as the reason for the second night.
Commentary (2)
Radakfollows אֶ֖מֶשׁ
Radak: the night just passed is called אֶמֶשׁ. The English 'last night' gives this sense.
Hebrew
הַלַּיְלָה שֶׁעָבְרָה נִקְרֵאת אֶמֶשׁ.

וַהֲוָה בְּיוֹמָא דְבַתְרוֹהִי וַאֲמֶרֶת רַבְּתָא לִזְעֶרְתָּא הָא שְׁכֵיבִית רַמְשָׁא עִם אַבָּא נַשְׁקִנֵּהּ חַמְרָא אַף בְּלֵילְיָא וְעוּלִי שְׁכִיבִי עִמֵּיהּ וּנְקַיֵּם מֵאֲבוּנָא בְּנִין:

Grammar
  • The verse repeats the frame of 19:33 with these changes: the subject (the younger), the verb of motion (וַתָּקׇם 'arose' for וַתָּבֹא 'came in'), the preposition (עִם for אֵת), the adverb גַּם 'also', the fuller הַהוּא 'that' (19:33 has הוּא), and the defective spelling בְּקֻמָהּ.
  • In both nights it is the daughters (plural) who make the father drink (19:33, 19:35); only the act of lying with him is done by one daughter each night, the elder first and then the younger. The father's ignorance is the same in both.
  • The adverb גַּם ties the second night to the first, as the speech in 19:34 had done.

19:36

And the two daughters of Lot became pregnant by their father.

and-they-became-pregnant the-two-of daughters-of Lot from-their-father

Grammar
  • The verb is a wayyiqtol of הָרָה in the feminine plural, with the two daughters as subject; the English 'became pregnant' is the sense of the verb's Qal 1 entry.
  • The construct phrase שְׁתֵּי בְנוֹת־לוֹט is 'the two daughters of Lot': a construct chain ending in a proper name is definite, so the whole phrase has the sense of the article.
  • The verse gives the conception without a separate night for each daughter: the reader is left to place it.
Commentary (3)
Rashirecords וַֽתַּהֲרֶ֛יןָ
Rashi: although a woman does not conceive from a first act of intercourse, these two took control of themselves and put their nakedness (their private parts) outward, and so conceived from the first act. The English does not adopt this physiological explanation; it is kept here because a reader may ask how both conceived after one night each.
Hebrew
אַעַ"פִּ שֶׁאֵין הָאִשָּׁה מִתְעַבֶּרֶת מִבִּיאָה רִאשׁוֹנָה, אֵלּוּ שָׁלְטוּ בְעַצְמָן וְהוֹצִיאוּ עֶרְוָתָן לַחוּץ וְנִתְעַבְּרוּ מִבִּיאָה רִאשׁוֹנָה:
Radakfollows וַֽתַּהֲרֶ֛יןָ

מֵאוֹתָהּ בִּיאָה הָרוּ, לְהוֹדִיעַ כִּי לֹא יָסְפוּ עוֹד לִשְׁכַּב עִמּוֹ, כִּי לֹא נִתְכַּוְּנוּ אֶלָּא לְהַשְׁאִיר זֶרַע.

The firstborn bore a son and named him Moab; he is the father of the Moabites to this day.

Grammar
  • The verse has two parts: the naming (wayyiqtol forms) and a nominal clause with a resumptive pronoun (הוּא אֲבִי מוֹאָב).
  • The name מוֹאָב is given as the son's name and then as the name of the people; the English uses 'Moab' for the son and 'the Moabites' for the people.
  • The final phrase עַד הַיּוֹם is a fixed idiom: 'to this day', a reference to the time of the telling.
Commentary (8)
Rashinot-applicable מוֹאָ֑ב
Rashi: the firstborn named her son with the explicit 'from my father', and the younger named hers in clean language, and was rewarded in the days of Moses. This is a homily on the two daughters and does not bear on the English.

Ibn Ezra: מוֹאָב is 'like' מֵאָב, 'from a father': the name is the sound-play of the daughter's words. The gloss and the note give this; the English line keeps the name, as the decisions require.

Hebrew
שֶׁיָּרְשׁוּ אֶרֶץ, כִּי מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהָיְתָה כַּוָּנַת הַנָּשִׁים רְצוּיָה, הָיָה זַרְעָם לִשְׁנֵי גּוֹיִם יוֹרְשֵׁי אַבְרָהָם בִּקְצָת, כְּאָמְרָם (משלי ג:ו) "בְּכָל דְּרָכֶיךָ דָעֵהוּ" אֲפִילוּ לִדְבַר עֲבֵרָה (נזיר כג).
Ancient Near East
  • Moab was a people of the plateau east of the Dead Sea, a neighbour of Israel in the Transjordan. Deuteronomy 2:9 says that the LORD gave Ar to the descendants of Lot as a possession.
  • Moab is known also from outside the Bible: it is a kingdom in the Mesha stele, a royal inscription of Moab from the ninth century BCE.
  • The text gives Moab and Ammon an origin: both descend from Lot through his daughters, after the destruction of the cities (19:24-29). It states only the descent; whether the account preserves a tradition of kinship with these peoples or expresses Israel's view of them is discussed.
  • The name is explained by sound, as many names in Genesis are: 'Moab' is joined to מֵאָב, 'from a father'. Such explanations are the narrator's wordplay and are not necessarily the name's linguistic origin.
19:38 · ס

And the younger also bore a son, and named him Ben-Ammi; he is the father of the Ammonites to this day.

and-the-younger also she bore son, and-named his-name Ben-Ammi, he father-of sons-of Ammon to the-day

Grammar
  • The verse repeats the frame of 19:37 with the younger daughter as subject. The emphatic pronoun גַם־הִוא is the one difference in the subject.
  • The name בֶּן־עַמִּי is the younger's naming of her son; its meaning ('son of my people') is in the note, not in the English line.
  • The Hebrew marks the end of a section after this verse (the ס in the Masoretic text), which closes the account of the two daughters.
  • בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן is a collective: 'the sons of Ammon' is the people, so the English gives 'the Ammonites'.
Commentary (3)
Radaknot-applicable בֵּ֔ן עַמִּ֑י
Radak: the name בֶּן־עַמִּי means 'from my family I had this son'. And this daughter was more modest than the firstborn, for she did not reveal that he was from her father (שֶׁלֹּא גִּלְּתָה מִן אָבִיהָ).
Hebrew
כְּלוֹמַר מִמִּשְׁפַּחְתִּי הָיָה לִי זֶה הַבֵּן, וְזֹאת הָיְתָה צְנוּעָה יוֹתֵר מִן הַבְּכִירָה שֶׁלֹּא גִּלְּתָה מִן אָבִיהָ.
Radakfollows בְנֵֽי עַמּ֖וֹן
Radak: the people is called the sons of Ammon, which is why the English gives 'the Ammonites' for the Hebrew phrase.

וּזְעֶרְתָּא אַף הִיא יְלִידַת בַּר וּקְרַת שְׁמֵיהּ בַּר עַמִּי הוּא אֲבוּהוֹן דִּבְנֵי עַמּוֹן עַד יוֹמָא דֵין:
Ancient Near East
  • Ammon was a people of the Transjordan, north-east of Moab and east of the Jordan, with its centre at Rabbah (later Amman). Deuteronomy 2:19 gives the land of the sons of Ammon to the descendants of Lot.
  • The name בֶּן־עַמִּי, 'son of my people', resembles בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן, 'sons of Ammon': as with Moab, the text joins the name of the people to the name of the child by sound.
Apparatus
  • The pronoun is written הוא and read הִיא (the Torah's regular ketiv/qere for the feminine pronoun); the pointing הִוא is the qere. The English follows the reading: 'she'.
20:1

Abraham set out from there for the land of the Negev, and he lived between Kadesh and Shur, and he sojourned in Gerar.

and-journeyed from-there Abraham to-land the-Negev and-dwelt between Kadesh and-between Shur and-sojourned in-Gerar

Grammar
  • Three wayyiqtol verbs (וַיִּסַּע, וַיֵּשֶׁב, וַיָּגָר) carry the narrative in sequence: a move, a stay, and a longer residence.
  • The repeated preposition in בֵּין־קָדֵשׁ וּבֵין שׁוּר gives two separate points, with Kadesh and Shur as the ends of the place where Abraham dwelt.
  • The accents divide the verse at the etnaḥta on שׁ֑וּר, so the first half gives the journey and the stay and the second gives the residence in Gerar.
  • The place-names carry no article: קָדֵשׁ, שׁוּר and גְּרָר are proper names; the lexicon's first sense for קָדֵשׁ is the Kadesh of the south.

The narrative of 20:1 moves without comment on the reason for the journey; the commentators supply motives (see commentary), which are not in the English.

Commentary (6)
Rashinot-applicable וַיִּסַּ֨ע מִשָּׁ֤ם אַבְרָהָם֙
Rashi gives a motive for leaving: the towns were ruined and travellers stopped, and Abraham moved away because of the bad name Lot had after his deeds with his daughters. This is a reason for the move, not the sense of the words.
Hebrew
כְּשֶׁרָאָה שֶׁחָרְבוּ הַכְּרַכִּים וּפָסְקוּ הָעוֹבְרִים וְהַשָּׁבִים, נָסַע לוֹ מִשָּׁם. דָּ"אַ לְהִתְרַחֵק מִלּוֹט, שֶׁיָּצָא עָלָיו שֵׁם רָע, שֶׁבָּא עַל בְּנוֹתָיו:
Radakrecords וַיִּסַּ֨ע מִשָּׁ֤ם
Radak takes 'from there' as the oaks of Mamre, where Abraham lived, and suggests he went into the land of the Philistines, which is within the land God gave him. The English keeps 'from there' and does not name the place.
