Hebrew
וַאֲקִים אַבְרָהָם יָת שְׁבַע חוּרְפַן דְּעָאן בִּלְחוֹדֵיהֶן:
21:29

Abimelech said to Abraham, "What are these, these seven ewe-lambs that you have set by themselves?"

and-said Abimelech to Abraham what these seven ewe-lambs these which you-set by-themselves

Grammar
  • מָה הֵנָּה (21:29.5–6) is a verbless question: 'what (are) these?'. The English supplies the copula 'are'. The answer is given by the apposition: 'these seven ewe-lambs'.
  • הָאֵלֶּה (21:29.9) repeats the demonstrative after the noun and carries the article though the noun שֶׁבַע כְּבָשֹׂת has none; the English repeats 'these'.
  • אֲשֶׁר הִצַּבְתָּ (21:29.10–11) is a relative clause with a Hifil qatal, 2nd masculine singular. The addressee is Abraham.
  • הֵנָּה and לְבַדָּנָה are feminine plural forms, agreeing with the ewe-lambs (שֶׁבַע כְּבָשֹׂת). English has no feminine; 'these' and 'by themselves' are plural.
  • The question ends with the silluq on לְבַדָּנָה (21:29.12). The zaqef qaton on הָאֵלֶּה (21:29.9) divides the question from the relative clause.

Ibn Ezra's reading of לְבַדָּנָה is in the commentary and the apparatus; the English keeps the plural.

Commentary (3)
Ibn Ezranormativefollows מָ֣ה הֵ֗נָּה
Ibn Ezra, on מָה הֵנָּה: «לְשׁוֹן נְקֵבוֹת», 'the language of females': הֵנָּה is the feminine plural pronoun, said of the ewe-lambs. English cannot show the gender; 'these' is plural.
Hebrew
לשון נקבות:
Ibn Ezranormativerecords לְבַדָּֽנָה׃
Ibn Ezra, on לְבַדָּנָה: «עִם ה״א וְהִיא לְבַדָּהּ», 'with a heh; and it is lebadah'. He takes the form as the feminine of 'by himself', 'alone' (a form ending in heh), the counterpart of לְבַדָּהּ, 'by herself'; he does not say it is plural. The English 'by themselves' gives the sense for the seven ewe-lambs; the suffix -nah is a feminine plural suffix by the pack's parse, so the English keeps the plural, and records his equation with the singular form.
Hebrew
לבדנה. עם ה"א והיא לבדה:
Targum Onkelos the whole verse
Hebrew
וַאֲמַר אֲבִימֶלֶךְ לְאַבְרָהָם מָה אִנּוּן שְׁבַע חוּרְפַן אִלֵּין דַּאֲקֵמְתָּא בִּלְחוֹדֵיהֶן:
Apparatus
  • Ibn Ezra equates לְבַדָּנָה with לְבַדָּהּ ('alone', feminine singular, 'by herself'). The English keeps the plural 'by themselves' for the seven ewe-lambs, the sense the feminine plural suffix -nah gives in the pack's parse.
21:30

He said, "You are to take seven ewe-lambs from my hand, so that it may be a witness for me that I dug this well."

and-said that [object] seven ewe-lambs you-will-take from-my-hand in-order-that she-will-be to-me for-a-witness that I-dug [object] the-well this

Grammar
  • Abraham's answer to Abimelech's question of 21:29 is one speech, which runs through this verse and ends with it. The verb in 21:30.1 has no named subject; the context identifies the speaker.
  • כִּי after וַיֹּאמֶר (21:30.2) is the recitative 'that' which introduces direct speech and is not translated; some read it as 'because' or 'indeed', answering Abimelech's 'what are these?' (21:29). The English leaves it out and opens the quotation.
  • The object שֶׁבַע כְּבָשֹׂת (21:30.4–5) stands before its verb תִּקַּח (21:30.6), a second masculine singular yiqtol addressed to Abimelech, with the force of an instruction. The fronting stresses the object; the English uses the normal order. The numeral שֶׁבַע has the form used with a feminine noun.
  • The purpose clause is בַּעֲבוּר with a yiqtol. תִּהְיֶה is third feminine singular, so its subject is not the plural 'ewe-lambs' as such: either the set of seven or the gift taken as a whole counts as a singular, or the subject is an implied 'this' (Rashi's זאת, Radak's הַמִּקְנָה הַזֹּאת). The English 'it' keeps the singular. לִי לְעֵדָה: 'for me as a witness', with לְ marking the predicate.
  • The second כִּי (21:30.12) introduces what the witness attests: 'that I dug this well', a qatal of חָפַר.
  • Accents: the zaqef gadol on וַיֹּאמֶר (21:30.1), the zaqef qaton on כְּבָשֹׂת, the etnaḥta on מִיָּדִי (21:30.7) and the silluq on הַזֹּאת (21:30.16): the etnaḥta ends the first half of the verse, the instruction; the second half gives its purpose.

The speaker is named by context only, so 'He said' is kept without a name. The verb תִּהְיֶה is singular and the English renders it 'it'; the commentators name the subject differently (see commentary). The second half of the verse gives the purpose of the gift: it is a witness to Abraham's claim to the well.

Commentary (10)
Rashifollows בַּעֲבוּר֙ תִּֽהְיֶה לִּ֣י
Rashi's gloss on 'in order that it may be to me' is the single word זאת, 'this': the feminine singular subject of תִּהְיֶה is 'this' (the gift), not the plural ewe-lambs. The English 'it' agrees.
Hebrew
זאת:
Rashifollows לְעֵדָ֔ה
Rashi reads לְעֵדָה as a feminine form of the noun for testimony, citing 'and the pillar is a witness' (Genesis 31:52). This agrees with Ibn Ezra and with the English 'a witness'.
Hebrew
לְשׁוֹן עֵדוּת שֶׁל נְקֵבָה, כְּמוֹ וְעֵדָה הַמַּצֵּבָה (בראשית ל"א):
Rashinot-applicable כִּ֥י חָפַ֖רְתִּי אֶת הַבְּאֵ֥ר
Rashi tells how the herdsmen of Abimelech quarrelled over the well, each side claiming 'we dug it'. They agreed that whoever was seen at the well, with the water rising to meet him, owned it, and the water rose to meet Abraham. This is the story behind the claim, not the sense of 'that I dug'.
Hebrew
מְרִיבִים הָיוּ עָלֶיהָ רוֹעֵי אֲבִימֶלֶךְ וְאוֹמְרִים אֲנַחְנוּ חֲפַרְנוּהָ, אָמְרוּ בֵּינֵיהֶם כָּל מִי שֶׁיִּתְרָאֶה עַל הַבְּאֵר וְיַעֲלוּ הַמַּיִם לִקְרָאתוֹ, שֶׁלּוֹ הִיא, וְעָלוּ לִקְרָאת אַבְרָהָם:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows לְעֵדָ֔ה
Ibn Ezra: לְעֵדָה is 'like לְעֵדוּת', 'as testimony', the same noun in a feminine form. He adds that the root of the word for oath, שְׁבוּעָה, is שִׁבְעָה (seven), and says he will explain this at Numbers 30:3 (אוֹ הִשָּׁבַע שְׁבֻעָה). The second remark bears on the name Beersheba (21:31), not on the English of this verse.
Hebrew
כמו לעדות ודע כי מלת שבועה עקרה. שבעה, ובמלת "או השבע שבועה" (במדבר ל, ג) אפרשנה:
Radakfollows תִּֽהְיֶה לִּ֣י לְעֵדָ֔ה
Radak supplies the subject of תִּהְיֶה: 'let this livestock (הַמִּקְנָה הַזֹּאת) which I give be to me for a witness'. A feminine singular subject, which suits the English 'it'.
Hebrew
תִּהְיֶה לִי הַמִּקְנָה הַזֹּאת שֶׁאֲנִי נוֹתֵן לְעֵדָה.
Targum Onkelosfollows the whole verse
Onkelos renders לְעֵדָה as לְסַהֲדוּ, 'as a witness'. The English agrees.
Hebrew
וַאֲמַר אֲרֵי יָת שְׁבַע חוּרְפַן תְּקַבֵּל מִן יְדִי בְּדִיל דִּתְהֵי לִי לְסַהֲדוּ אֲרֵי חֲפָרִית יָת בֵּירָא הָדֵין (נ"י הָדָא):
Sfornorecords כִּ֚י אֶת שֶׁ֣בַע כְּבָשֹׂ֔ת תִּקַּ֖ח מִיָּדִ֑י
Sforno compares Ruth 4:7 (a man drew off his shoe and gave it to his fellow, 'and this was the attestation'): taking the lambs was testimony of the owners' agreement and their acknowledgment of the matter. He makes the lambs a sign of consent; the English keeps the plain 'a witness'.
Hebrew
עַל דֶּרֶךְ "שָׁלַף אִישׁ נַעֲלוֹ וְנָתַן לְרֵעֵהוּ וְזֹאת הַתְּעוּדָה" (רות ד:ז) כִּי הָיָה זֶה עֵדוּת הַסְכָּמַת הַבְּעָלִים וְהוֹדָאָתָם בַּדָּבָר.
Sfornorecords בַּעֲבוּר֙ תִּֽהְיֶה לִּ֣י
Sforno's one word on 'in order that it may be to me' is הַבְּרִית, 'the covenant': he supplies the feminine singular subject, the covenant, which is to be a witness for Abraham. The English keeps 'it' without naming it.
Hebrew
הַבְּרִית
Sfornorecords לְעֵדָ֔ה
Sforno glosses לְעֵדָה as 'on your acknowledgment' (עַל הוֹדָאָתְךָ), taking the witness to be Abimelech's acknowledgment. The English keeps 'a witness'.
Hebrew
עַל הוֹדָאָתְךָ
Sforno כִּ֥י חָפַ֖רְתִּי אֶת הַבְּאֵ֥ר הַזֹּֽאת׃
Hebrew
.
Ancient Near East
  • The seven ewe-lambs were set apart by Abraham in 21:28; the text gives only their purpose, a witness. Nothing in the verse says they were a price, a fee or a sacrifice, and the English does not say so.
  • In dry country a dug well was valuable, and who had dug it was the ground of a claim to it: compare 26:15–22, where the Philistines stop up the wells that Abraham's servants dug, and Isaac's servants dig them again and quarrel over them.
21:31

Therefore he called that place Beersheba, because there both of them swore.

on-so he-called to-the-place the-that well-of-seven that there they-swore the-two-of-them

Grammar
  • עַל כֵּן (21:31.1–2) is the compound 'therefore', 'on so'; it begins the explanation of the name. Radak takes it to refer to the seven lambs.
  • The naming construction is קָרָא with לְ, a place, and then the name: 'he called that place Beersheba'. The verse does not name the subject of קָרָא (Abraham in context); Radak reads 'they called'.
  • The name has two words, בְּאֵר and שֶׁבַע. The verse gives the reason for the second, 'because there they swore' (כִּי שָׁם נִשְׁבְּעוּ), which plays on the root שׁבע: 'seven' and 'swear'.
  • נִשְׁבְּעוּ (21:31.10) is the Niphal, third common plural, of שָׁבַע. The dual שְׁנֵיהֶם (21:31.11) stands in apposition to the subject inside the verb: the oath was sworn by both.
  • Accents: the revia on כֵּן (21:31.2) and the tevir on קָרָא (21:31.3) divide the first half; the etnaḥta on שָׁבַע (21:31.7) ends the first half, after the name, and the second half gives the reason; the silluq on שְׁנֵיהֶם ends the verse.

The English gives the place name as the text gives it. The meaning of the name is in the grammar notes and the commentary; the English does not explain it.

Commentary (2)
Radakrecords the whole verse
Radak: the ו of conjunction is left out (בְּאֵר and שֶׁבַע are joined without 'and', as in 'sun, moon', Habakkuk 3:11, and 'Reuben, Simeon', Exodus 1:2). 'Therefore' means on account of the seven lambs, and because they both swore there, on these two things they called the place 'Sheba'; 'Beer' was added for the well Abraham dug. The naming was a great sign that he would inherit the land, since whatever he said and named came true.
Hebrew
חָסֵר וי״ו הַשִּׁמּוּשׁ כְּמוֹ ״שֶׁמֶשׁ יָרֵחַ״ (חבקוק ג:יא), ״רְאוּבֵן שִׁמְעוֹן״ (שמות א:ב), וְהַדּוֹמִים לָהֶם, רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר, עַל כֵּן עַל שֶׁבַע כְּבָשׂוֹת, וְכִי שָׁם נִשְׁבְּעוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עַל שְׁנֵי הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה קָרְאוּ לַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא שֶׁבַע, וְנִשְׁתַּתֵּף ״בְּאֵר״ עִם ״שֶׁבַע״ עַל הַבְּאֵר שֶׁחָפַר שָׁם אַבְרָהָם. וְזֶה הָיָה אוֹת גָּדוֹל לִירַשׁ אֶת הָאָרֶץ שֶׁהָיָה מְקֻבָּל כָּל מַה שֶׁהָיָה אוֹמֵר וְקוֹרֵא שֵׁם לַמָּקוֹם, וְהָיָה כֵן.
Targum Onkelosrecords the whole verse
Onkelos renders נִשְׁבְּעוּ as 'they confirmed' (קַיָּמוּ) rather than 'swore'. The English 'swore' follows the Niphal sense of שָׁבַע.
Hebrew
עַל כֵּן קְרָא לְאַתְרָא הַהוּא בְּאֵר שָׁבַע אֲרֵי תַמָּן קַיָּמוּ תַּרְוֵיהוֹן:
Ancient Near East
  • The name Beersheba is read as 'well of seven' or 'well of the oath'. Both words are in the text: שֶׁבַע, 'seven' (21:28–30), and נִשְׁבְּעוּ, 'they swore', in this verse. The English gives the name only, and the notes give both readings.
  • Beersheba lies in the northern Negev, at the southern edge of the settled land.
21:32

So they made a covenant at Beersheba, and Abimelech rose, and Phichol, the commander of his army, and they returned to the land of the Philistines.

and-they-cut covenant at-well-of-seven and-rose Abimelech and-Phichol commander-of-his-army and-they-returned to-land-of Philistines

Grammar
  • Three wayyiqtols carry the narrative: וַיִּכְרְתוּ (making the covenant), וַיָּקׇם (the rising of Abimelech) and וַיָּשֻׁבוּ (the return).
  • כָּרַת בְּרִית is the idiom 'cut a covenant'. The object is בְּרִית with no object marker. The English 'made a covenant' gives the sense of the idiom.
  • The singular וַיָּקׇם has Abimelech as subject. וּפִיכֹל, 'and Phichol', is added after it with its appositive שַׂר־צְבָאוֹ, and the plural וַיָּשֻׁבוּ takes both men as subject.
  • שַׂר־צְבָאוֹ is 'commander of his army': the construct, with a third masculine singular suffix on 'army'.
  • Accents: the etnaḥta on שָׁבַע (21:32.4) ends the first half of the verse, the covenant; the zaqef qaton on צְבָאוֹ, the tipḥa on וַיָּשֻׁבוּ (21:32.10) and the silluq on פְּלִשְׁתִּים (21:32.13) mark the rest.

The English keeps the plural and singular verbs as the Hebrew has them: one subject is named first, then the second is added. 'So' renders the ו of the first wayyiqtol.

Commentary (4)
Rambanrecords וַיָּשֻׁ֖בוּ אֶל אֶ֥רֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּֽים׃
Ramban takes 'they returned to the land of the Philistines' to mean they returned to their city in that land: Abimelech and Phichol lived in Gerar, which is in Philistine territory, while Abraham lived in Beersheba, also in that land. The English keeps the Hebrew's 'the land'.
Hebrew
עִנְיָנוֹ וַיָּשׁוּבוּ אֶל עִירָם אֲשֶׁר בְּאֶרֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּים, כִּי בְּאֶרֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּים הָיוּ, אֲבָל הֵם יוֹשְׁבִים בִּגְרָר שֶׁהִיא מְדִינַת הַמֶּלֶךְ וְהוּא יוֹשֵׁב בִּבְאֵר שֶׁבַע שֶׁהִיא בְּאֶרֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּים בְּנַחַל גְּרָר:
Radaknot-applicable וַיָּ֣קׇם אֲבִימֶ֗לֶךְ
Radak has Abraham stay at the well with his flocks a day, two days or longer, and then return to his house in Gerar. This supplies a stay the text does not state.
Hebrew
וְאַבְרָהָם נִשְׁאַר שָׁם עִם צֹאנוֹ יוֹם אוֹ יוֹמַיִם אוֹ יוֹתֵר, וְאַחַר כָּךְ שָׁב אֶל אֶרֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּים אֶל בֵּיתוֹ לִגְרָר.
Targum Onkelosrecords the whole verse
Onkelos renders the covenant-making with 'they decreed' (גְּזָרוּ) and 'a confirmation' (קְיָם), and the return as 'they returned to the land of the Philistines'. The English keeps 'made a covenant'.
Hebrew
וּגְזָרוּ קְיָם בִּבְאֵר שָׁבַע וְקָם אֲבִימֶלֶךְ וּפִיכֹל רַב חֵילֵיהּ וְתָבוּ לְאַרַע פְּלִשְׁתָּאֵי:
Sfornorecords וַיָּשֻׁ֖בוּ אֶל אֶ֥רֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּֽים׃
Sforno: they returned from Beersheba, which was not in Philistine territory. They had come there to speak with Abraham, who had gone to look at his flocks, and there Abraham gave sheep, cattle and ewe-lambs to cut the covenant. The English keeps 'returned to the land' as the Hebrew has it.
Hebrew
שָׁבוּ מִבְּאֵר שֶׁבַע שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בְּאֶרֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּים, שֶׁהָלְכוּ שָׁם לְדַבֵּר עִם אַבְרָהָם שֶׁהָלַךְ שָׁם לִרְאוֹת מִקְנֵהוּ, וְשָׁם נָתַן צֹאן וּבָקָר וְכִבְשׂוֹת לִכְרוֹת הַבְּרִית.
Ancient Near East
  • Abimelech is the king of Gerar in these chapters (20:2; 21:22). The title שַׂר צָבָא, 'commander of the army', is a royal military office.
  • 'Cut a covenant' is the standard Hebrew idiom for making a treaty or pact. It is generally linked with the slaughter of animals that accompanied an oath (compare 15:9–10, 17 and Jeremiah 34:18–19); the origin of the idiom is debated. Here the text names only the sheep and cattle given to Abimelech (21:27) and the seven ewe-lambs (21:28–30).
  • The Philistines of the Bible are generally identified with a people that settled the southern coast of Canaan in the early twelfth century BCE. Whether the patriarchal narrative uses the name for a people already there, or applies a later name to the region, is disputed; the English keeps the text's name.
21:33

And he planted a tamarisk tree at Beersheba, and called there on the name of the LORD, El Olam.

and-he-planted tamarisk at-well-of-seven and-he-called there on-name-of the-LORD El Olam

Grammar
  • וַיִּטַּע is a wayyiqtol, third masculine singular, of נָטַע. Its object אֶשֶׁל follows it and carries no object marker.
  • וַיִּקְרָא־שָׁם continues the narrative. 'Call on the name' (קָרָא בְּשֵׁם) is the phrase used of worship at other patriarchal sites (12:8; 26:25); it can also mean 'proclaim the name'.
  • The name יְהֹוָה (21:33.8) is rendered 'the LORD' as the decisions set. The epithet אֵל עוֹלָם (21:33.9–10) is two nouns, 'El' in the construct and 'eternity, long duration'; it is transliterated in the English. It occurs in Genesis only here.
  • Accents: the etnaḥta on שָׁבַע (21:33.4) divides the verse into planting and calling; the qadma on וַיִּקְרָא (21:33.5) and the tipḥa on יְהֹוָה (21:33.8) mark the second half; the silluq on עוֹלָם (21:33.10) ends it.

El Olam is the name in apposition to 'the LORD' in the English, as the Hebrew has it. Its meaning (God of eternity, everlasting God) and the commentators' readings are in the commentary and the context notes.

Commentary (10)
Rashirecords אֶ֖שֶׁל
Rashi, quoting Rav and Shmuel, gives two readings of אֶשֶׁל: an orchard that brought fruit to feast the guests, or an inn with every kind of fruit. He also cites the planting of tents (Daniel 11:45). Neither is the tree of the English; a reader may take the word as an orchard or an inn.
Hebrew
רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל, חַד אֲמַר פַּרְדֵּס לְהָבִיא מִמֶּנוּ פֵּרוֹת לָאוֹרְחִים בַּסְּעוּדָה, וְחַד אֲמַר פֻּנְדָּק לְאַכְסַנְיָא וּבוֹ כָּל מִינֵי פֵּרוֹת. וּמָצִינוּ לְשׁוֹן נְטִיעָה בְּאֹהָלִים, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וְיִטַּע אָהֳלֵי אַפַּדְנוֹ (דניאל י"א):
Rashinot-applicable וַיִּ֨קְרָא שָׁ֔ם
Rashi's midrash on וַיִּקְרָא שָׁם: through that tree the name of the Holy One was called God of the world, because guests were told to bless the one whose food they had eaten. This is homily, not the sense of the words.
Hebrew
עַל יְדֵי אוֹתוֹ אֵשֶׁל נִקְרָא שְׁמוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּבָּ"ה אֱלוֹהַּ לְכָל הָעוֹלָם, לְאַחַר שֶׁאוֹכְלִים וְשׁוֹתִים אוֹמֵר לָהֶם בָּרְכוּ לְמִי שֶׁאֲכַלְתֶּם מִשֶּׁלּוֹ, סְבוּרִים אַתֶּם שֶׁמִּשֶּׁלִּי אֲכַלְתֶּם? מִשֶּׁל מִי שֶׁאָמָר וְהָיָה הָעוֹלָם אֲכַלְתֶּם (סוטה י'):
Ibn Ezranormativefollows אֶ֖שֶׁל
Ibn Ezra: אֶשֶׁל is a tree (אִילָן), and Abraham planted it as a sign (לְאוֹת). The English 'a tamarisk tree' follows the tree reading; the identification with the tamarisk is the lexicon's. The sign is a reason, so it stays out of the English.
Hebrew
אילן גם ויטע לאות:
Rambanrecords וַיִּ֨קְרָא שָׁ֔ם בְּשֵׁ֥ם יְהֹוָ֖ה אֵ֥ל עוֹלָֽם׃
Ramban takes 'on the name of the LORD' as a proclamation of the LORD who governs time by his strength, and El Olam as the one who rules the whole world. He cites Maimonides (Guide II.13), who took El Olam to point to God's existence before time. Onkelos reads וַיִּקְרָא as prayer. The English keeps 'called'.

Ancient Near East
  • Tamarisks grow in dry country where there is water near the surface. The planting at a well suits the place; the identification of אֶשֶׁל as a tamarisk is the lexicon's, and Ibn Ezra says only 'a tree'.
  • El is the ordinary Northwest Semitic word for 'god' and the name of the head of the Canaanite pantheon known from Ugarit; Genesis uses El with an epithet for the God worshipped at particular places (El Elyon 14:18–22; El Roi 16:13; El Bethel 35:7). Whether the title El Olam takes over a local shrine title is debated. עוֹלָם means a long or remote time, past or future; the title is rendered 'God of eternity', 'the everlasting God' or 'God of old', and the commentators read it as God who rules time or the world (Ramban, Sforno, Onkelos).
  • 'Call on the name of the LORD' is an act of worship in the patriarchal narratives (12:8; 26:25).
21:34 · פ

And Abraham sojourned in the land of the Philistines for many days.

and-sojourned Abraham in-land-of Philistines days many

Grammar
  • וַיָּגׇר is a wayyiqtol, third masculine singular: the verb opens the clause, and the subject follows it.
  • יָמִים רַבִּים has no preposition: it is an adverbial phrase of duration, 'many days'. English adds 'for'.
  • The adjective רַבִּים agrees with יָמִים in gender and number.
  • Accents: the tipḥa on פְּלִשְׁתִּים (21:34.4) divides the verse; the silluq on רַבִּים (21:34.6) ends it. The פ after the verse marks a paragraph division in the Masoretic layout.

The verse closes the section about the well and the covenant. The English gives 'many days' without a number, as the Hebrew does.

Rashi counts the years: Abraham's stay in Hebron was twenty-five years, and here it was twenty-six, so 'many days' exceeds the earlier stay. This is chronology, not the sense of the words.

22:1

It happened after these things that God tested Abraham. He said to him, "Abraham." He said, "Here I am."

and-it-happened after the-things these and-the-God tested [object] Abraham and-he-said to-him Abraham and-he-said here-I

Grammar
  • וַיְהִי is a wayyiqtol of הָיָה that opens a new episode; the English keeps the formula 'it happened'.
  • וְהָאֱלֹהִים נִסָּה: the subject comes before the qatal, which gives the situation before the speech. It is not a sequential verb.
  • The etnaḥta on אַבְרָהָם divides the verse. The silluq on הִנֵּנִי closes it.
  • The name Abraham is repeated as the address of the call, and הִנֵּנִי is the reply that accepts it.

The English keeps 'God' for הָאֱלֹהִים and reads נִסָּה as 'tested', the sense Ibn Ezra fixes. The two wayyiqtols of speech carry the call and the answer.

Commentary (9)
Rashideclines אַחַר֙ הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֔לֶּה
Rashi, citing the Sages (Sanhedrin 89b): 'after these things' is after the words of the Adversary, who accused that of all the feasts Abraham made he offered no bull or ram; God replied that Abraham did it all for his son, and that if told to sacrifice him he would not hold back. Another reading: after the words of Ishmael, who boasted to Isaac that he had been circumcised at thirteen and did not protest; Isaac answered that if God told him to offer himself he would not hold back. The English keeps 'these things' open.
Hebrew
יֵשׁ מֵרַבּוֹתֵינוּ אוֹמְרִים (סנהדרין פ"ט) אַחַר דְּבָרָיו שֶׁל שָׂטָן, שֶׁהָיָה מְקַטְרֵג וְאוֹמֵר מִכָּל סְעוּדָה שֶׁעָשָׂה אַבְרָהָם לֹא הִקְרִיב לְפָנֶיךָ פַּר אֶחָד אוֹ אַיִל אֶחָד; אָמַר לוֹ כְּלוּם עָשָׂה אֶלָּא בִּשְׁבִיל בְּנוֹ, אִלּוּ הָיִיתִי אוֹמֵר לוֹ זְבַח אוֹתוֹ לְפָנַי לֹא הָיָה מְעַכֵּב; וְיֵ"אֹ אַחַר דְּבָרָיו שֶׁל יִשְׁמָעֵאל, שֶׁהָיָה מִתְפָּאֵר עַל יִצְחָק שֶׁמָּל בֶּן י"ג שָׁנָה וְלֹא מִחָה, אָמַר לוֹ יִצְחָק בְּאֵבֶר א' אַתָּה מְיָרְאֵנִי? אִלּוּ אָמַר לִי הַקָּבָּ"ה זְבַח עַצְמְךָ לְפָנַי, לֹא הָיִיתִי מְעַכֵּב.
Rashifollows הִנֵּֽנִי׃
Rashi: הִנֵּנִי is the answer of the righteous, a word of humility and of readiness (זִמּוּן). The English 'Here I am' carries readiness; the humility is in the commentary only.
Hebrew
כָּךְ הִיא עֲנִיָּתָם שֶׁל חֲסִידִים, לְשׁוֹן עֲנָוָה הוּא וּלְשׁוֹן זִמּוּן:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows וְהָ֣אֱלֹהִ֔ים נִסָּ֖ה אֶת אַבְרָהָ֑ם
Ibn Ezra: נִסָּה is to be read in its plain sense, 'tested'; a reading that changes the letters is refuted by the whole passage. He sets aside the Gaon's reading, that the test was to show Abraham's righteousness to people, since no one was present at the binding. The test was for reward, and the verse's first words remove the objection that a command could be countermanded.

Ramban takes the test (נִסָּיוֹן) as a trial of the one tested: God commands so that the act passes from potential to deed, and Abraham receives the reward of a good deed and not only of a good heart. This is the sense 'tested' that the English gives.

Radakrecords וַיְהִ֗י אַחַר֙ הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֔לֶּה
Radak: after Abraham's dealings with Abimelech, his long stay there and his coming to live at Beersheba, God tested him over his only son. He finds the idea of a test hard to say of God, who searches hearts and knew Abraham would obey; and if it was to inform people, none was present at the binding but Abraham and Isaac, not even the servants. He concludes that the test was to show later generations, who believe the Torah, the fullness of Abraham's love, so that they learn to love the LORD. The English does not name the referent of 'these things'.

וּבָנִים וְלֹא נֶהֱנָה מִן הָעוֹלָם, וְאִם יָמוּת הוּא יִהְיֶה הַדָּבָר קָשֶׁה לְאַבְרָהָם מְאֹד. וְעוֹד שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ בֶּן זְקֻנִים, וּכְשֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הָאֵל שֶׁיַּעֲלֵהוּ שָׁם לְעוֹלָה, הָיְתָה כָּל כַּמָּה שָׁנִים מִיּוֹם שֶׁבָּטְלָה עֲבוֹדַת הַצְּלָמִים וְהָאֱלִילִים, מַאֲמִינִים רֹב הָעוֹלָם בְּתוֹרַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ וּבְסִפּוּרֶיהָ, אֶלָּא שֶׁחוֹלְקִים עָלֵינוּ עַל הַמִּצְווֹת, שֶׁאוֹמְרִים לָאָדָם לִלְמֹד הֵימֶנּוּ דֶּרֶךְ אַהֲבָתוֹ.
Radakrecords וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֔יו אַבְרָהָ֖ם
Radak takes the call as made in a night vision, since Abraham is said to rise early in the morning (22:3). The English says nothing of a vision.
Hebrew
בְּמַרְאַת הַלַּיְלָה אָמַר לוֹ, שֶׁהֲרֵי אָמַר ״וַיַּשְׁכֵּם אַבְרָהָם בַּבֹּקֶר״ (בראשית כב:ג).
Targum Onkelosrecords the whole verse
Onkelos renders the divine name here as 'the LORD' (ייָ) and Abraham's answer as 'Here I am' (הָא אֲנָא). The English keeps 'God' for הָאֱלֹהִים, as the decisions set for the God of Israel.
Hebrew
וַהֲוָה בָּתַר פִּתְגָּמַיָּא הָאִלֵּין וַייָ נַסִּי יָת אַבְרָהָם וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבְרָהָם וַאֲמַר הָא אֲנָא:
Sfornonot-applicable נִסָּ֖ה אֶת אַבְרָהָ֑ם
Sforno: the test was so that Abraham's love and fear would pass from potential into act and he would resemble his Maker, who is good to the world in act (cf. 1:26). It gives a reason for the test, not the sense of the word.
Hebrew
כֵּיוָן שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּפֹעַל אוֹהֵב וְיָרֵא כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה בַּכֹּחַ, וּבָזֶה יִדְמֶה יוֹתֵר לְבוֹרְאוֹ שֶׁהוּא טוֹב לָעוֹלָם בְּפֹעַל, כִּי אָמְנָם הַכַּוָּנָה בִּמְצִיאוּת הָאָדָם הָיְתָה שֶׁיִּדְמֶה לְבוֹרְאוֹ כְּפִי הָאֶפְשָׁר, כַּאֲשֶׁר הֵעִיד בְּאָמְרוֹ "נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ" (בראשית א:כו).
Apparatus
  • 22:1.6: the reading 'tested' is the one the Hebrew gives; Ibn Ezra notes another reading of the letters and the Gaon's reading of the sense (see commentary).
22:2

He said, "Please take your son, your only one, whom you love, Isaac, and go to the land of Moriah and offer him up there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains that I will tell you of."

and-he-said take I-pray [object] your-son [object] your-only-one which you-loved [object] Isaac and-go to-yourself to land the-Moriah and-cause-to-ascend-him there to-burnt-offering upon one the-mountains which I-will-say to-you

Grammar
  • קַח נָא is an imperative with the particle of entreaty: 'Please take'. The request tone is Rashi's reading (see commentary).
  • The son is described in stages: your son, your only one, whom you love, and then Isaac. The name comes after the relative clause, as an apposition.
  • אָהַבְתָּ is a qatal in the relative clause, a love that holds; the English uses the present, 'whom you love'.
  • וְלֶךְ־לְךָ is an imperative with the dative; the idiom is the one of 12:1, and the English keeps 'go'.
  • וְהַעֲלֵהוּ is a hifil imperative with the suffix 'him'; the aim, 'as a burnt offering', follows with the preposition ל.

The English keeps 'your only one' and 'Moriah' as the Hebrew has them. 'Offer him up' is the sense of the hifil with a burnt offering as its aim; it does not add a slaughter, which the words do not state.

Commentary (15)
Rashifollows קַח נָ֠א
Rashi: נָא is only a term of request. God says, 'I ask you, stand firm for me in this trial', so that the earlier trials will not be said to have had no substance (שֶׁלֹּא יֹאמְרוּ הָרִאשׁוֹנוֹת לֹא הָיָה בָהֶן מָמָּשׁ). The English 'Please take' takes the request sense.
Hebrew
אֵין נָא אֶלָּא לְשׁוֹן בַּקָשָׁה, אָמַר לוֹ בְּבַקָּשָׁה מִמְּךָ, עֲמֹד לִי בְּזֶה הַנִּסָּיוֹן, שֶׁלֹּא יֹאמְרוּ הָרִאשׁוֹנוֹת לֹא הָיָה בָהֶן מָמָּשׁ:
Rashirecords אֶת בִּנְךָ֨
Rashi (Sanhedrin 89b): a dialogue. 'I have two sons.' 'Your only one.' 'Each is the only one of his mother.' 'Whom you love.' 'I love both.' 'Isaac.' Why was it not said at once? So as not to confuse him suddenly and unsettle his mind, to make the command dear to him, and to give him reward for each word. The English keeps the words as they stand.
Hebrew
אָמַר לוֹ שְׁנֵי בָנִים יֵשׁ לִי, אָמַר לוֹ אֶת יְחִידְךָ; אָמַר לוֹ זֶה יָחִיד לְאִמּוֹ וְזֶה יָחִיד לְאִמּוֹ, אָמַר לוֹ אֲשֶׁר אָהַבְתָּ; אָמַר לוֹ שְׁנֵיהֶם אֲנִי אוֹהֵב, אָמַר לוֹ אֶת יִצְחָק (סנהדרין פ"ט). וְלָמָּה לֹא גִּלָּה לוֹ מִתְּחִלָּה? שֶׁלֹּא לְעַרְבְּבוֹ פִּתְאוֹם וְתָזוּחַ דַּעְתּוֹ עָלָיו וְתִטָּרֵף, וּכְדֵי לְחַבֵּב עָלָיו אֶת הַמִּצְוָה וְלִתֵּן לוֹ שָׂכָר עַל כָּל דִּבּוּר וְדִבּוּר:
Rashirecords אֶ֖רֶץ הַמֹּרִיָּ֑ה
Rashi: the land of Moriah is Jerusalem, as in 2 Chronicles 3:1; the Sages say instruction went out from there, and Onkelos renders it 'the land of worship' for the incense of the place. The English keeps the name.
Hebrew
יְרוּשָׁלַיִם, וְכֵן בְּדִבְרֵי הַיָּמִים לִבְנוֹת אֶת בֵּית ה' בִּירוּשָׁלִַם בְּהַר הַמּוֹרִיָּה (דברי הימים ב ג'). וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ פֵּרְשׁוּ עַל שֵׁם שֶׁמִּשָּׁם הוֹרָאָה יוֹצְאָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל. וְאֻנְקְלוֹס תִּרְגְּמוֹ עַל שֵׁם עֲבוֹדַת הַקְּטֹרֶת שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ מוֹר נֵרְדְּ וּשְׁאָר בְּשָׂמִים:
Rashifollows וְהַעֲלֵ֤הוּ
Rashi: הַעֲלֵהוּ means bring him up the mountain to make him a burnt offering; God did not say 'slaughter him', and after the ascent God said to take him down (22:12). The English 'offer him up' adds no slaughter.
Hebrew

Rashi: God keeps the righteous in suspense (מַתְהֵא) and then reveals it to them, all to increase their reward, as in 'to the land which I will show you' (12:1) and, in Jonah, 'proclaim to it the proclamation' (Jonah 3:2). A homily on why no mountain is named; not the sense of the words.

Ibn Ezra: the house was built there, as 2 Chronicles 3:1 says; it is not a high mountain, and the threshing floor of Araunah was there. The English keeps 'mountains', since har is mountain or hill and the height of the site is not in the verse. His claim of a low height is recorded, not adopted.

Ramban: Isaac is called 'your only one' because he is the son of the free wife and alone is called seed, and the word magnifies the command: take your son, the only one, the beloved. The English keeps the word as it stands.

Rambanrecords הַמֹּרִיָּ֑ה
Ramban gives Rashi's view (Moriah is Jerusalem, as in 2 Chronicles 3:1), the Sages' saying that instruction went out from there, and Onkelos' 'land of worship', which he questions. He cites Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer for a derivation from 'fear' (מוֹרָא). The right way by the plain sense (הַנָּכוֹן עַל דֶּרֶךְ הַפְּשָׁט), he says, is that the name is like 'the mountain of myrrh' (Song of Songs 4:6), since myrrh and spices were found there, or that it was named in praise of Israel; 'the land of Moriah' is the city, and the mountain alone is 'Mount Moriah'. Abraham knew the land but not the mountain, so God said He would show him one of the mountains there.

, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ ״אֶל הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר אַרְאֶךָּ״ (בראשית יב:א). וְכֵן זֶה לְהַגְדִּיל סִפּוּר אַהֲבַת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ לָאֵל; לֹא שָׁאַל וְלֹא נִסָּה, לָמָּה לֹא אָמַר, וְלָמָּה אָמַר לְהַעֲלוֹתוֹ בְּמָקוֹם רָחוֹק שְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים, וְלֹא אָמַר לוֹ לְהַעֲלוֹתוֹ מִיָּד שָׁם בִּמְקוֹמוֹ. וְזֶה הָיָה לִשְׁתֵּי סִבּוֹת, הָאֶחָד לְהַגְדִּיל אַהֲבַת אַבְרָהָם, כִּי אִלּוּ אָמַר לוֹ הָאֵל הַעֲלֵהוּ עַתָּה בִּמְקוֹמְךָ, הָיָה הַדָּבָר פִּתְאֹם וְנִבְהָל לַדָּבָר וְלֹא הִתְבּוֹנֵן בּוֹ וְעָשָׂה מִצְוַת הָאֵל פִּתְאֹם כְּמוֹ שֶׁצִּוָּהוּ, אֲבָל בְּהַאֲרִיכוֹ לוֹ זְמַן הַעֲלוֹתוֹ עַד שְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים וְהָיָה לוֹ שָׁעוֹת לְהִתְבּוֹנֵן בַּדָּבָר וְעִם כָּל זֶה מִהֵר לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹן הָאֵל, זֶה הָיָה דָּבָר גָּדוֹל. וְהַסִּבָּה הַשֵּׁנִית שֶׁהוֹרוּהוּ מְקוֹם הַנִּבְחָר שֶׁיִּבְנוּ בָּנָיו בַּיִת לַה׳ וּמִזְבֵּחַ לְהַעֲלוֹת עָלָיו עוֹלוֹת וּזְבָחִים וְלַחֲנֹךְ הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא בְּנֶפֶשׁ הַנִּבְחָר וְהָאָהוּב, כִּי אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא נִשְׁלַם הַדָּבָר וְלֹא נִשְׁחַט הֲרֵי הָיָה לְרָצוֹן לִפְנֵי הָאֵל כְּאִלּוּ נַעֲשָׂה, וְהִנֵּה הוּעֲלָה עַל הַמִּזְבֵּחַ נֶעֱקַד כַּשֶּׂה.

Onkelos renders the land of Moriah as 'the land of worship' and 'offer him up' as 'offer him up before me', with 'before me' not in the Hebrew. The English keeps the name and adds nothing.
Hebrew
וַאֲמַר דְּבַר כְּעַן יָת בְּרָךְ יָת יְחִידָךְ דִּי רְחַמְתָּ יָת יִצְחָק וְאִיזֵל לָךְ לְאַרְעָא פּוּלְחָנָא וְאַסְקֵיהּ קֳדָמַי תַּמָּן לַעֲלָתָא עַל חַד מִן טוּרַיָּא דִּי אֵימָר לָךְ:
Ancient Near East
  • Moriah: the name occurs here and in 2 Chronicles 3:1, where it is the mountain on which Solomon's house was built in Jerusalem. Rashi, Ramban and Radak identify the land with Jerusalem. The verse itself names no city, and the meaning of the name is disputed; ancient versions read it differently (the Septuagint has 'the high land').
  • An olah (a burnt offering) is an animal burnt whole on the altar, not eaten by the worshipper. The Hebrew word comes from the root 'go up' and is usually taken to refer to the offering going up in smoke.
  • Child sacrifice was practised in the ancient Near East, and the Bible prohibits it (Leviticus 18:21, 20:2–5; Deuteronomy 12:31, 18:10) and condemns it through the prophets (Jeremiah 7:31). The Bible also knows the rule that the firstborn belongs to God and is redeemed (Exodus 13:11–15). What this chapter is for is disputed: the commentators here take it as a test of Abraham's obedience and love (Ibn Ezra, Ramban, Radak); some modern readers take it as a story against child sacrifice, or as an account of the founding of a sanctuary. The text says only that God tested Abraham.
Apparatus
  • 22:2.5: WLC note c: the edition reads one or more accents differently from BHS. No effect on the English.
  • 22:2.22: the height of the mountain is not stated. Ibn Ezra says the place is not high; the English keeps 'mountains' (see commentary).
22:3

Abraham rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey, and took his two servants with him and Isaac his son. He split the wood for a burnt offering, got up, and went to the place that God had told him of.

and-he-rose-early Abraham in-the-morning and-he-bound-on [object] his-donkey and-he-took [object] two his-servants with-him and [object] Isaac his-son and-he-split [object] wood-of burnt-offering and-he-arose and-he-went to the-place which he-had-said to-him the-God

Grammar
  • A chain of wayyiqtols (וַיַּשְׁכֵּם, וַיַּחֲבֹשׁ, וַיִּקַּח, וַיְבַקַּע, וַיָּקָם, וַיֵּלֶךְ) gives the order of the acts; each takes 'and' or none, as the English sense needs.
  • The verb חָבַשׁ names the binding on of the donkey's gear. The Hebrew names no saddle; the English 'saddled' gives its sense.
  • עֲצֵי עֹלָה is a construct chain: 'the wood of a burnt offering'. The English adds 'for'.
  • The relative clause אֲשֶׁר אָמַר לוֹ הָאֱלֹהִים has a qatal verb: the speech came before the going, so the English has 'had said'.
  • The etnaḥta on בְּנוֹ divides the verse into two halves: the preparations, and the splitting and going. The silluq on הָאֱלֹהִים closes the verse.

The English keeps 'the place' without naming the mountain: the place is the one of 22:2, and the commentators differ on its name. 'Saddled' gives the sense of the verb חָבַשׁ, 'bind on', which names no saddle.

Ancient Near East
  • The donkey was the usual pack and riding animal of the period; the journey of three days (22:4) is made with a donkey carrying the wood and the gear.
22:4

On the third day, Abraham lifted his eyes and saw the place from afar.

in-the-day the-third and-he-lifted Abraham [object] his-eyes and-he-saw [object] the-place from-far

Grammar
  • בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי: the preposition ב with the article and the ordinal. The point from which the third day is counted is not stated (Ibn Ezra).
  • נָשָׂא אֶת־עֵינָיו is the idiom 'lift the eyes', for looking up; the English keeps 'lifted his eyes'.
  • The two wayyiqtols, וַיִּשָּׂא and וַיַּרְא, carry the narrative on, with Abraham as subject.
  • מֵרָחֹק closes the sentence: the seeing is at a distance, and the English places 'from afar' last, as the Hebrew does.

The English keeps 'the third day' open as to its reckoning point. Ibn Ezra's count from the departure is recorded in the commentary.

Rashinot-applicable בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁ֗י
Rashi: why was the place not seen at once? So that they would not say he was dazed and his mind was confused; had he had time to take counsel with himself, he would not have gone. A reason for the delay.

22:5

Abraham said to his servants, "Stay here with the donkey. The boy and I will go as far as there, and we will bow down and we will return to you."

Grammar
  • שְׁבוּ לָכֶם פֹּה: the imperative 'stay' with the dative; the English 'stay here'.
  • The verbs נֵלְכָה, וְנִשְׁתַּחֲוֶה, וְנָשׁוּבָה are first-person plural: 'we' are Abraham and the boy. The pack parses נֵלְכָה and נָשׁוּבָה as cohortatives and נִשְׁתַּחֲוֶה as a yiqtol.
  • The subject 'I and the boy' comes before its verb, and the English keeps that order.
  • The etnaḥta on כֹּה divides the verse: the staying and the going first, then the three verbs of Abraham's plan.

Abraham's words are the speech; the English keeps 'we will return' as a statement of plan. The commentators differ on what he meant by it (see commentary).

Commentary (6)
Rashirecords עַד כֹּ֑ה
Rashi: 'as far as there' (עַד כֹּה) means a short way, to the place before us. Another reading, playing on כֹּה: 'I will see where is that which the Place said to me, "So (כֹּה) shall your seed be"' (15:5). The English keeps the distance open.

Ibn Ezra asks how Abraham could say 'and we will return'. Others answer that he meant to bring back Isaac's remains, or that he put them off with words so that they would not turn back and Isaac would not perceive and flee. He rejects the Sages' age of thirty-seven for Isaac, takes him to be near thirteen and bound against his will, and gives as evidence that his father hid the secret; the English keeps the words and takes no side on the intention.

22:6

Abraham took the wood for the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son, and took in his hand the fire and the knife, and the two of them went together.

Grammar
  • A chain of wayyiqtols gives the order: he took the wood, laid it on Isaac, took the fire and the knife, and they went.
  • וַיָּשֶׂם has no expressed object in the Hebrew; the wood of the previous clause is understood, and the English 'it' only repeats it.
  • מַאֲכֶלֶת is a feminine noun from the root אכל; its etymology is Rashi's (see commentary).
  • וַיֵּלְכוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם יַחְדָּו: the dual 'two of them' and the adverb 'together'. The same words close 22:8.

The English 'laid it on Isaac his son' repeats the wood of the previous clause, which the verb carries over. 'The knife' is the sense the lexicon gives.

22:7

Isaac said to Abraham his father, and he said, "My father." And he said, "Here I am, my son." And he said, "Here are the fire and the wood, but where is the sheep for a burnt offering?"

and-he-said Isaac to-Abraham father-his and-he-said my-father and-he-said here-I my-son and-he-said here the-fire and-the-wood and-where the-sheep to-burnt-offering

Grammar
  • The dialogue turns on the address 'father' (אָבִי) and 'son' (בְנִי), both with the first-person suffix.
  • הִנֵּה הָאֵשׁ וְהָעֵצִים is a sentence with no verb; the English adds 'are'.
  • הַשֶּׂה has the article, 'the sheep' that the offering needs; לְעֹלָה has none. Isaac asks where the sheep is.
  • Each speech opens with wayyiqtol 'and he said'. The speaker changes between Isaac and Abraham.

The English keeps the repeated 'and he said' of the Hebrew, which marks each speech. Speakers are named from the context.

Commentary (2)
Radaknot-applicable הִנֶּ֣נִּֽי
Radak notes the form הִנֶּנִּי with the dagesh in the second nun. A remark on the form; the English 'Here I am' is unchanged.
Hebrew
בְּדָגֵשׁ עִם הַנּוּ״ן הַשְּׁנִיָּה.
Targum Onkelosrecords the whole verse
Onkelos reads 'lamb' (אִמְרָא) for the sheep (שֶׂה), an animal of the flock. The English keeps 'sheep', the Hebrew's word.
Hebrew
וַאֲמַר יִצְחָק לְאַבְרָהָם אֲבוּהִי וַאֲמַר אַבָּא וַאֲמַר הָא אֲנָא בְרִי וַאֲמַר הָא אֶשָּׁתָא וְאָעַיָּא וְאָן אִימְרָא לַעֲלָתָא:
Ancient Near East
  • The sheep (שֶׂה) is one of a flock. The word covers a sheep or a goat, and the text names neither the kind nor the age; Leviticus 1:10 allows a sheep or a goat as a burnt offering.
Apparatus
  • 22:7.16: שֶׂה is one of a flock, a sheep or a goat; Onkelos reads 'lamb'. The English keeps 'sheep'.
22:8

Abraham said, "God will see for himself the sheep for a burnt offering, my son." And the two of them went together.

and-he-said Abraham God will-see for-him the-sheep to-burnt-offering my-son and-they-went the-two-of-them together

Grammar
  • The subject אֱלֹהִים comes before the yiqtol יִרְאֶה, and לּוֹ is 'for himself'.
  • יִרְאֶה לּוֹ הַשֶּׂה: the verb of seeing takes 'the sheep' as its object. Its sense 'see for himself' is open between the readings in the commentary and the apparatus.
  • The vocative 'my son' comes last, after the words for the sheep; the English keeps the Hebrew order.
  • The last clause repeats 22:6 word for word.

The English 'God will see for himself' keeps the verb's sense and does not choose between providing the sheep and the sheep being Isaac. Both readings are recorded.

and-came to-the-place which said to-him the-God and-built there Abraham [object] the-altar and-arranged [object] the-wood and-bound [object] Isaac his-son and-laid [object] him on the-altar from-above to-the-wood

Grammar
  • The verse is a chain of wayyiqtols: they came (22:9.1), built (22:9.8), arranged (22:9.13), bound (22:9.16) and laid (22:9.20). Each takes ו and continues the one before.
  • אֲשֶׁר אָמַר לוֹ הָאֱלֹהִים is a relative clause: literally 'which God said to him', in English 'that God had told him of'. The verb is a qatal, so it is earlier than the coming (the saying is in 22:2).
  • The object marker אֶת comes before each definite object (הַמִּזְבֵּחַ, הָעֵצִים, יִצְחָק) and has no English counterpart. אֹתוֹ (22:9.21) is the object marker with a suffix, the object being Isaac.
  • מִמַּעַל לָעֵצִים (22:9.24–25): an adverb of place with the preposition ל and the noun, 'on top of the wood'.
  • Accents: the etnaḥta on הָעֵצִים (22:9.15) divides the verse, and the silluq on לָעֵצִים (22:9.25) ends it.

The English is the plain reading of the chain. The place is not named in the verse.

Commentary (8)
Rashirecords וַֽיַּעֲקֹד֙
Rashi: his hands and feet were bound behind him. Binding hands and feet together is called עֲקִידָה (Shabbat 54), and the word is of the same family as עֲקֻדִּים (the striped goats of Jacob's flock, 30:35), whose ankles were white, so that the place where they are bound is recognizable. The English keeps the ordinary 'bound'.
Hebrew
יָדָיו וְרַגְלָיו מֵאֲחוֹרָיו; הַיָּדַיִם וְרַגְלַיִם בְּיַחַד הִיא עֲקִידָה (שבת נ"ד), וְהוּא לְשׁוֹן עֲקֻדִּים, שֶׁהָיוּ קַרְסוּלֵיהֶם לְבָנִים, מָקוֹם שֶׁעוֹקְדִין אוֹתָן בּוֹ הָיָה נִכָּר:
Rambannot-applicable וַיָּבֹ֗אוּ אֶֽל הַמָּקוֹם֮ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אָֽמַר ל֣וֹ הָאֱלֹהִים֒
Ramban identifies the place as Mount Moriah. The verse does not name it, so the English says only 'the place'.
Hebrew
עַתָּה, הוּא הַר הַמּוֹרִיָּה, שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ "הִנֵּה זֶה הָהָר אֲשֶׁר אָמַרְתִּי לְךָ":
Radaknot-applicable וַיָּבֹ֗אוּ אֶֽל הַמָּקוֹם֮
Radak also identifies the place as the mountain of Moriah (הַר הַמֹּרִיָּה). The English does not name it.

הוּא הַר הַמֹּרִיָּה.

Radak: when they came together God spoke to Abraham and showed him the place in a prophetic vision (מַרְאֵה הַנְּבוּאָה). In the midrash (Bereshit Rabbah 56:2) Abraham saw a cloud tied over it or a pillar of fire, and on that view the 'saying' is this showing (radak:22:9:3). The English keeps 'told' and does not say how it was told.
Hebrew
וּבְבוֹאָם יַחְדָּיו אָמַר לוֹ וְהֶרְאָהוּ בְּמַרְאֵה הַנְּבוּאָה. וּבַדְּרָשׁ (בראשית רבה נו:ב) שֶׁרָאָה עָנָן קָשׁוּר עָלָיו אוֹ עַמּוּד אֵשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְנוּ לְמַעְלָה. וּלְדַעַת הַדְּרָשׁ יִהְיֶה פֵּרוּשׁ
Radak אֲשֶׁ֣ר אָֽמַר ל֣וֹ
Hebrew
, כְּשֶׁהֶרְאָה לוֹ אֶת הֶעָנָן אוֹ הָעַמּוּד זֶהוּ הָאֲמִירָה.
Radakfollows וַֽיַּעֲרֹ֖ךְ אֶת הָעֵצִ֑ים
Radak says the wood was arranged so that it could be lit. The English gives 'arranged the wood' and leaves the purpose to the context.

עֲרָכָם עַל הָאֵשׁ לְהַדְלִיקָם.
Radaknot-applicable וַֽיַּעֲקֹד֙ אֶת יִצְחָ֣ק
Radak: he bound Isaac's hands and feet so that he would not kick (יִבְעָט). Although Isaac was willing and was bound by his own will, he feared that the angry spirit would overcome him, and he told his father to bind him well. The verse does not state this, and the English does not add it.

עֲקָדוֹ בְּיָדוֹ וּבְרַגְלָיו כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יִבְעָט, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁבִּרְצוֹנוֹ הָיָה וּבִרְצוֹנוֹ נֶעֱקַד, פָּחַד שֶׁלֹּא תִגְבַּר עָלָיו הָרוּחַ הַכּוֹעֶסֶת, וְאָמַר לְאָבִיו שֶׁיַּעַקְדֶנּוּ יָפֶה.

Hebrew
וְאָתוּ לְאַתְרָא דִּי אֲמַר לֵיהּ יְיָ וּבְנָא תַמָּן אַבְרָהָם יָת מַדְבְּחָא וְסַדַּר יָת אָעַיָּא וַעֲקַד יָת יִצְחָק בְּרֵיהּ וְשַׁוִּי יָתֵיהּ עַל מַדְבְּחָא עֵיל מִן אָעַיָּא:
22:10

Abraham stretched out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son.

and-stretched-out Abraham [object] his-hand and-took [object] the-knife to-slaughter [object] his-son

Grammar
  • The clauses are joined by wayyiqtols: he stretched out (22:10.1) and took (22:10.5). The infinitive לִשְׁחֹט (22:10.8) gives the purpose of taking the knife.
  • לִשְׁחֹט is an infinitive construct with the preposition ל. The object is בְּנוֹ, marked with אֶת.
  • יָדוֹ is the noun יָד with the third person masculine singular suffix: 'his hand'.
  • Accents: the zaqef qaton on יָדוֹ (22:10.4) and the etnaḥta on הַמַּאֲכֶלֶת (22:10.7) divide the verse; the silluq on בְּנוֹ (22:10.10) ends it.
Commentary (2)
Radaknot-applicable לִשְׁחֹ֖ט אֶת בְּנֽוֹ׃
Radak says Isaac was to be slaughtered first on the altar and the fire would then consume him, in the manner of a sacrifice. The verse does not state this, and the English does not add it.
Hebrew
לְשָׁחֳטוֹ תְּחִלָּה עַל הַמִּזְבֵּחַ וְאַחַר כֵּן תֹּאכְלֵהוּ הָאֵשׁ כְּדֶרֶךְ הַזֶּבַח.
Targum Onkelos the whole verse
Hebrew
וְאוֹשֵׁיט אַבְרָהָם יָת יְדֵיהּ וּנְסֵיב יָת סַכִּינָא לְמֵיכַס יָת בְּרֵיהּ:
22:11

The angel of the LORD called to him from the heavens and said, "Abraham, Abraham." He said, "Here I am."

and-called to-him angel-of the-LORD from the-heavens and-said Abraham Abraham and-said here-I

Grammar
  • קָרָא with אֵלָיו is 'call to him' (22:11.1–2). The call comes from the heavens, the source marked by מִן (22:11.5–6).
  • The name is repeated in the vocative, אַבְרָהָם אַבְרָהָם (22:11.8–9). The repetition is discussed in the commentary.
  • Each speech is introduced by a wayyiqtol of אָמַר (22:11.7, 22:11.10).
  • Accents: the tipḥa on וַיֹּאמֶר (22:11.7) and the etnaḥta on the second אַבְרָהָם (22:11.9) divide the verse; the silluq on הִנֵּנִי (22:11.11) ends it.

Rashirecords אַבְרָהָ֣ם אַבְרָהָ֑ם

Hebrew
לְשׁוֹן חִבָּה הוּא, שֶׁכּוֹפֵל אֶת שְׁמוֹ:

Ibn Ezra: פעמים כמו בחפזון, 'twice, as in haste' (or 'sometimes, as in haste'): the name is doubled as a call made in haste. The English keeps the doubled name and gives no reason for it (Rashi: affection; Radak: so that Abraham would hear quickly and not slaughter).

וּקְרָא לֵיהּ מַלְאָכָא דַיְיָ מִן שְׁמַיָּא וַאֲמַר אַבְרָהָם אַבְרָהָם וַאֲמַר הָא אֲנָא:
22:12

He said, "Do not stretch out your hand against the boy or do anything to him, for now I know that you fear God, and you have not withheld your son, your only one, from me."

and-said not stretch-out your-hand to the-boy and-not do to-him anything for now I-have-known that fearing God you and-not withheld [object] your-son [object] your-only-one from-me

Grammar
  • The prohibitions use אַל with the jussive: תִּשְׁלַח (do not stretch out) and תַּעַשׂ (do not do). The second is joined by וְאַל, so 'or do not' carries the same prohibition on.
  • כִּי עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי: the first כִּי gives the reason, 'for now I know'. The second כִּי introduces what is known, 'that you fear God'.
  • יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים is an adjective with its object: 'fearing God'. The English 'fear God' keeps the verb's sense.
  • The qatal חָשַׂכְתָּ (22:12.19) is negated with לֹא: 'you have not withheld'. The English uses the same tense.
  • Accents: the etnaḥta on מְאוּמָה (22:12.10) divides the speech at the end of the prohibition; the silluq on מִמֶּנִּי (22:12.24) ends the verse.

Rashirecords אַל תִּשְׁלַ֤ח
Rashi glosses 'do not stretch out' as 'do not slaughter', and the rest of his comment is a dialogue in which Abraham offers only to wound the boy. The English keeps 'stretch out' and lets the context of the speech give its sense.

22:13

Abraham lifted his eyes and saw, and here was a ram that had been caught in the thicket by its horns. Abraham went and took the ram and offered it up as a burnt offering instead of his son.

and-lifted Abraham [object] his-eyes and-saw and-here ram after caught in-the-thicket by-his-horns and-went Abraham and-took [object] the-ram and-caused-to-ascend-him for-burnt-offering instead-of his-son

Grammar
  • A run of wayyiqtols carries the narrative: lifted (22:13.1), saw (22:13.5), went (22:13.12), took (22:13.14), offered (22:13.17).
  • נֶאֱחַז is a niphal qatal, third person masculine singular, 'was caught'. With אַחַר read as 'after' it gives 'after (it) was caught' (Ibn Ezra, Radak: אחר שנאחז). Ibn Ezra adds that if the form is pointed as a participle (נֶאֱחָז, with qamats) the verb 'was' is understood: אחר היותו נאחז, 'after its being caught'. The English 'after being caught' renders this.
  • Some join אַחַר to the preceding clause: 'Abraham lifted his eyes after these things' (the Targum and Rashi). Ibn Ezra rejects this: the text would then have said אַחֲרֵי, אַחַר כֵּן or אַחֲרֵי זֹאת. The zaqef gadol on אַחַר sets it apart from נֶאֱחַז; אַחַר can also be 'behind' (BDB 2.a). The English follows Ibn Ezra.
  • וַיַּעֲלֵהוּ is the hiphil wayyiqtol of עָלָה with the object suffix -הוּ. The offering, 'as a burnt offering', is לְעֹלָה.
  • תַּחַת בְּנוֹ, 'instead of his son', is the preposition with the suffix; it closes the chain.
  • Accents: the zaqef gadol on אַחַר (22:13.8) and the etnaḥta on בְּקַרְנָיו (22:13.11) divide the verse; the silluq on בְּנוֹ (22:13.20) ends it.

Ancient Near East
  • An עֹלָה (burnt offering) is an animal offered whole and burnt on the altar. The word is from the root עלה, 'go up'.
Apparatus
  • אַחַר: 'after' (Ibn Ezra, Radak), or, joined to the preceding clause, 'after these things' (Rashi, Onkelos). On the lexicon it can also be 'behind' (BDB אַחַר 2.a), 'a ram behind (him), caught'; the zaqef gadol after אַחַר sets it apart from נֶאֱחַז. Ibn Ezra takes 'after'.
  • נֶאֱחַז: the text has patah, a niphal qatal ('was caught'); Ibn Ezra also allows the participle נֶאֱחָז (qamats), with 'was' (היה) understood.
22:14

Abraham named that place Adonai-yireh, as it is said today, "On the mountain of the LORD it will be seen."

and-called Abraham name-of the-place that Adonai-yireh as is-said today on-the-mountain of-the-LORD it-will-be-seen

Grammar
  • The verb is the qal wayyiqtol of קָרָא in the sense 'name' (Qal 6), with שֵׁם: 'named the place'. The name is given as read, Adonai-yireh, in the English.
  • יְהוָה יִרְאֶה is a sentence-name, 'the LORD will see' (qal yiqtol). The saying in the second half uses the niphal, יֵרָאֶה, 'it will be seen' (or 'he will appear', Niph 1): the verb is the same, the stem changes. The name also echoes 22:8, אֱלֹהִים יִרְאֶה־לּוֹ הַשֶּׂה, 'God will see for himself the sheep'.
  • אֲשֶׁר יֵאָמֵר הַיּוֹם: the niphal yiqtol of אָמַר with the relative, 'as it is said today'. The saying in double quotes is its content.
  • Accents: the tipḥa on הַהוּא (22:14.5) and the etnaḥta on יִרְאֶה (22:14.7) divide the verse; the silluq on יֵרָאֶה (22:14.13) ends it.

The second יְהֹוָה in the saying is the LORD, written as in the text.

  • Naming a place after an event is a regular feature of the patriarchal stories (for example Bethel, 28:19; Beersheba, 21:31): the name carries the story.

Grammar
  • בִּי נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי is the oath formula: 'by myself I have sworn'. Radak compares it with 'as I live'.
  • נְאֻם יְהוָה is the formula 'declares the LORD', set inside the speech. The English keeps it inside the quotation.
  • כִּי יַעַן אֲשֶׁר gives the cause of the oath: 'because you have done this thing'. The relative clause and the verb עָשִׂיתָ are one unit; וְלֹא חָשַׂכְתָּ names the same deed from the other side.
  • Accents: the zaqef gadol on וַיֹּאמֶר (22:16.1) and the tipḥa on נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי (22:16.3) mark pauses in the oath formula; the etnaḥta on יְהוָה (22:16.5) ends the oath and 'declares the LORD', the main division of the verse; the revia on כִּי (22:16.6) and the yetiv on יַעַן (22:16.7) set off the reason; the silluq on יְחִידֶךָ (22:16.18) ends the verse.
  • The speech does not end here. The main clause of 'because you have done this' is in 22:17 (כִּי בָרֵךְ אֲבָרֶכְךָ), so the quotation is left open at the end of this verse.

Ancient Near East
  • A person swears by a higher power called as witness (Abraham makes his servant swear 'by the LORD', 24:3); the LORD, with none higher, swears by himself (here; also Exod 32:13, Isa 45:23, Jer 22:5).

22:17

I will surely bless you, and I will surely multiply your offspring like the stars of the sky and like the sand which is on the shore of the sea, and your offspring will possess the cities of his enemies,

that blessing I-will-bless-you and-multiplying I-will-multiply [object] your-offspring like-stars-of the-sky and-like-the-sand which upon edge-of the-sea and-will-possess your-offspring [object] gate-of his-enemies

Grammar
  • כִּי בָרֵךְ אֲבָרֶכְךָ: the infinitive absolute before the finite verb of the same root gives emphasis, 'I will surely bless you'. The same construction returns in וְהַרְבָּה אַרְבֶּה.
  • The clause is the content of the oath sworn in 22:16 (נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי): 'that I will surely bless you' is what God swears.
  • Two similes are joined by ו: כְּכוֹכְבֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם and וְכַחוֹל אֲשֶׁר עַל־שְׂפַת הַיָּם. The etnaḥta on הַיָּם divides the verse: the promise of number first, then the promise of land.
  • וְיִרַשׁ זַרְעֲךָ: the yiqtol has future sense; the subject 'your offspring' follows the verb. The object is 'the gate' (שַׁעַר) with the marker אֵת.
  • אֹיְבָיו: the suffix 'his' refers to זֶרַע, which is singular, so the enemies are those of the offspring, not of Abraham.

The English gives 'the cities of his enemies' because Ibn Ezra, the normative commentator, reads 'gate' as the walled town. The literal line keeps 'gate'. Radak's reading, the land of the enemies, is recorded in the commentary.

Ancient Near East
  • A city gate was the place of a town's defence and of its public business, so the gate could stand for the town and its authority. 'The gate of his enemies' names their towns by a part for the whole; the commentators differ on the extent (see the commentary).

22:18

and all the nations of the earth will bless themselves by your offspring, in return for your having obeyed my voice."

Grammar
  • וְהִתְבָּרְכוּ is a weqatal that carries on the promise of 22:17, so it is future in sense: 'will bless themselves'.
  • The hitpael of בָּרַךְ is reflexive. The English keeps it; the passive reading ('be blessed') of Onkelos is recorded in the commentary.
  • עֵקֶב אֲשֶׁר: 'in return for that'. The perfect שָׁמַעְתָּ is rendered 'your having obeyed', so that the English stays a noun phrase after 'in return for'.
  • This verse ends the angel's speech, which began in 22:16. The closing quotation mark is here.

The English follows Ibn Ezra's reading of עֵקֶב as reward ('in return for'). Radak and Sforno agree on the word; they differ on how the nations come to bless themselves, and that is recorded.

Abraham returned to his servants. They rose and went together to Beersheba, and Abraham lived in Beersheba.

Grammar
  • Four wayyiqtol verbs run in sequence (וַיָּשָׁב, וַיָּקֻמוּ, וַיֵּלְכוּ, וַיֵּשֶׁב): the narrative past of the English.
  • The two plural verbs (וַיָּקֻמוּ וַיֵּלְכוּ) have no stated subject. They follow the singular וַיָּשָׁב אַבְרָהָם, so the company is Abraham and his young men; Radak and Ibn Ezra include Isaac, who is in Abraham's keeping. יַחְדָּו, 'together', marks one company.
  • Isaac is not named in this verse. The English adds nothing; see the commentary on Ibn Ezra's reading.
  • A petuḥah (פ) follows this verse in the Masoretic text: a section ends here.

The English names only Abraham and his young men. Ibn Ezra's comment on the silence about Isaac is recorded in the commentary, not in the English.

The English keeps 'lived', as the verb means; Rashi's chronology is not in the English.

22:21

Uz his firstborn, and Buz his brother, and Kemuel the father of Aram.

[object] Uz his-firstborn and-[object] Buz his-brother and-[object] Kemuel father-of Aram

Grammar
  • The verse has no verb. Each name follows the object marker אֵת, and the names are the sons of Nahor, the list continuing the sentence of 22:20.
  • בְּכוֹר is 'firstborn': Uz is the eldest of Nahor's sons, and the 'his' refers to Nahor.
  • The English keeps the apposition 'the father of Aram' as the Hebrew has it, with Aram the grandson.

The lexicon glosses Kemuel as 'son of Nahor' and Aram as 'grandson of Nahor'. The Hebrew says only 'Kemuel the father of Aram'; Aram as Kemuel's son follows from the lexicon. Radak's suggestion that 'father of Aram' names a notable man is recorded; Ramban's suggestion of another Kemuel is recorded at 22:23.

Radak says Kesed is the ancestor of the nation called Kasdim (Chaldeans), as he wrote earlier. A link to a later people; the English keeps the name and adds nothing.

וּמִמֶּנּוּ יָצָא הַגּוֹי הַנִּקְרָא כַּשְׂדִּים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְנוּ (בראשית יא:כח).

וְיָת כֶּשֶׂד וְיָת חֲזוֹ וְיָת פִּלְדָּשׁ וְיָת יִדְלָף וְיָת בְּתוּאֵל:
Ancient Near East
  • The Chaldeans (Kasdim) are named in 11:28 as the people of Ur. Radak's link between Kesed and them is the commentator's claim, not stated in the text.
22:23

And Bethuel fathered Rebekah; these eight Milcah bore to Nahor, Abraham's brother.

and-Bethuel fathered [object] Rebekah eight these bore Milcah to-Nahor brother-of Abraham

Grammar
  • The verse sums up the family: 'these eight' are the sons of Milcah listed in 22:21–22.
  • Bethuel fathers Rebekah, the subject of the next part of the story; the verse does not give further children of Bethuel.
  • The construct 'brother of Abraham' identifies Nahor by his relation to Abraham.

The English moves the number after the demonstrative: Hebrew 'eight these' is 'these eight'.

Commentary (5)
Rashinot-applicable וּבְתוּאֵ֖ל יָלַ֣ד אֶת רִבְקָ֑ה
Rashi: all these lists of descent are written only for this verse, which names Rebekah. A reason for the genealogy, not a reading of its words.
Hebrew
כָּל הַיִּחוּסִין הַלָּלוּ לֹא נִכְתְּבוּ אֶלָּא בִּשְׁבִיל פָּסוּק זֶה:
Rambanrecords וּבְתוּאֵ֖ל יָלַ֣ד אֶת רִבְקָ֑ה
Ramban: the verse does not name Laban, though he may be older than Rebekah, because the subject is Rebekah. He reads 'father of Aram' as identifying Kemuel, and suggests that another Kemuel may have lived in that generation. The English gives the names as the Hebrew does.
Hebrew
לֹא הִזְכִּיר הַכָּתוּב לָבָן וְאִם הוּא גָּדוֹל מֵרִבְקָה, כִּי לֹא בָּא לְהַזְכִּיר רַק הַשְּׁמוֹנָה שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִלְכָּה לְנָחוֹר. אֲבָל הִזְכִּיר רִבְקָה כִּי לְהוֹדִיעַ יִחוּסָהּ בָּאָה הַפָּרָשָׁה. וְטַעַם "אֲבִי אֲרָם" לֹא הִזְכִּיר אֲרָם רַק לְהוֹדִיעַ וּלְהַכִּיר קְמוּאֵל, כִּי אֲרָם הָיָה נִכְבָּד מֵאָבִיו, וְאוּלַי קְמוּאֵל אַחֵר הָיָה בְּדוֹרָם, וְזֶה אֲבִי אֲרָם:
Radaknot-applicable וּבְתוּאֵ֖ל יָלַ֣ד אֶת רִבְקָ֑ה
Radak: the text does not mention Laban because the story is about Rebekah.

Sfornonot-applicable וּבְתוּאֵ֖ל יָלַ֣ד אֶת רִבְקָ֑ה
Sforno: the report is that Bethuel, of the principal wife's sons, fathered Rebekah, so that a wife would be found in his father's house. A reason for the news, not a reading of the words.

22:24 · פ

And his concubine, whose name was Reumah, she too bore Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah.

and-his-concubine and-her-name Reumah and-bore also she [object] Tebah and-[object] Gaham and-[object] Tahash and-[object] Maacah

Grammar
  • The concubine is the subject of 'bore' (וַתֵּלֶד). Her name comes first, as a parenthesis, before the verb.
  • גַּם הִוא: 'she too' resumes the subject with emphasis. Radak reads גַּם as standing for 'to him too', after the suffix in וּפִילַגְשׁוֹ.
  • The four names follow the object marker: the sons are named, not counted.
  • With the eight sons of Milcah (22:23) these make twelve sons of Nahor.

The Hebrew pilegesh is a secondary wife, of lower standing than the principal wife; the English keeps the term as 'concubine'. Her sons are counted in the family here.

Commentary (5)
Rambannot-applicable וּפִֽילַגְשׁ֖וֹ וּשְׁמָ֣הּ רְאוּמָ֑ה
Ramban: the verse records all the good news brought to Abraham about his brother's sons, and the whole of Nahor's line is fit to cling to Abraham's seed. A reason for the list, not a reading of the words.
Hebrew
יְסַפֵּר הַכָּתוּב כָּל הַבְּשׂוֹרָה שֶׁבִּשְּׂרוּ אֶת אַבְרָהָם בִּבְנֵי אָחִיו. וְיִתָּכֵן שֶׁנִּכְתַּב זֶה לְהוֹדִיעַ כָּל יִחוּס נָחוֹר, כִּי כֻּלָּם רְאוּיִים לְהִדָּבֵק בְּזַרְעוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם, וְעַל כֻּלָּם אָמַר "אִם לֹא אֶל בֵּית אָבִי תֵּלֵךְ וְאֶל מִשְׁפַּחְתִּי" (בראשית כ"ד:ל"ח):
Radakfollows וּפִֽילַגְשׁ֖וֹ וַתֵּ֤לֶד גַּם הִוא֙
Radak explains 'she bore to him, also she': after 'and his concubine' with ו, the pronoun 'also' stands as if it said 'to him'. The English follows: 'she too bore'.

פֵּרַשׁ ״וַתֵּלֶד לוֹ גַּם־הִיא״, וְאַחַר שֶׁאָמַר וּפִילַגְשׁוֹ בְּוָי״ו הַכִּנּוּי וְאָמַר גַּם כְּאִלּוּ אָמַר לוֹ.
